articles.title: Cultural Representations of Memory in Contemporary Greek Audiovisual Culture: The Synthetic Revival of the Kaisariani Photographs as a Case Study
articles.authors: Nikolaos Aletras
articles.abstract: This article examines how the memory of the past is represented today within Greek audiovisual culture, taking as its case study the algorithmic colouring and animation of a set of rare photographs documenting the execution of two hundred Greek resistance fighters at the Kaisariani rifle range on 1 May 1944. The photographs, taken from the perspective of the perpetrators, were acquired by the Greek state, designated as a cultural monument, and shortly afterwards processed by users through generative artificial intelligence tools and disseminated across YouTube, TikTok, and the online press. Drawing on cultural memory theory, on recent scholarship concerning synthetic pasts, and on empirical evidence regarding the mnemonic effects of AI generated video, the study argues that the AI revival of archival photographs constitutes a new representational practice rather than a technical enhancement. Through a threefold methodology of structural image analysis, platform based performance analysis, and digital reception ethnography, the article demonstrates that the same source archive gives rise to divergent representations conditioned by the affordances of each platform, and that these synthetic representations exert measurable mnemonic and ideological effects on their audiences. The Kaisariani case thereby provides both an empirical demonstration and a methodological template for a wider research programme situated at the intersection of cinema, documentary, digital archives, and generative artificial intelligence.

articles.title: How does the level of media propaganda literacy differ among individuals under 18, between 18 and 30, and over 30 in Uzbekistan, and how does this difference impact their vulnerability to misinformation and critical thinking skills?
articles.authors: Jamshidbek Rasulov
articles.abstract:
This research investigates how varying levels of media propaganda literacy across
different age groups in Uzbekistan impact susceptibility to misinformation and critical
thinking. By categorizing participants into three distinct age groups—those under 18,
between 18 and 30, and over 30—the study identifies generational differences shaped by
historical and technological contexts. Data collected through surveys and interviews reveal
that while younger generations rely more on social media and demonstrate greater
adaptability to digital information, older individuals remain dependent on traditional media
like television, often lacking critical fact-checking skills. Despite a high level of self-reported
understanding of concepts like "propaganda," significant knowledge gaps persist, particularly
among older participants, highlighting the enduring impact of Soviet-era media practices. The
findings underscore the need for targeted media literacy initiatives tailored to age-specific
vulnerabilities to bridge generational divides and empower all citizens to evaluate
information critically

articles.title: An Integrated Multi-Method Approach to Television Studies in the Streaming Era: the Production, Representation, and Reception of Gender Violence on Norwegian Screens
articles.authors: Maud Ceuterick
articles.abstract: By merging textual analysis with production interviews and audience studies, this article aims to develop a multi-method approach to television texts. The method proves particularly useful to investigate audiences’ interpretation of gender violence on screen and how this is integrated within a Public Service Broadcaster’s societal mission and national audiences’ perception of the broadcaster. The article focuses on the most popular Norwegian TV series to date Exit (2019-2023) distributed by the national NRK, as a product of enlightening entertainment. It questions how aesthetic choices create realism and how different audiences relate to the reality presented as authentic and relatable. It also interrogates how audiences’ perception of the national broadcaster affect their interpretation of the series.

articles.title: Assessment of facilitators and barriers to open science implementation in the Brain-Heart Interconnectome Research Program: a qualitative study
articles.authors: Edward Xu; Marc Antonino Albert; Gustavo de Paula Dídimo; Anna Catharina Vieira Armond; David Moher; Emilio I. Alarcón; Ian D Graham; Krystina B. Lewis; Alexandra King; Malcolm King
articles.abstract: Open science improves research transparency, reproducibility, and equity. This qualitative study assessed facilitators and barriers to implementing open science practices within the Brain-Heart Interconnectome (BHI), an interdisciplinary research program funded by the Canada First Research Excellence Fund (CFREF) to advance prevention and treatment of brain-heart conditions (e.g., stroke and cardiac disease). The study aimed to explore perceptions and behaviours of BHI-funded investigators and teams regarding open science mandate implementation. Data were collected through virtual focus groups with 36 participants from 17 funded projects. Participants include principal investigators, research staff, trainees, and Indigenous Elders and Knowledge Holders. Focus groups were designed and analyzed using the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF). Barriers included limited financial and logistical resources, intellectual property and ethical concerns, and a lack of guidance and training. Facilitators included mandates from journals and funders, along with perceived improvements in research accountability and quality. Findings were mapped onto the Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW) using the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation – Behaviour (COM-B) model, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding behaviour change and informed implementation strategy development. These insights will be critical to effective and efficient open science uptake within BHI and are likely transferable to other biomedical and interdisciplinary research programs.

articles_hidden.title: Structured-data reporting shapes the apparent causes of phase-3 trial failure: an automated decomposition of ClinicalTrials.gov records
articles_hidden.authors: Tommy Carstensen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective. To decompose the causes of phase-3 failure from ClinicalTrials.gov automatically, to identify where the registry misleads, and to compare the result with the manual study of Hwang et al. (2016).

Methods. Cross-sectional study of registry records: every phase-3 registration with posted results or with status terminated, withdrawn or suspended (18,466 in all). A failure is a trial that stopped early for a reason other than benefit, or that completed and missed its primary endpoint. The primary analysis covers trials that enrolled and started in 2017-2026; registrations withdrawn before enrollment enter a sensitivity analysis only. Primary-endpoint success was read from the structured statistical-analysis records. Termination reasons were classified by large-language-model agents, and a sample of first-pass labels was adjudicated blind by a stronger model. A stratum of 17 large pharmaceutical companies ("big pharma") is compared with Hwang et al., who classified failed drug programs of 1998-2008.

Results. Among trials that enrolled, efficacy (37.1%, 95% CI 34.9 to 39.5) and operational causes (36.5%, 34.3 to 38.8) were the two largest causes of failure. Counting withdrawn registrations as failures put operational causes first (operational 40.2%, efficacy 27.2%). Only 47.3% of completed trials with posted results carried a usable primary p-value; imputing misses for the others that had a comparator arm raised the efficacy share to 46.8% and lowered the operational share to 30.9%. In big pharma, efficacy accounted for 53.7% of failures (program-clustered 95% CI 47.6 to 59.6), not distinguishable from the 56.7% of Hwang et al. (clustered p = 0.46; 95% CI of the difference -11.0 to 5.0 points). The share was 48.3% among trials of drugs with no earlier phase-3 win (difference -17.1 to 0.2 points, unclustered p = 0.057), and 45.8%, lower than theirs, with withdrawn registrations counted (clustered p = 0.0052). Safety accounted for 3.1% of big-pharma failures (2.5% for all sponsors) against 17.2% in Hwang et al. First-pass labels agreed with the adjudication for 83.3% of a balanced sample (95% CI 77.0 to 88.2).

Conclusions. A registry-only decomposition of phase-3 failure depends on whether registrations that never enrolled count as failures and on how completed trials without a usable primary p-value are treated. With the former set aside, efficacy is the leading cause of failure in big pharma; its observed share is not distinguishable from the 2016 manual estimate, a comparison by proxy that does not establish agreement. For all sponsors efficacy is only slightly ahead of operational causes as observed, and further ahead under an imputation or a stricter win rule, each resting on assumptions. Safety is recorded far less often than in the manual estimate; the registry fields cannot show how many safety-driven stops are registered as sponsor or business decisions. The validation was model-based and covered the first classification pass only.

articles_hidden.title: An evaluation of the quality of published papers from researchers affiliated with the Australian Institute of Sport
articles_hidden.authors: Adrian Barnett; Alexander Gibson; Ran Tian; David N Borg; Paolo Menaspà
articles_hidden.abstract: The Australian Institute of Sport (AIS) has a central role in high-performance sport in Australia. An important part of this role is to support research in a range of sports disciplines. Sports science research has had many reproducibility issues; therefore, it is important to consider whether the research supported by the AIS is of high quality. To examine this, we conducted a retrospective audit of published papers to estimate the prevalences of good research practice and identify areas for improvement. We extracted information from papers using automated text extraction and research assistants. We identified 280 papers published between 2020 and 2024 with at least one author who was affiliated with the Australian Institute of Sport. The results showed a low engagement with robust study planning, including pre-registration, analysis plans, and sample size calculations. More encouraging results were that almost all papers had research questions that were well justified and answered. Overall, we found many areas where research quality could be improved by better adherence to established good research practices.

articles_hidden.title: Can grant evaluation still distinguish scientific excellence?
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Bulla; James Wilsdon; Peter Mikula
articles_hidden.abstract: Grant peer review increasingly depends on fine-grained numerical scores to rank many formally excellent proposals. In the era of generative and agentic AI, this architecture may be losing resolution. We analyse score-distribution data from EU Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) Postdoctoral Fellowships and show sharp compression of evaluation scores in the 2025 call. Compared to 2024, there was a 64.6% increase in the volume of applications received, low-scoring proposals became rare, and ~20% of proposals received evaluation scores of ≥95%. The timing is consistent with AI-assisted optimization, but alternative structural explanations remain possible. Nonetheless, the score compression exposes a structural vulnerability of highly standardized evaluation systems: evaluation precision near the top of the scale may be more apparent than real. We thus propose three testable predictions for cross-funder comparison: compression should be strongest in schemes with explicit scoring rubrics, become more visible after broad diffusion of advanced AI drafting and reasoning tools, and intensify as these tools gain capabilities. Data from Human Frontier Science Program (HFSP) Postdoctoral Fellowships and Research Grants, which first screen short Letters of Intent before inviting selected applicants to submit Full Proposals, show broadly similar score distributions across years, with no comparable compression. Systematic cross-funder score tracking is therefore needed to distinguish scheme-specific disruptions from broader temporal shifts and identify designs that preserve evaluative resolution. If compression is becoming more widespread, funders should reconsider whether fine-grained ranking remains an efficient and fair way to select among many excellent proposals.

articles.title: Biased Motive Inferences of Online Outrage Undermine Cross-Partisan Conversations
articles.authors: Chen-Wei Yu; William J. Brady
articles.abstract: Moral outrage spreads widely in online political discourse, but how do people understand others’ outrage expressions? Across three studies (N = 1,855), including behavioral experiments and a field study, we discovered that partisan-biased motive inferences underlie the divergent effects of online outrage expression: While people typically inferred that their in-partisans’ motives for expressing outrage were to raise awareness or inspire action, they tended to infer their political opponents’ motives were to shame or troll. These motive inferences were linked to greater political sectarianism and lower willingness to have a conversation about politics with the outrage expressor. In a fourth study (N = 720), we developed an intervention that changed people’s motive inferences, which improved willingness to have a conversation about politics. These findings highlight the role of motive inferences in shaping contemporary online political discourse filled with strong emotions, and suggest key levers to foster civil interactions among cross-partisans.

articles.title: “Puzzling, Yet So Refreshing”: Experiencing the Value of Neurodiversity Within an Inclusive Choir
articles.authors: Nicolas Petit; Géraldine Dessertenne; Fanny Aprile; Lucie Jurek
articles.abstract: The social challenges encountered by autistic people are increasingly understood as a double empathy problem: a mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic individuals, rather than an autistic deficit. It is thus critical to cultivate inclusive spaces that foster mutual understanding, where autistic people can fit in while allowing the general population to experience high-quality neurodiverse contacts. Choral singing offers a promising medium to do so and to facilitate cross-neurotype dynamics, as it is thought to have evolved as a biological mechanism to foster social bonding. Accordingly, this qualitative study explored how 12 general population adult choristers experienced a 6-month neurodiverse choir shared with 8 autistic adolescents and 3 autism specialists. We used a two-stage qualitative design, first capturing individual experiences through a thematic analysis of an open-ended online questionnaire, and subsequently deepening our results through a discussion with a community stakeholder panel. The findings revealed an intrinsically demanding experience, especially emotionally and cognitively, counterbalanced by important benefits, as it was also described as joyful and powerful, encouraging personal growth among the choristers and a shift in their perceptions of autism. These findings support the neurodiversity paradigm and suggest that choral singing may support double empathy experiences, facilitating intergroup contact in the social majority, to reduce prejudice and thereby remove social barriers to the inclusion of autistic voices.

articles.title: Impacts of voice pleasantness and familiarity on enjoyment and engagement with spoken narratives
articles.authors: Carolyn McGettigan; Hannah Jones; Victor Rosi; Emma Soopramanien; Amrita Bains; Saloni Krishnan
articles.abstract: Recent experimental reading research has found that situational enjoyment of texts plays an important role in predicting both comprehension and motivation to continue reading. Here, we used narrative listening to test whether these findings generalise to spoken narratives, and to further investigate how different aspects of the narrator’s voice affect the experience and outcomes of listening. In Experiment 1, participants heard spoken book excerpts produced by a highly-naturalistic synthesised voice. After each excerpt, participants rated their enjoyment of the excerpt, answered a multiple-choice content comprehension question, and finally chose whether to wait to hear more of the narrative (or skip to the next one; a measure of motivation). Replicating the findings from reading research, we found that greater enjoyment was associated with increased probability of both correct comprehension and waiting. In Experiment 2, participants heard the same book excerpts, now narrated by 2 different synthesised voices that significantly differed in perceived pleasantness. Here, we found higher enjoyment for excerpts read by the more pleasant-sounding voice, but no effects of pleasantness on comprehension or waiting. In Experiment 3, we harnessed personalised voice cloning to show that both enjoyment and waiting were increased when listening to personally-familiar narrators (self, friend), compared with unfamiliar narrators. Our findings offer mechanistic evidence for the rewarding role of voice identity perception in spoken language processing, and present interesting implications for how personalised narrators could improve engagement with spoken book language.

articles.title: The effect of unconventional gender role advertisements (femvertising) on female purchase intentions and brand attitude: attitudes towards motherhood and culture: Korea vs. UK
articles.authors: Erin Lim; Adrian Furnham; Alastair McClelland
articles.abstract: This study examined the impact of culture and attitudes towards motherhood (ATM) on the effectiveness of traditional/non-traditional gendered advertisements. Korean and British participants viewed either traditional or non-traditional female portrayals in adverts and rated them for purchase intention and brand attitude. They also completed the Attitudes towards Fertility and Childbearing Scale (AFCS) containing three subscales: Fertility, Hindrance, and Social Identity. The results showed that there was a significant difference between cultures on ATM with more negative attitudes in Korean participants. However, there was no interaction effect between culture and advert type on advertising effectiveness, but main effects of culture and advert type were found. Favourable attitudes towards motherhood significantly positively correlated with the effectiveness of traditional adverts, but not non-traditional adverts except for Hindrance with PI.

articles.title: When Different Relational Experiences with AI Become Visible in Conversation: Linguistic and Dyadic Evidence from Naturalistic ChatGPT Interactions
articles.authors: Nadine Nicole Schmitt; Lennart Seizer; Fanny Alexandra Dietel; Lea Grimm-Keßler; Björn Schuller; Johanna Schuller
articles.abstract: People may experience large language models (LLMs) as therapeutically allied, emotionally close, or socially substitutive, but whether these relationships become visible in conversations is unknown. We distinguished what users discussed, what unfolded relationally, and how they experienced the AI relationship. We linked self-reports from 94 adults to donated, personally meaningful ChatGPT conversations using 21 outcome-blind frozen topics, blinded triple annotation of 500 sequences, and participant-grouped machine learning frozen before outcome access. Digital Therapeutic Alliance (DTA) and AI Attachment were related but showed different conversational correlates. Validation (R²_CV = .423) and uptake (R²_CV = .260) were recoverable out of sample, yet, neither formed a generalizable DTA signature. Conversely, a post-registration multivariate analysis identified a distributed Social Substitution fingerprint beyond conversation length and 21 topics (ΔR²_CV = .070) and improved prediction in 98% of repetitions. Ruptures were rare and consistently repaired; their association with DTA was fragile. Thus, different human–LLM relationships leave different—and sometimes no readily observable—conversational traces.

articles.title: Ulyssean Self-Control: Pre-commitment is effective, but choosing it freely requires good self-control
articles.authors: Hallgeir Sjåstad; Mathias Ekström
articles.abstract: Can pre-commitment strategies be a solution to self-control problems, or do they mainly help those who are already successful at regulating their behavior? In Study 1 (N=1,012), pre-commitment causally improved effort performance in an incentivized matrix-solving task. However, in Study 2 (N=1,010) participants with low (vs. high) self-control as a general trait were 35 percentage points less likely to choose the pre-commitment strategy, which in turn was associated with worse performance and earnings. Information about strategy effectiveness led to a small increase in uptake, whereas a “paternalistic” policy with forced pre-commitment led to superior performance. Study 3 (N=1,037) found that participants with high trait self-control were more likely to choose pre-commitment strategies across work, education, and health domains, mediated by higher future focus, strategy familiarity, and temptation avoidance. Pre-commitment is an effective strategy, but it is most often chosen by those who are already doing well: Individuals with good self-control.

articles.title: The Associations between Social Network Size and Preschool Children’s Visual Perspective-Taking and Non-Verbal Cue Understanding
articles.authors: Esmee Miron Aalders; Stephanie Wermelinger; Moritz M. Daum
articles.abstract:
Exposure to diverse communicative environments fosters a broader, more flexible
repertoire of communicative behaviour. Children’s social networks may constitute a
meaningful, yet underexplored, factor contributing to environmental diversity. In a
cross-sectional study, we examined whether social network size in preschool children
(N = 128, Mage = 4.06, SDage = 0.29) is associated with their communicative behaviour
indicated via three aspects: visual perspective-taking, non-verbal cue understanding,
and theory of mind (ToM). We ran two different types of analysis: first, the
conventional weekly contact threshold to operationalise social network size. This
analysis revealed no significant associations with the outcome variables. Second, we
conducted a data-driven grid search to identify the contact frequency threshold that
best predicted each outcome. The results suggest distinct candidate thresholds across
the three communicative behaviours assessed, indicating that each behaviour is
associated with a different relevant level of contact frequency. Visual perspective-taking
was positively associated with social network size calculated using a threshold of
approximately monthly contact. For non-verbal cue understanding, the best-fitting
threshold was about four interactions per week, at which social network size was
negatively associated with task performance. We found no significant associations
between social network size and children’s ToM. The findings show associations between
children’s social networks and pragmatic communication behaviour, but these
associations are sensitive to how social network size is operationalised.

articles.title: Aging and Hearing Loss in Emotional Prosody Processing: Divergent Neural Adaptation and Behavioral Performance
articles.authors: Yi Lin; Yangfan Lu; Hongwei Ding; Yang Zhang
articles.abstract: Emotional prosody perception is vulnerable in later adulthood, yet the contributions of central aging and peripheral hearing loss remain unclear. Across two experiments, we combined event-related potentials (ERPs) , time-frequency analyses and behavioral measures to examine how aging and hearing sensitvity shape emotional prosody processing. Experiment 1 used acoustically matched speech and nonspeech stimuli in a passive oddball paradigm to assess preattentive processing. Experiment 2 examined explicit emotion identification and implicit stimulus judgment to evaluate goal-directed performance and its associations with neural responses. Aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between emotions and lower behavioral efficiency, alongside enhanced P3a amplitude. Older adults also responded more slowly than younger adults during emotion identification. Hearing sensitivity showed no significant main effect on accuracy or reaction time, despite associations with delayed early neural processing and stronger theta- and alpha-band activity. Hearing-related neural effects were most evident in older adults and varied across emotions and stimulus types. Brain–behavior associations were selective: reduced mismatch negativity (MMN) was associated with slower responses during stimulus identification, whereas longer MMN latencies were associated with lower accuracy and slower responses during emotion identification. These findings indicate that aging and hearing loss have distinct yet interacting associations with emotional prosody processing, with neural responses not necessarily corresponding to behavioral performance. We propose an “asymmetric adaptation” account in which neural responses to degraded auditory input reorganize selectively across processing stages and contexts, potentially explaining this neural-behavioral divergence and informing more sensitive assessment of socioemotional communication in later adulthood.

articles.title: Effects of a Web-Based Debiasing Intervention on Brazilian Psychologists’ Accuracy on Major Depressive Disorder Diagnostic Tasks: A Randomized Training Intervention
articles.authors: Kalil Maihub Manara; Eric A. Youngstrom; Joshua A Langfus; Clarissa Marceli Trentini
articles.abstract: This randomized experimental study evaluated a web-based debiasing intervention designed to improve clinical judgment in the assessment of adult major depressive disorder (MDD) in Brazil. The intervention, adapted from prior work on pediatric bipolar disorder, taught Bayesian probability estimates and other debiasing strategies. Brazilian psychologists (N = 535) were assigned to either the intervention or an active control condition featuring a brief educational video, and were assessed post-intervention (n = 299). Outcomes were decision-making errors and diagnostic accuracy in response to vignettes, which depicted diagnostic challenges that could elicit cognitive biases. Assignment to intervention was associated with significantly fewer decision-making errors and greater diagnostic accuracy. Intervention effects were stronger for the vignette involving diagnostic risk estimation, as supported by intervention-by-vignette interaction effects. Intervention effects across vignettes were not statistically significant when only categorical diagnostic tasks were considered. Years of clinical practice and postgraduate training were largely unrelated to outcomes, and decision-making errors were not associated with treatment decisions. Overall, findings provide preliminary evidence of the transferability of this brief, web-based debiasing intervention to a distinct clinical and cultural context, although effect sizes were substantially attenuated compared with those observed in the original intervention.

articles.title: Identifying the Critical Period of Academic Burnout: A Computational Simulation Approach Based on Large-Scale Assessment Data
articles.authors: Xin Tang; Xiaofeng Wen; Jianxiao Jiang; Danhua Lin; Yiqun Gan; Yu Zhang
articles.abstract: Understanding student engagement and burnout has long been a central concern in educational research. While prior studies have extensively examined levels and correlates of them, far less is known about the timing at which students transition into amotivation (i.e., burnout) state from motivated state. In present study, based on Cox proportional hazards modeling and using large-scale data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), we develop a computational simulation model to infer individual- and group-level distributions of academic burnout onset across study weeks. Results demonstrate systematic variation in the timing of academic burnout onset as a function of weekly study time, with longer study hours associated with an earlier increase in burnout risk. To facilitate practical application, we further implement an interactive ShinyApp that allows users to estimate academic burnout onset periods at the individual, classroom, and school levels. This study contributes a novel methodological framework for temporally locating motivational breakdown and offers a scalable tool for translating large-scale assessment data into actionable educational insights.

articles.title: PRELIMINARY FRAMEWORK FOR A DYNAMIC SOCIO-ACOUSTIC MODEL OF SPEECH PERCEPTION
articles.authors: Meghan Sumner
articles.abstract: Listeners store detailed acoustic information and access social information cued by variation fast and early. Yet, how we understand all we understand remains an open question. I propose a Dynamic Socio-Acoustic Model that frames perception as a continuous, multidimensional tracking system where speech variation functions as primary cognitive information. This listener-driven model includes the fluid topological stretching of cognitive space, an acoustic exemplar space that is untethered to linguistic units and allows for multidimensional cross-context categorization. Listeners maintain a sub-lexical, macro-exemplar landscape where incoming acoustic-kinematic trajectories drive real-time resonance. Rather than matching signals to static templates, listeners construct ad-hoc categories on the fly, dynamically scaling an active grid in response to immediate environmental contrasts. By uniting continuous sensory tracking with fluid, experience-dependent spatial restructuring, this framework offers an ecological account of perception and memory that rethinks structural variation from a hurdle into a pathway to social meaning.

articles.title: Beyond Initial Crisis Recognition: Suicide-Risk Responses of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini Across 14-Turn Ukrainian-Language Conversations
articles.authors: Hryhorii Kuzyk; Oleg Salamon; Liliia Andreieva; Kateryna Drozdova
articles.abstract: Nine deployed conversational systems mostly recognised the crisis, but it disappeared from their behaviour once the conversation moved on. We ran 16 scenarios in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini as 14-message conversations (48 dialogues): crisis signals alternated with distraction, turn 13 introduced a new person at risk, and turn 14 was sent a day later. Coding was binary, as in the previous study, with clinical verification; two crisis-contour specifications were tested separately. New crisis signals drew a reaction in 87, 95, and 76 of 96 responses, respectively; the crisis stopped being mentioned mainly at an everyday message. The new person at risk drew a reaction in 44 of 48 responses; after a day, 29 retained crisis content. All 14 turns drew a 'yes' code in 4, 7, and 0 of 16 conversations. Reacting to the new person did not guarantee correct allocation of roles and actions. Both contour specifications produced safety-relevant errors. Neither hypothesis was supported: the systems behaved differently, and the same rule, introduced as a single package, did not stabilise their behaviour. Recognition, retention, and reconfiguration at a transition are distinct properties; the weakest is retention of the prior state and tracking of each person's trajectory.

articles.title: Assessing User-Subjective Experience with Conversational Agents for Behavioral and Mental Health Interventions: Design and Psychometric Evaluation of CUE-Chat
articles.authors: Esther Mertens; Janis Butz; Jean-Louis van Gelder
articles.abstract:
While AI-conversational agents are increasingly integrated into behavioral and mental health interventions, standardized instruments to assess their performance remain scarce. To address this gap, we developed an instrument to measure user-subjective experience with AI-driven agents in the healthcare domain. We focused on user perception due to its direct contribution to intervention effects, and on healthcare given that the rapid adoption of AI-agents in this domain continues to outpace the development of validated evaluation instruments. 
Across four studies, we developed and tested the Chatbot User Evaluation instrument (CUE-Chat). First, we identified relevant assessment domains and items through literature review, existing instruments, input from AI-driven agents, and the research team’s domain expertise. Following this, we requested feedback on draft subscales, definitions, and items from expert and laypeople panels. We then tested the structure of the instrument’s concept version. Finally, we conducted a psychometric evaluation and finalized the instrument.
CUE-Chat consists of four factors: Perceived Efficacy (4 items), Usability (4 items), Intelligence (4 items), and Safety and Risk Management (4 items). Reliability and validity of the total score and each subscale was good to excellent (Cronbach’s α = .73-.92; Ω = .74-.93). Predictive validity was strong with all scales predictive of users’ overall rating of an AI-agent’s performance.
We conclude that CUE-Chat’s strong psychometric properties are promising, and that it is particularly useful for researchers integrating AI-driven agents into behavioral and mental health interventions in both developmental and evaluative stages.

articles.title: Consensus Embedding Geometry for Taxonomy Discovery in Psychological Domains
articles.authors: Daniel Steven Stutts; Jeffrey Humpherys; Ting Shen
articles.abstract: Psychological domains contain many constructs whose meanings are specified through natural-language definitions and examples. Organizing these vocabularies requires methods that connect semantic representations to interpretable categories and expose the effects of analytical choices. We present a researcher-guided framework combining construct prototypes, consensus similarity across embedding models, classical multidimensional scaling, and clustering in theory-guided feature spaces. Averaging model-specific cosine matrices produces a positive-semidefinite consensus kernel that accommodates different embedding dimensions. Global geometry supports broad organization, domain features support intermediate grouping, and local geometry supports finer subdivision. We demonstrate the framework on 224 abuse constructs represented by working definitions supplied by generative artificial intelligence and seven synthetic examples per construct. The resulting hierarchy distinguishes psychological domination from environmental violation and provides finer categories within each branch. Comparisons with single-model, definition-only, example-only, and direct-clustering alternatives identify the roles of representation and subdivision choices. The contribution is a reproducible workflow and stage-specific evaluation for exploratory taxonomy discovery. The case study establishes the dependence of its output on identifiable modeling choices, with category validity and cross-domain transfer remaining questions for further study.

articles.title: Familiar Content Changes Performance and Processing in Matrix Reasoning in Early Adolescence
articles.authors: Paulo Guirro Laurence; Marcela M. Weiss; Elizeu Macedo
articles.abstract: Matrix-reasoning assessments commonly use abstract geometric figures, although familiar content may change both performance and processing. This within-participants study compared accuracy and gaze-defined patterns of visual exploration for abstract and contextual items requiring corresponding relational rules. Participants were 56 children and adolescents recruited from a public school in São Paulo, Brazil, aged 11 to 15 years. Each participant completed six abstract and six contextual 3 × 3 matrices while gaze was recorded. Trial-level transition matrices were constructed from fixation sequences across nine matrix cells and the response alternatives, and k-means clustering identified two recurring patterns. Contextual items were answered more accurately than abstract items, with 2.44 times higher odds of a correct response. Completion time, fixation count, and fixation duration were similar between conditions. Cluster 1 was characterized by localized transitions involving the final row and response alternatives, whereas Cluster 2 involved broader, more sequential exploration across the matrix. Contextual items had lower odds of Cluster 1 classification, indicating that representational format modestly altered the distribution of gaze patterns. A significant condition-by-cluster interaction further showed that Cluster 2 was associated with higher accuracy for abstract items, but no cluster difference was detected for contextual items. These exploratory findings suggest that familiar content changes how matrices are explored, indicating that abstract and familiar matrix items should not be treated as interchangeable.

articles.title: What is there to explain about free will? An “easy problem” of consciousness downstream of agency
articles.authors: Nicolas Rouleau
articles.abstract: Free will is one of the most enduring problems in philosophy and cognitive science, yet what, exactly, requires explanation remains unclear. The most tractable target is the experience of free will – the vivid sense of self-authorship, control, and a felt capacity to have done otherwise. As with the scientific study of mystical experiences, this phenomenology can be investigated without resolving the metaphysical claims implied by its content. Here, I argue that free will is an “easy problem” of consciousness: a phenomenon that can be measured, manipulated, predicted, and mechanistically explained. Taking causal determinism as a working postulate, I consider whether prediction and reinforcement could generate the experience of controlling one’s own actions through causal misattribution and superstitious conditioning, without granting consciousness independent causal power. If the experience can be explained under deterministic constraints, the core scientific explanandum of the free will phenomenon has been addressed. Free will can then be distinguished from agency, which remains a causally consequential, graded capacity for goal-directed, adaptive, and self-regulating action across living systems, machines, and hybrids thereof.

articles.title: Making good decisions with counterfactuals
articles.authors: Ma Ricky; Scott Mueller; Thomas Icard; Tobias Gerstenberg
articles.abstract: Making a good decision often requires knowing something counterfactual: whether a person would be better off if we acted than if we didn't. Formal work shows how both experimental and observational data ought to be combined to inform good decisions. Here, we ask whether people's intuitions follow this normative standard. In three experiments (N = 354), participants decided whether or not to act based on observational and experimental data. Participants performed better than chance but far from optimally. Trial-by-trial feedback about the consequences of their choices, including what would have happened had they chosen otherwise, didn't improve performance. The breakdown was at the inference step: participants' estimates of whether a person would benefit from the treatment, be harmed by it, or be left unaffected were almost unrelated to normative predictions. Yet, participants' decisions followed coherently from those (incorrect) estimates. Experts in statistics, economics, and data science made better decisions than novices, but their counterfactual inferences were no more accurate. Counterfactual reasoning is critical for making good decisions from experimental and observational data, but its logic doesn't come naturally to people.

articles.title: Breaking Common Ground through Reciprocal Misalignment
articles.authors: Siham Abu Ali; Tatiana Philippova; Isaac Fradkin
articles.abstract: Establishing shared meaning is widely considered the normative, almost ubiquitous trajectory of linguistic interaction, while moments of misalignment are typically viewed as temporary interruptions that individuals attempt to repair. However, it is not uncommon to experience communication breakdowns that actively escalate rather than resolve. This raises a fundamental question: does interaction inherently lead people toward shared meaning, or is semantic alignment a reciprocal, socially contingent process? We conducted four experiments using a novel multiplayer word association task, where participants generated semantic associations while interacting with either human or simulated partners varying in semantic typicality. Our results show that, in general, social interaction motivates individuals to produce more conventional associations to support alignment. However, this tendency depended on partner’s behavior: when interacting with an atypical or difficult-to-align-with partner, individuals actively reduced their own typicality and tendency to match partner’s associations, effectively sacrificing semantic alignment. Such ‘reciprocal misalignment’ persisted even when participants were incentivized to maximize alignment. Our findings suggest that semantic misalignment may reflect a reciprocal, socially-motivated modulation of identity and differentiation, rather than solely a failure of coordination. This work sheds light on the interactional mechanisms underlying interpersonal distancing, communication breakdowns in neurodivergence, and potentially broader patterns of social polarization.

articles.title: Health and Personality Contributions to Cybersickness in Virtual Reality
articles.authors: Jonathan Kelly; Taylor Doty; Sydney Hicks; Stephen B. Gilbert; Michael Dorneich
articles.abstract:
Background
Cybersickness reflects interactions between system (hardware and software) properties and user characteristics. Although motion sickness susceptibility is a known predictor, individual differences including transient and enduring health, psychological, and personality factors have rarely been examined and never simultaneously.

Method
Participants (N = 252) were exposed to one of five VR games. Cybersickness was assessed using self-reported symptoms (Simulator Sickness Questionnaire; SSQ) and tolerance (time in VR). Hierarchical regression models evaluated whether health, psychological functioning (affective state, psychological distress), and personality predicted outcomes after accounting for game, sex, and motion sickness susceptibility.

Results
Fatigue, pain sensitivity, and sex were key predictors of symptom severity: higher fatigue, greater pain sensitivity, and female sex were associated with higher SSQ scores. Motion sickness susceptibility and agreeableness predicted reduced tolerance. Final models explained 29.3% of variance in SSQ and 23.8% in tolerance.

Conclusion
Cybersickness reflected established stimulus and susceptibility factors as well as outcome-specific user characteristics: health-related factors and sex were associated with symptom severity; susceptibility and agreeableness were associated with tolerance.

Application
User state (e.g., fatigue), sex, motion sickness susceptibility, and tolerance-related individual differences should be considered in the design and deployment of immersive systems to improve comfort and support sustained VR use.

articles.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between technology acceptance, classroom distraction, and academic engagement among Chinese high school students: A reassessment of Li and Chen (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Li and Chen concluded reciprocal prospective associations between technology acceptance, classroom digital distraction, and academic engagement among high school students. However, significant cross-lagged parameters do not by themselves establish genuine prospective influence because similar estimates may arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data that reproduced the sample size and correlation matrix reported by Li and Chen, I examined whether their conclusions were robust across several defensible analytic specifications. The pattern of results depended strongly on analytic choice: some models suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or null effects. When estimates from all specifications were combined using meta-analytic methods, no overall effect reached statistical significance. Accordingly, the available evidence does not provide a firm basis for concluding that technology acceptance, classroom distraction, and academic engagement exert reciprocal prospective influences on one another. In line with multiverse-analysis recommendations, conclusions should be drawn from the collective pattern across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than from a single model.

articles.title: “Oh No, the Robots Are Here”: AI identity labels, social uptake and sanctioning in mixed human–AI communities
articles.authors: Sara Major; Aleksandar Tomašević; Ana Vranić; Darja Cvetkovic; Dušan Vudragović; Boris Stupovski; Marija Mitrovic Dankulov
articles.abstract: Social media users can now encounter autonomous AI accounts that post, reply and vote alongside other users. In a longitudinal field experiment, we examined how labelling these accounts relates to whom people answer and how they evaluate AI contributions. YSocial is a Reddit-like hybrid platform for social media simulation, where people interact with language-model agents. On it, 36 participants discussed popular culture with 72 AI accounts powered by an uncensored language model over 21 experiment days. The AI accounts kept persistent personas and remembered previous exchanges. They were visibly labelled in one community and unlabelled in the other. Among 2,143 human replies, Bayesian models estimated that the probability of replying to an AI-authored post or comment was 3.5 percentage points higher in the hidden-label community, given the same earlier posts and comments available in the thread (95% credible interval 0.5–6.5). In both communities, participants were more likely to reply to an AI account after it had replied to them and less likely after they had replied to it. The gap in criticism, including polite disagreement, between replies to AI and human accounts was 13.3 percentage points larger in the visible-label community (95% credible interval 5.1–21.4). The toxicity difference was uncertain. Visible labels were associated with less engagement with AI contributions and more criticism of them.

articles.title: Persecutory and Grandiose Thinking in Mental Disorder, Religion, and Politics: Common Causes, Processes, and (Dys)Functions
articles.authors: Ari Brouwer; Charles L Raison
articles.abstract: Persecutory and grandiose thinking (PGT) is evident in mental disorder, religion, and politics. This paper offers an interdisciplinary explanation of PGT with a focus on common causes, mechanisms, and functions. First, psychopathological and ideological variants of PGT are introduced and compared. Theories of stress-induced psychological and social change are invoked next to explain shifts towards PGT in individuals and groups. These include a Status Threat/Reward Model of psychopathological PGT and a relative deprivation theory of political violence. Potential functions and dysfunctions of PGT are considered next, with a focus on how persecutory and grandiose thinking may orient individuals towards mitigating social threats and gaining social rewards, respectively. Conditions for collective PGT are then explored, including systemic stress and exposure to redemptive ideological narratives. Finally, we consider how religious and political institutions regulate PGT.

articles.title: Maturational constraints on tracking of temporal attention in infant language acquisition.
articles.authors: Tineke M. Snijders; Katharina Menn
articles.abstract: Children are active learners: they selectively attend to important information. Rhythmic neural tracking of speech is central to active language learning. This chapter evaluates recent research showing that neural oscillations in the infant brain synchronise with the rhythm of speech, tracking it at different frequencies. This process predicts word segmentation and later language abilities. We argue that rhythmic neural speech tracking reflects infants’ attention to specific parts of the speech signal (e.g., stressed syllables), and simultaneously acts as a core mechanism for maximising temporal attention onto those parts. Rhythmic neural tracking of speech puts a constraint on neural processing, which maximises the uptake of relevant information from the noisy multimodal environment. We hypothesise this to be influenced by neural maturation. We end by evaluating the implications of this proposal for language acquisition research, and discuss how differences in neural maturation relate to variance in language development in autism.

articles.title: Ongoing thought varies around individualised defaults in an experiential state space across contexts and depressive symptoms
articles.authors: Clara Wakonigg Alonso; Sian Panton; Dominique Makowski; Giulia Poerio; Theodoros Karapanagiotidis
articles.abstract: Ongoing thought varies continuously, yet previous research has shown that people engage in a small set of recurring thought patterns that are consistent across contexts and individuals. However, it remains unclear whether individuals show idiosyncratic, stable configurations, akin to a default experiential state from which momentary experiences deviate. We combined an emotional-induction task with Multidimensional Experience Sampling of ongoing thought in the lab and daily life. Dimensionality reduction revealed five dominant population-level patterns of thought, forming orthogonal axes of a shared experiential space. Within this space, thought patterns were more similar within individuals than between, supporting person-specific signatures. Position within this space carried psychological meaning: depressive symptom severity predicted both the intensity and frequency of negative intrusive thought in daily life. Default thought patterns were then estimated as each participant's geometric median across daily-life experiences and we assessed how affective contexts displaced thought from these defaults. Positive and negative stimuli shifted thought away from default thought patterns in systematic context-dependent ways, and these shifts varied with depressive symptom severity. Together, the findings suggest that default thought patterns define stable regions within an experiential space, while emotional states and individual differences relate to how momentary experience is displaced from these defaults.

articles.title: Personalized Impulse Control Training in Prison:  A Mixed-Methods Proof-of-Principle Study
articles.authors: Tilia Linthout; Rune Verhoeyen; Emilie A. Caspar; Yannick Boddez; Pieter Van Dessel
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Impulse control difficulties are relevant in prison settings, yet little is known about whether theory-based impulse control interventions can be implemented in detention contexts. This study examined the feasibility and preliminary effects of two personalized impulse control interventions in a Flemish prison: an intervention targeting goal-directed predictive processing (GDPP) and a go/no-go intervention.
Design/methodology/approach: Six incarcerated men completed a mixed-methods study. Participants were assigned to either the GDPP condition or the go/no-go condition and completed daily paper questionnaires during three consecutive seven-day phases: a baseline, intervention, and post-intervention phase. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively and through exploratory single-case analyses. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.
Findings: Participants in both conditions showed descriptive reductions in self-reported target impulsive behaviors. The reduction appeared larger in the GDPP condition, but the small sample and missing data preclude strong conclusions about comparative efficacy. Qualitative findings indicated that participants generally experienced the interventions as acceptable and meaningful. Several change processes were reported, including daily self-monitoring, perceived accountability, repeated researcher contact, awareness of alternative behaviors, and confidence in future behavior. Participants also identified barriers related to prison stressors, personal stressors, and limited opportunities to demonstrate change in detention.
Originality/value: This study provides an initial test of the transferability of personalized impulse control interventions to a prison context. It suggests that GDPP-based training can be adapted for detention settings and highlights practical and methodological challenges for future controlled studies.
Keywords: impulse control; prison; goal-directed predictive processing; go/no-go training; mixed methods; single-case analysis

articles.title: The Perceived Utility and Scope of Ecological Momentary Assessment and Interventions for Non-Suicidal Self-Injury: A Needs-Based Dynamic Risk Perspective
articles.authors: Mirthe Luijsmans; Laurence Claes; Ruth Tatnell; Marlies Houben; Thomas Vaessen; Tom Smeets; Inez Myin-Germeys; Glenn Kiekens
articles.abstract:
Background: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a serious mental health problem characterized by rapid within-person fluctuations in thoughts and urges. Yet, treatments rely on retrospective and static approaches for assessments and interventions. Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) and Ecological Momentary Interventions (EMIs) may enable more dynamic support in real time. This study examined the perceived utility and scope of these new digital modalities from the perspectives of treatment-seeking individuals and mental health professionals.
Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 30 treatment-seeking individuals engaging in NSSI, after completing a four-week EMA period, and with 14 professionals who used EMA in treatment. Interviews explored experiences with EMA and perspectives on EMIs and were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.  
Results: Three themes were identified. First, EMA and EMIs were perceived as extending therapeutic 
support by enhancing awareness, reflection, and skill use in daily life. Second, participants emphasized that EMIs must be tailored to changing needs in function of changing risk. This informed the development of a Needs-Based Dynamic Risk and Intervention Model for NSSI, distinguishing needs and interventions through a traffic-light analogy across low (i.e., mental health promotion), moderate (i.e., vulnerability regulation), and high (i.e., behavioral interruption) risk states. Third, EMIs were viewed as valuable when embedded in blended care and implemented through shared decision-making, balancing system- and user-initiated support.
Conclusion: Integrating EMA and EMIs into treatment has potential to provide needs-tailored support for individuals who self-injure. Future work should focus on empirically validating the proposed dynamic model and co-designing EMI components that address fluctuating needs in daily life.

articles.title: A Three-Domain Framework for Trust in Digitally Mediated Social Life
articles.authors: anonymous; YUAN SHEN; Ke Shen; Jinliang Qin
articles.abstract: Digital technologies increasingly mediate information access, social interaction, and institutional participation, raising the question of how trust in digital systems is organized in relation to trust in people and institutions. Across three independent samples of Chinese young adults, we tested a three-domain framework of trust in digitally mediated social life and developed a concise measure distinguishing interpersonal trust, institutional/rule trust, and digital system trust. Study 1 (N = 1,495) identified a three-factor structure using parallel analysis and exploratory factor analysis. Study 2 (N = 1,333) confirmed this structure: the three-factor model outperformed a unidimensional model and all pairwise-collapsed two-factor alternatives, although the three domains remained strongly correlated. Study 3 (N = 901) provided evidence consistent with measurement invariance across gender and initial nomological differentiation. Learning-oriented digital engagement was more strongly associated with institutional/rule and digital system trust, everyday/relational engagement with interpersonal and digital system trust, and digital information judgment with institutional/rule trust. Sensitivity analyses reproduced the primary patterns. Together, the findings support a three-domain framework in which digital system trust is strongly interconnected with, but not reducible to, trust in people or institutional arrangements.

articles.title: Navigating Autistic College Students’ Career Development: A Capability-Oriented Perspective on Agency and Advocacy
articles.authors: Yilun Jiang; Karly Ball Isaacson; Bradley E. Cox; Brett Ranon Nachman
articles.abstract: Autistic college students navigate career development through their interests and strengths, while encountering deficit-oriented assumptions about autism. Research on autistic students’ career development usually focuses on career support and skill development, while limited studies have examined how they pursue career pathways from a strengths-based perspective. Drawing on a secondary analysis of semi-structured interviews from a national mixed-methods study (n = 36), we examined how autistic college students in four-year U.S. colleges navigate career development. Applied thematic analysis identified three themes: participants developed purpose-driven career goals through long-standing interests, lived experiences, and community exposure; navigated judgments about capability and professional fit across academic and career contexts; and assembled career support across career centers, faculty, and autism support groups. Our findings highlight autistic participants’ capability to explore career pathways that reflect their interests and goals and suggest an agency-beyond-advocacy interpretation, in which agency refers to broader forms of action through which students shape their career development and advocacy represents one important form of agency. Finally, we offer suggestions for universities and employers to develop resources more tailored to autistic students’ career goals and needs.

articles.title: Recovering Hierarchical Structures in Psychological Measurement
articles.authors: Alexander P. Christensen; Sydney Mckenna Goldberg; Ashley L. Watts; Luis Eduardo Garrido
articles.abstract: Psychological constructs are often organized hierarchically, making accurate identification of their narrowest dimensions essential to recover broader levels of organization. Existing network methods for this task are limited by either the resolution limit of modularity or the variability introduced by terminating community detection prematurely. We introduce Pairwise Resolution Iteration via Subgraph Modularity (PRISM), a community detection procedure designed to identify dimensions below the resolution limit without requiring a tunable parameter. We evaluated PRISM using 320,000 samples generated from second order factor models across 3,200 conditions that varied the numbers of first and second order factors, factor loadings, indicators per factor, sample size, skew, overlapping dimensions, population error, and correlations among second order factors. PRISM was compared with lower order Louvain and exploratory factor analysis (EFA) paired with several traditional dimensionality methods, many of which set the depth of the bass-ackward estimation procedure. Recovery was evaluated using dimensionality accuracy, bias, and structural accuracy. PRISM generally provided the most accurate and least biased recovery at both levels and maintained strong performance at smaller sample sizes and extreme skew. overlapping dimensions reduced performance across methods, and both network methods performed poorly when overlapping dimensions were combined with few indicators, weak first order loadings, and strong second order loadings. EFA paired with parallel analysis based on principal component eigenvalues was the strongest traditional alternative, particularly in exceptionally large samples. These findings support PRISM as a robust general procedure to recover each level of a hierarchical structure.

articles.title: Temporal choice dynamics track opponent-dependent adaptation in autism
articles.authors: Tahmineh Godazgar; Rana Ghamari; Abolfazl Nadi; Atiye Sarabi-Jamab
articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder involves differences in social communication, interaction and behavioral flexibility, yet conventional single-response Theory-of-Mind tasks rarely capture the trial-by-trial dynamics of social adaptation. We examined how autistic and non-autistic young people organized recent choice history, how they adjusted it across opponents, and how these patterns related to task performance. Twenty-seven autistic children and adolescents and 24 healthy controls completed the same two-choice hide-and-seek task under social and non-social framing against artificial opponents of graded sophistication. We compared aggregate performance, Bayesian model-based estimates of latent strategy use, and model-free history kernels measuring how current choices depended on recent self-actions and opponent actions. History kernels showed that autistic participants switched away from their previous choice more strongly against every opponent, whereas controls added lag-2 and opponent-coupled structure when the opponent adapted to them and reconfigured their kernels across opponents more. Within the same dataset, replaying participants’ kernels against empirically fitted opponents reconstructed accuracy (r = .86) and the direction of the group difference against the first-order opponent, against which switching provided less benefit than against the zero-order opponent. Against the first-order opponent, controls were more often described by first-order opponent modelling (influence learning) and autistic participants by heuristic policies. These findings suggest that autism-related differences in repeated interaction are expressed in how choice history is organized and reconfigured across opponents, beyond categorical differences in inferred strategies.

articles.title: When Are Less Precise Predictions More Credible?
articles.authors: Eitan David Rude; Amin Shiri; Felipe M. Affonso; Hal Hershfield; Craig R. Fox
articles.abstract: People expressing uncertain values frequently offer point predictions or intervals of varying widths (e.g., “I’d say your investment will be worth $6,000” versus “I’d say your investment will be worth $5,000–$7,000”). Interestingly, prior research has drawn conflicting conclusions concerning the credibility of more versus less precise predictions. We resolve this inconsistency by identifying a key moderator: the perceived nature of uncertainty. Specifically, we find that under epistemic (“knowable”) uncertainty, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ degree of confidence, and more precise predictions are seen as more credible. Under aleatory (“random”) uncertainty, however, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ assessments of the degree of outcome variability, and less precise predictions are seen as more credible (provided they are within reasonable bounds). These results inform literatures on both the communication of uncertainty and the interpretation of confidence intervals.

articles.title: Beyond Weight Gain in Family-Based Treatment for Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder: A Response to Lock et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Laurence Cobbaert
articles.abstract: Family-based treatment for avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (FBT-ARFID) has recently been defended as addressing more than weight gain. This Commentary argues that therapeutic intent should be distinguished from demonstrated comparative benefit. In the primary randomized trial, FBT-ARFID showed its clearest advantage for weight restoration, while broader domains of ARFID symptomatology and psychological functioning did not consistently show between-group superiority. High treatment completion and absence of serious adverse events likewise cannot establish psychological, relational, sensory, or autonomy-related safety when these outcomes are not systematically assessed. These limitations are particularly consequential in ARFID, where sensory processing differences, fear of aversive consequences, low interest in eating, and neurodivergence may shape treatment needs and experiences. Future trials should incorporate direct child-reported outcomes, treatment burden, agency and participation, sensory distress, psychosocial functioning, adverse effects, reasons for discontinuation, and durability of change. If FBT-ARFID is to be understood as more than weight gain, its evaluation should be broader than weight gain too.

articles.title: Music-Based Interventions for  Cognition and Brain Health: the ARM framework
articles.authors: Psyche Loui; Jonathan E. Peelle; Jessica Adrienne Grahn
articles.abstract: Music-based interventions (MBIs) have shown promise in addressing cognitive, motor, and language impairments across neurological and neurodevelopmental conditions. Despite an increasing number of controlled studies that have assessed the potential rehabilitative effects of music, neural mechanisms underlying therapeutic benefits remain poorly understood. Here we present the ARM framework: a neurobiologically-informed model integrating three key systems: Auditory processing networks that encode temporal and spectral features; Reward circuitry activated by musical pleasure and prediction, and Motor systems engaged through auditory-motor coupling and rhythmic entrainment. We examine how specific MBIs leverage these systems to varying degrees and show how understanding these mechanisms is essential for predicting individual treatment response, personalizing interventions, and developing next-generation therapeutic approaches that optimize engagement of specific neural systems.

articles.title: Expertise Diversity Enhances Information Sharing in Wiki settings: Evidence from Sequential Collaboration
articles.authors: Maren Mayer; Joachim Kimmerle
articles.abstract: Online collaborative projects such as Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap rely on sequential collaboration, where contributors iteratively revise a shared product over time. While previous research has examined wikis for computer-supported collaborative learning and sequential collaboration for numerical judgment tasks, little is known about the cognitive mechanisms underlying information sharing in such settings. The present study bridges research on computer-supported collaborative learning, group information sharing, and cognitive models of sequential collaboration. Drawing on a computational model of sequential collaboration, we tested the prediction that higher variation in contributors' expertise facilitates the integration of information into a shared product. In an experimental study with 413 participants we demonstrate that information accumulation increased throughout the sequential chain but at a decreasing rate. Consistent with model predictions, higher expertise variation significantly increased the likelihood that information was incorporated into the shared text. Contrary to expectations, expertise variation did not affect the timing of information inclusion across chain positions, nor did it increase information deletions. These findings demonstrate that predictions derived from a cognitive model of numerical judgment formation generalize to information-sharing contexts. More broadly, the results suggest that diversity in contributors' knowledge can improve collaborative knowledge construction in sequential environments. This research adds to evidence that sequential collaboration is an effective mechanism for integrating distributed knowledge in online collaborative systems.

articles.title: Can personality be deliberately changed? Effects of a randomized, placebo-controlled intervention on character strengths and Big Five personality traits
articles.authors: Lisa Wagner; Valentina Vylobkova; Sonja Heintz; Jessie Sun; Fabian Gander
articles.abstract: The promise of intentional change in adult personality traits attracts broad interest, even as convincing evidence remains scarce and methodologically challenging. In a preregistered randomized placebo- and waitlist-controlled study with N = 3,434 adults, we tested whether an eight-week online training of a self-selected character strength produces short- and long-term changes in character strengths (states and traits) and Big Five personality traits. Participants in the intervention condition increased targeted strengths states more than both placebo and waitlist control conditions. However, intervention and placebo participants experienced similar gains in targeted strengths traits, extraversion, and agreeableness, as well as similar decreases in neuroticism relative to the waitlist condition. Thus, some effects may result from non-specific aspects of the structured activity. Informants did not observe any between-condition differences in strengths trait change. These findings underscore the importance of using rigorous control conditions in research on volitional personality change.

articles.title: Techno-Optimism Reduces Willingness to Address Climate Change
articles.authors: Jonas M B Haslbeck; Maien S. M. Sachisthal; Fabian Dablander
articles.abstract: Technological innovation is essential for mitigating climate change, but so are wider socio-economic transformations as well as lifestyle changes. Techno-optimism, the belief that technological innovation alone is sufficient to address climate change, may reduce public willingness to engage in climate action. Here we use a structural causal model to estimate the causal effect of techno-optimism on willingness to contribute 1\% of one's monthly household income to address climate change using a large, population-weighted sample from the Netherlands (N = 23, 395). We find that being a techno-optimist reduces the probability of being willing to contribute by 18.7% (95% CI: 15.6, 20.7). In addition, we find that the causal effect is much smaller for respondents on the political right, where overall willingness is already very low. We close by discussing the importance of adequately framing the role of technology when discussing climate change mitigation.

articles.title: Neural Racing Accumulator Model Estimation With Lightweight Monotonic Flows
articles.authors: Malte Lüken; Stefan T. Radev; Lourens Waldorp; Andrew Heathcote
articles.abstract: Race models describe speeded decision-making as a race between competing runners that accumulate evidence in favor of available choice options. Their parameters can be estimated through the model likelihood that combines the probability and cumulative density functions of each runner. However, estimating parameters of complex race models whose runners have intractable densities with (hierarchical) Bayesian inference has been challenging: Numerical density approximations tend to be slow and amortized neural posterior estimation methods require complex network architectures that can be expensive to train and, in classical settings, tie the trained estimator to a specific prior distribution and generative model. We propose a flexible neural estimation method that decouples training from the choice of prior distribution or model parameterization. We train a small neural network together with a monotonic neural spline flow to simultaneously learn the runners' conditional probability density and cumulative density functions. We then combine both functions to efficiently estimate race model likelihoods that can be used in combination with modern samplers. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both tractable and intractable versions of the popular racing diffusion model. Based on our results, we argue that, when flexibility in choosing prior distributions or model parameterizations is needed, learning the model likelihood with lightweight neural density estimators is advantageous.

articles.title: Consistency: A Critical but Often Overlooked Requirement for Causal Inference in Psychological Research
articles.authors: Lukas Junker; Michael P. Grosz
articles.abstract: Psychologists are often interested in specific causal quantities (“What is the effect of reducing social-media scrolling by 20 minutes on well-being?”) but tend to focus on vague questions (“Does ‘time spent on social media’ predict well-being?”). There is a mismatch between the causal effects researchers care about and the associations and correlations they compute. In this article, we highlight consistency as a foundational requirement for causal inference that can bridge this mismatch and make statistical estimates causally interpretable. Consistency shows how causal quantities are interpretable only when (a) the causal quantity of interest—the causal estimand—is described precisely enough that it does not bundle different versions of the treatment (e.g., passive scrolling, reading distressing news, or chatting with friends on social media) that have different effects, and (b) the way that the treatment variable changes in the data matches this causal estimand of interest. We clarify these requirements and illustrate how to state and assess them in settings common in psychological research, with a focus on indirect experimental manipulations and multidimensional constructs. Making this step explicit helps researchers articulate their estimands more transparently and is a prerequisite for other concerns such as confounding and model specification.

articles.title: Attentional Experience, Autonomic Function and Network Dynamics During the ISAAA Observational Stage of Mindfulness Training
articles.authors: GAO JUNLING; Hank Leung; Kin Cheung Lee; Bonnie Wai Yan Wu; Qiqi Chen; Andrew Bakaki; Hin Hung Sik
articles.abstract:
Objectives. 
To characterize attentional experience, pulse rate variability (PRV), and interpersonal pulse-rate networks during the observational stage of Interoceptive Sensitivity for Attentional–Autonomic Alignment (ISAAA) training.
Methods. 
In an uncontrolled five-day meditation camp, 48 participants provided linked pre- and post-camp questionnaires. Post-camp wrist photoplethysmography recorded five minutes of rest followed by four five-minute practice blocks (n = 14). Exploratory analyses related three questionnaire scores to proportional rest-to-meditation RMSSD change (n = 12) and examined interpersonal pulse-rate networks (n = 14).
Results. 
On the Toronto Mindfulness Scale (TMS), Curiosity increased by 2.70 points (95% CI [1.45, 3.95], dz = .63, p < .001, Holm-adjusted) and Decentering by 2.82 points ([1.80, 3.84], dz = .81, p < .001, Holm-adjusted); both remained Holm-significant across six alternative pre-post linkage reconstructions. RMSSD block means were lower during practice than at rest (50.36–68.80 vs. 96.70 ms), with no detected difference across practice blocks (p = .2773). Pulse rate showed no detectable change. Emotional Awareness correlated with the meditation/rest RMSSD ratio (ρ = −.68, p = .015, did not survive correction). Mean absolute interpersonal correlation was .070 at rest and .057 during the first practice block; no network comparison was significant.
Conclusions. 
Stage 1 training was accompanied by increased curiosity and decentering. The physiological pattern is compatible with engaged observation, indicating a potential attention-autonomic correlation, while the baseline and processing need more data on a firm autonomic interpretation. Interpersonal networks provide an exploratory group-level perspective without establishing increased synchrony or social connection.

articles.title: Real-time Associations Between Psychological States and Context in University Students with Suicidal Ideation: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Ana Portillo-Van Diest; Gemma Vilagut; Laura Ballester; Johan Bjureberg; Paula Carrasco; Raquel Falcó; Margalida Gili; Mathilde Husky; Glenn Kiekens; Francisco H. Machancoses
articles.abstract: Suicidal ideation (SI) is dynamic and linked to emotion regulation difficulties that may be reflected in associations between momentary psychological states and context. In a 2-week ecological momentary assessment (EMA) study, 476 students reported passive daily SI, momentary psychological states (affect, stress, tiredness, concentration difficulties) and contexts four times per day. Multilevel network analysis compared contemporaneous, temporal, and between-person networks across three groups: one without SI or psychopathology (No-MD/SI), and two with low and high 14-day passive SI (Low- and High-SI). Low- and High-SI groups showed more temporally self-reinforcing negative affect and weaker affect-context connections. No-MD/SI students showed stronger positive affect recovery following negative affect. High-SI students spent less time with loved ones and were more likely to engage in conversation after stress than after positive emotions. Findings suggest that passive SI is associated with greater negative emotion rigidity and a shift in social connectedness from enjoyment to distress-driven coping.

articles.title: fMRI hyperscanning reveals widespread neural coupling during natural conversations
articles.authors: Laetitia Mwilambwe-Tshilobo; Lily Tsoi; Sebastian Speer; Zaid Zada; Shannon M. Burns; Emily B. Falk; Diana Tamir
articles.abstract: Conversation is one of the most powerful tools that people have for building and maintaining social connections. How does conversation bring two minds together? Here we tracked the neural dynamics between dyads during real-time conversation using fMRI hyperscanning, where both people were scanned simultaneously, to explore whether and how conversation aligns brains. Dyads engaged in natural, free-flowing conversation as they co-constructed the content of their dialogue. In a control condition, partners read aloud scripted dialogue from another dyad’s conversation, preserving the turn-taking structure while removing the co-construction. To examine neural alignment, we compared whole-brain intersubject correlation between partners in each condition, assessing both synchronous and predictive neural dynamics. Results showed that naturalistic conversation led to significant widespread neural alignment across brain regions implicated in attention, audition, affect, executive control, and social cognition, compared to scripted conversation. Temporally refined analyses showed that during naturalistic conversation, relative to scripted conversation, both speakers and listeners anticipated each other within a short temporal window, with brain activity preceding their partner’s in the same neural systems. These findings show that live, turn-taking conversations align neural activity well beyond passive or asynchronous communication, providing a foundation for future research examining how spontaneous, co-constructed dialogue allows people to communicate effectively.
