articles.title: Developing an adolescent self-report measure of social media experience: Insights from cognitive interviews
articles.authors: Jo Hickman Dunne; Louise Black; Jade Davies; Frederick Jones; Molly Anderton; Pratyasha Nanda; Felicitas Beissel; Lauren Burke; Reihaneh Farzinnia; Margarita Panayiotou
articles.abstract: Despite a rapid increase in research exploring the relationship between adolescent social media use and mental health, the field is hindered by poor quality tools that lack the validity and precision to assess this relationship. The current study presents findings from cognitive interviews that aimed to refine a multidimensional measure of adolescents’ social media experiences relevant to their mental health and wellbeing. We conducted 20 individual, paired or group interviews with 35 adolescents aged 11-16, across three rounds of interviews, testing 83 of a possible 107 items. Through iterative testing, issues relating to comprehension; inapplicability and assumptions within items; and items not addressing their intended experience, were identified and addressed. The interviews also highlighted two wider conceptual issues: (1) the impact of parental restrictions on adolescents’ experiences, and (2) difficulties in responding to items about abstract, identity-based experiences. In addition, the interviews supported an understanding of preferred response options and format. Findings from this study informed specific revisions to measure items to enhance validity, as well as broader considerations for assessing adolescent social media experience. Our study also reinforces the importance of cognitive interviewing in refining adolescent measures more broadly. We identify the need for the development of a set of general recommendations to guide item writing for adolescents, and further work to understand optimal response label options and wording for longer recall periods. Development of such guidance, alongside the greater use of cognitive interviews to pre-test measures, is crucial for improving instrument validity in the field of adolescent mental health.

articles.title: Understanding the role of generative artificial intelligence in mental health support: Survey of user experiences, engagement patterns, and perceived risks and benefits
articles.authors: Jake Linardon; Zoe McClure; Cleo Anderson; Claudia Liu; Olivia Marie Soliman; Mariel Messer
articles.abstract: Generative AI – especially ChatGPT – is increasingly used for mental health purposes, but users’ subjective experiences of these tools remain unclear. We characterized how individuals utilize ChatGPT for mental health support through a web-based survey completed by 308 adults (Mage=31.5, SD=5.3; 54% men) who reported prior use of this tool. Around half reported use of ChatGPT for mental health support more than once a week, 80% have used it for more than 3 months, and a third reported increased use over time. Depression (55%), anxiety (74%), stress (66%), and relationship conflict (49%) were the problems most frequently discussed with ChatGPT, with the severity of these problems typically rated as mildly or moderately severe. Endorsed reasons for use were its on-demand availability (71%), free cost (69%), and anonymous nature (54%), while common functions the platform served included obtaining advice (71%), providing a safe space for expression (63%), and to learn coping strategies (61%). Experiences were largely positive, with 8 in 10 agreeing that ChatGPT helped them feel understood, better process their emotions, and improve their mental health literacy. Concerns were also evident, with around half expressing worry about data privacy, and a quarter feeling overly reliant on the platform and reducing their motivation to seek help. Few indicated that ChatGPT had replaced professional help (7%) or discouraged help-seeking (12%). Findings shed light on how users are engaging with generative AI for mental health support and highlight the importance of rigorous research designed to evaluate its safety and long-term efficacy.

articles.title: The Description–Experience Gap in Loss Aversion
articles.authors: Nuno Busch; Thorsten Pachur
articles.abstract: Humans make different decisions under risk when they acquire information about their options through experience than when they learn it from a summary description. Research on this description–experience gap has largely focused on differences in probability weighting—for instance, how low-probability events are reflected in people’s decisions. Here, we show that the gap manifests much more broadly and also occurs with regard to the influence of outcomes. Specifically, we investigated how description- and experience-based decisions differ in loss aversion—the tendency for loss outcomes to have a greater impact on choice than equivalent gain outcomes. We first conducted a meta-reanalysis synthesizing raw data of all available datasets that directly compared description- and experience-based decisions involving mixed-domain lotteries (88,409 choices in total across N_Desc = 439 and N_Exp = 468). The results indicate that loss aversion, measured with cumulative prospect theory (CPT), is more pronounced in experience-based than in description-based choices. We then replicated this description–experience gap in loss aversion in a large-scale experiment with preregistered methods (19,435 choices by N_Desc = 202 and N_Exp = 202) tailored to address potential limitations of the studies included in the meta-analysis, and also showed the gap in an analysis that does not depend on estimating a latent loss aversion parameter. An analysis of the experience-based choices with a reinforcement learning model suggests that a possible mechanism for the apparently higher loss aversion in decisions from experience could be asymmetric learning after positive versus negative prediction errors during experiential sampling.

articles.title: In AI Do We Trust? Comparing a Transformer-Based Natural Language Processing Model Against a Traditional Content Analysis Approach to Qualitative Research
articles.authors: Matthew Baron; Catherine Stein
articles.abstract:
Central to debates about the use of artificial intelligence (AI) models for qualitative
research are concerns about comparability and trust in AI generated findings. The present
methodological study compared findings from a transformer-based Natural Language Processing
(NLP) model, BERT, against a traditional content analysis approach to qualitative research using
the same text data. We examined claims that AI models generate findings that are identical or
similar to traditional qualitative approaches. The study assessed three aspects of comparability
between the BERT model solution and human-coded findings that included topic labeling,
classification overlap, and AI replicability. Results indicated broad similarity in the semantic
meaning of topic categories generated by the BERT model and themes from content analysis.
There was low overlap in the classification of individual participant responses between BERT
and content analysis categories, even for categories similar in semantic meaning. Running the
BERT model a second time on the same input data resulted in differences in topic categories and
document classification between the two approaches. Study implications and research
recommendations for the use of NLP models are discussed.

articles.title: Social Support among LGBTQ, Cisgender, and Heterosexual Undergraduate Students:  An Ego-Centric Social Network Study
articles.authors: Allyson Marie Blackburn; Nathan Todd; Nicole Allen
articles.abstract: While the population and acceptance of LGBTQ people are growing, there are persistent mental health disparities for LGBTQ individuals, especially for emerging adults. Social support is critical for the promotion of well-being. Yet, who receives support and the nature of the support provided can vary based on social identity, including sexual orientation and gender identity. In this study, we demonstrate the benefit of using ego-centric social network analysis (ESNA) to advance research about emotional support for sexual minorities. Using a sample of 1,215 undergraduate students (253 sexual minorities) from a large Midwestern university, we show that sexual minorities reported a greater proportion of LGBTQ people yet a lower proportion of family in their social network. We also show that sexual minorities reported that they were less likely to receive support but were more likely to be nominated by both heterosexuals and sexual minorities as network members who provide support. Finally, sexual minority participants relied more on friends than parents for emotional support, whereas the opposite was true for heterosexual students. These (and other) findings show how ESNA allows for testing hypotheses that capture the interconnected context of relationships. We discuss how findings advance the literature along with limitations and implications. Overall, we show that ESNA is a valuable tool to use to understand social networks as a critical context for development and well-being.

articles.title: Towards a multi-component framework of grammar development: Links with rhythm processing and executive functions
articles.authors: Eniko Ladanyi; Christine S. Schipke; Agnieszka Hearder; Flavia Adani; Barbara Höhle; Natalie Boll-Avetisyan; Isabell Wartenburger
articles.abstract: Grammar acquisition is central to language development, yet its interplay with non-linguistic abilities such as executive functions (EFs) and rhythm processing remains unclear. Clarifying these relations is important for understanding the mechanisms underlying grammar development. In a preregistered individual-differences study, we examined whether EF and rhythm measures were uniquely associated with sentence comprehension in German-speaking children aged 6–8 years. Children completed three sentence–picture matching tasks targeting comprehension of atypical structures (object-initial declarative sentences and object-relative clauses), along with non-verbal EF tasks assessing inhibition (Flanker) and working memory updating (n-back), and with rhythm tasks assessing rhythm discrimination and rhythm synchronization tapping. Sentence comprehension was associated with both rhythm discrimination and inhibition when accounting for other non-linguistic abilities and covariates. However, the association with rhythm discrimination was substantially attenuated after controlling for short-term memory (digit-span). Together, these findings support a multi-component account of grammar development in which non-linguistic abilities, particularly inhibition, rhythm processing, and short-term memory, are linked with individual differences in grammar development.

articles.title: srifm: Role of lexical information for perceptual learning
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia; Annika Hultén; Holger Mitterer
articles.abstract: Linguistic representations continue to be updated, probably implicitly, as a side effect of normal language use. In particular, a large body of work shows that we learn novel pronunciations of well-established phonemic categories rapidly (Norris, McQueen, & Cutler, 2003). This learning is thought to be automatic, such that it operates quickly once there is sufficient information to disambiguate the identity of that novel pronunciation: Effects are seen after encountering 10 instances of the ambiguous sound within unambiguous lexical items. Here, we uses perceptual learning to test predictions from two types of theories of speech perception, lexical feedback models (e.g., TRACE, McClelland & Elman, 1986; Magnuson et al., 2003) and autonomous models (e.g., Shortlist, Norris, 1994; Merge, McQueen & Cutler, 2010). According to TRACE, phonemes, and words are tracked in the input in parallel, and decisions at both of these levels are influenced online by the other levels. In this model, disambiguation is driven by the lexical level. In contrast, Merge postulates that listeners accumulate knowledge of sublexical representations, such as diphone probabilities, in addition to lexical knowledge.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of care-resistant behavior in dementia patients on nurses’ occupational burnout: A comment on Ding et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Ding et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking care-resistant behavior in dementia patients to nurses’ occupational burnout. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported care-resistant behavior, psychological detachment, professional calling, and occupational burnout are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Cross-linguistic affective iconicity
articles.authors: José Antonio Hinojosa; Daniele Gatti
articles.abstract: Whether relationships between word form and affect reflect shared human constraints or language-specific conventions remains largely unresolved. Addressing this, here we tested whether affective mappings learned in one language zero-shot predict estimations for the emotional dimensions of valence and arousal in another using 85,375 lexical entries from ten languages diverse in origin and culture across eight (sub)lexical representations spanning orthographic, phonological, articulatory, and distributional semantic information. Results revealed a strong semantic transfer, greater for valence than arousal, while form-based transfer was smaller but consistently above zero across all seven representations for arousal, with the strongest effects for articulatory features. Language-distance analyses further revealed that valence-related orthographic and phoneme-bigram transfer was stronger between more closely related languages, particularly genealogically and the modest correspondence between fitted form coefficients indicated that transferable prediction coexisted with differences in feature weighting across languages. These findings characterize affective iconicity as graded and representation-dependent: valence generalizes most strongly through distributional meaning, whereas arousal leaves a more consistent cross-linguistic trace in word form. This pattern motivates an account in which culturally and historically shaped evaluative mappings coexist with activation-related mappings that may draw more broadly on shared embodied constraints, connecting linguistic form with the conceptual organization of affective experience.

articles.title: Using conversational artificial intelligence to dissect the psychoneuroimmunology of social safety and threat
articles.authors: Julian Packheiser; Sigrid Elsenbruch; Harald Engler; Dirk Scheele
articles.abstract: Human health is profoundly shaped by the quality of our social environments, yet the mechanisms through which social experiences become biologically embedded remain poorly understood. Social Safety Theory (SST) proposes that perceived social safety and threat influence health through neuroendocrine and immune pathways, but it remains unclear which features of social interaction engage these pathways. Here, we argue that conversational artificial intelligence (AI) provides a powerful experimental tool to address this mechanistic gap. Synthetic agents allow researchers to systematically vary core social signals, including responsiveness, reciprocity, empathic cues, agency, and multimodal information, while holding other features of the interaction relatively constant. This controllability creates a unique opportunity to identify which social signals are necessary or sufficient to generate perceived safety or threat and to engage downstream biological responses. Building on SST, we propose a psychoneuroimmunological framework linking experimentally controlled features of synthetic social interaction to neuroendocrine and immune processes and derive testable hypotheses concerning perceived humanness, social-signal strength, and multimodal embodiment. By enabling the causal decomposition of social interaction, conversational AI could help reveal what makes an interaction biologically social and clarify the mechanisms linking social disconnection to health.

articles.title: Re. The influence of personality on the risk of myocardial infarction in UK Biobank cohort
articles.authors: Alexander Weiss
articles.abstract: Dahlén, Miguet, Schiöth, and Rukh1 used items from UK Biobank2 to construct “proxies” of the five domains of human personality—Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Extraversion, and Openness3. However, the items used came from an existing Neuroticism scale. In my analyses, I demonstrated that the discriminant validities of these proxies are poor, and so should not be used to study personality in UK Biobank or any other dataset.

articles.title: A Risk-Formulation Framework and Candidate Screening Items for Dangerous Use of Large Language Models in Clinical Psychiatry
articles.authors: Armando N. Braz; Punit Matta; Joshuah Muthee; Eren M Veziroglu; Daniel Price
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and related conversational artificial intelligence (AI) systems have moved rapidly from novelty into ordinary use across education, work, social life, and mental-health-related help seeking. Members of the public now use these systems for advice, companionship, self-disclosure, emotional support, psychoeducation, and quasi-therapeutic interactions. Existing instruments assess problematic or dependent AI use, but they do not ask whether AI has entered a pathway toward serious harm by entrenching ideation, operationalizing capability, displacing human support, or amplifying harmful conduct. To our knowledge, no brief, clinically oriented psychiatric screener has yet been developed and validated specifically for this purpose. We define dangerous AI use as generative AI use that appears to increase the likelihood, feasibility, persistence, organization, or scale of serious harm to self or others. This paper describes LLMs as interactive capability amplifiers and quasi-social systems rather than informational technologies alone, situates their risk within the technical problems of alignment and behavioral stability, and proposes a four-dimensional clinical formulation: Ideational Entrenchment, Operationalized Capability, Relational Displacement, and Broader Amplification. We then introduce two candidate instruments awaiting formal validation: the STEPS-5, a brief screen for AI involvement in acute self-harm and suicide risk, and the HEAT-4, a research-oriented framework addressing broader harmful-use amplification. These tools are intended to open clinical inquiry rather than diagnose, predict behavior, or determine disposition. Ultimately, we argue for the need to avoid both over-pathologizing ordinary AI use and ignoring when AI has become meaningfully relevant to psychiatric safety.

articles.title: Jargon as a Psychological Construct? A Multidecade Analysis of Communication Failure in Evaluation Reports
articles.authors: John Hite
articles.abstract: For seven decades, studies have asked whether the people who receive psychological evaluation reports understand what they say. Existing research has largely measured reader satisfaction rather than what readers comprehend, recall, or interpret. This narrative synthesis identified six studies, conducted between 1984 and 2025 in school psychology and, most recently, child neuropsychology, in which 253 readers were assigned to a standard-format report and had their comprehension scored directly. Comprehension ranged from 46.6% to 61.1% (weighted mean = 55.2%) and showed no detectable change across four decades. In every study that also scored an accessible version of the same report, readers understood it better, with scores from 60% to 82%. Recent evidence from pediatric neuropsychology shows the same gap: parents rated their understanding of their child's report highly, yet almost half could not state the child's diagnoses without error. Effective formats combined plain-language wording with one or more of domain-based organization, concrete behavioral examples, and elaborated recommendations. These findings suggest that jargon-related comprehension failure is a persistent, measurable, and modifiable problem spanning specialties within psychology. Implications for training, supervision, and evidence-based communication practice across school and clinical psychology are discussed.

articles.title: How to Select, Retain, Delete and Replace Items in IRT-Based Scale Development: A Multi-Criteria Framework for Psychometric Optimisation
articles.authors: Enoch Oluwatomiwo Oladunmoye
articles.abstract: Decisions about which items to keep, delete or replace shape the validity, precision and fairness of a scale, yet they are still often made with single statistics, such as the lowest discrimination parameter or the change in Cronbach’s alpha after deletion. This study proposes a multi-criteria framework for item decisions under Item Response Theory (IRT) and examines by simulation how single-criterion rules compare with it. Evidence is organised into six domains (information and targeting, model fit, local dependence and redundancy, differential item functioning, response categories, and content representation) and combined through a flag, investigate, compare and decide sequence. Counterfactual deletion and replacement are formalised as a purpose-weighted, constrained optimisation, and an Item Utility Profile is proposed as a decision aid rather than an index. A Monte Carlo study (500 replications) generated 60-item, six-domain two-parameter logistic pools containing locally dependent pairs and items labelled as functioning differently across groups. Five strategies for choosing 24 items were compared under two measurement purposes. Classical and slope-based rules each retained about four DIF-labelled items among the 24 chosen, and kept between 2.8 and 3.8 of six redundant pairs intact on average. An information-only rule left a content domain empty in 33% of replications when precision was needed near a screening threshold. The multi-criteria strategy kept about one DIF-labelled item, fewer than one redundant pair and every domain, at a cost of 13% to 17% of nominal weighted information. Conclusions. Item deletion is better handled as a documented measurement-design decision than as a statistical filter. The simulation is illustrative and uses known item parameters, so its findings need confirmation with estimated parameters and empirical data.

articles.title: The Global Measure of Masturbation Satisfaction (GMMAST): Scale Development and Preliminary Validation
articles.authors: David Cornelius de Jong; Nantje Fischer; Maximiliane Uhlich
articles.abstract:
Solo masturbation is a common sexual behavior, but its role in well-being is poorly understood.
One reason is that the extant literature has generally focused on how engagement in masturbation
(e.g., in the past 4 weeks) relates to well-being while neglecting how the subjective experience of
masturbation (e.g., as valuable and positive, or not) might impact well-being. This report
describes the development of the brief, five-item Global Measure of Masturbation Satisfaction
(GMMAST). The measure was developed using a sample of 2,486 adults who had masturbated
in the past month, drawn from the Masturbation and Sexual Health Survey, a U.S. national
survey. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, and tests of measurement invariance,
suggested the scale has strong psychometric properties. Associations with related constructs
(e.g., positive and negative masturbation attitudes, masturbation motives, receipt of sexual
education) provide preliminary evidence of validity.

articles.title: Perceived parents’ relationship quality and young adults’ dating experiences
articles.authors: Le Hoai Linh Vu; Aida Fernandez-Jimenez; Savannah M. Bodden; Simran Rooprai; Nicholas Daniel Ramcharran; Michael Petrovski; Aldo Spina; Sintayehu Daba Wami; Joseph FX DeSouza
articles.abstract: Based on the combination of attachment theory, social learning theory and family system theory, the purpose of this survey study is to examine the influence of the quality of interparental relationships on the early dating experiences of young adults, as well as to investigate the mediating role of parent-child bonds in this association. Data was collected from 122 York University undergraduate students (mean age 19.4 years) through an online survey portal (QuestionPro). Perceived parents’ levels of conflict and affection were measured with adapted Children’s Perception of Interparental Conflict Scale (CPIC) and Dyadic Adjustment Scale (DAS). Parental Bonding Instrument (PBI) was used to measure parent-child bond, while dating experiences were evaluated using Relationship Assessment Scale (RAS) and modified Conflict Tactics Scale (CTS2-Short). Correlational analysis and structural equation modelling (SEM) were conducted to analyze the data. It was found that higher perceived parental conflict predicted worse mother-child and father-child bonds. Neither parental relationship quality nor parent-child bonds significantly predicted relationship satisfaction or constructive conflict behaviours. Mediation effects were not supported. In conclusion, the findings indicate that the early perceptions of parents' relationship quality may not influence young adults’ early dating experiences; however, it may predict the bond between parents and child.

articles.title: Feasibility and acceptability of smartwatch-delivered micro-ecological momentary assessment (µEMA) during in situ exercise among breast cancer survivors
articles.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Aislinn E. Mitcham; Paget E. Chung; Carly Bobak; Hannah C. Edmonds; Sivakumar P. Kandasamy; Calie S. Sorenson; Hollin R. Hakimian; Kathleen Doyle Lyons; Amanda J. Emerson
articles.abstract:
Objectives. Micro-ecological momentary assessment (µEMA) facilitates in-real-time data capture using succinct prompts delivered to a smartwatch. µEMA overcomes limitations of smartphone-based EMA for activities where carrying a smartphone would be burdensome/impractical. To date, µEMA during exercise has only been conducted with younger, non-clinical samples. We evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of µEMA during in situ, self-directed exercise among breast cancer survivors within 5-years of completing cancer treatment.

Method. A µEMA app was installed on Fitbit Versa 3 smartwatches. N = 27 stage 0-III breast cancer survivors enrolled and 22 (81.5%) submitted ratings of affective response (via modified Feeling Scale) and physical effort (via modified Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale) during exercise sessions completed over 10 consecutive days. Feasibility was assessed as µEMA app response rates. Acceptability was assessed via User-Friendliness Scale ratings from daily dairy surveys as well as System Usability Scale (SUS) scores and exit interviews collected at end-of-study.

Results. Participants (Mage = 60.8 years, SD = 11.5) completed M = 4.7 (SD = 2.4) exercise sessions (walking most common) while responding to µEMA. The overall µEMA response rate across all exercise sessions was 77.7% (SD = 19.5). SUS scores (M = 82.9, SD = 15.5) exceeded the threshold for adequate usability (i.e., ≥ 68) and overall average person-weighted user-friendliness was ‘satisfactory’—‘good,’ M = 4.7 (SD = 1.1). Interviews revealed preference for µEMA over smartphone-based EMA during exercise. Notably, some technical issues were common. 

Conclusions. Results support the feasibility and acceptability of µEMA during in situ exercise among breast cancer survivors.

articles.title: Synthometricon: A search engine to identify conceptual overlap in measures in the behavioral sciences
articles.authors: Björn Erik Hommel; Annika Iris Külpmann; Ruben C. Arslan
articles.abstract: Every month, scores of new measures and constructs enter the behavioral science literature. Researchers struggle to keep an overview of their subfields, let alone the wider field, with an estimated number of allegedly different constructs now exceeding 30,000. Proposing constructs is easy, finding redundancies and overlaps is not. The effort of finding redundancies using participant responses grows quadratically with the number of measures. This cost motivates the use of language models, which can simplify and speed up the process without requiring new data collection. Earlier work employed latent semantic analysis (LSA) to make use of the textual nature of questionnaires in the social and behavioral sciences. However, LSA treats sentences as bags of words and ignores word order, syntax, and negation, all of which shape how respondents interpret items. Recent advances demonstrate that transformer-based sentence embedding models offer a more viable solution for predicting empirical relatedness between survey items. In the presented work, we use a fine-tuned language model, the SurveyBot3000, to introduce the Synthometricon, an open-access web application for systematic detection of conceptual overlap. The application indexes over 570,000 items across more than 97,000 scales from approximately 28,000 instruments in the APA PsycTests database and other sources.

articles.title: Understanding Medical Invalidation from the Patient Perspective: A Qualitative Interview Study Across Diseases and Healthcare Settings
articles.authors: Seraina Petra Lerch
articles.abstract:
Objective 
Research on patients feeling that their symptoms are not taken seriously (medical invalidation) has predominantly focused on individual diseases. This study explored patients' experiences across different medical conditions and healthcare contexts to identify common characteristics, contributing factors, consequences, and opportunities for prevention. 
Methods
The study was conducted in Germany between January and March 2025 using interviews undertaken remotely or in person. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis following Kuckartz and Rädiker. Thirty-one adults (≥18 years) with self-reported experiences of not being taken seriously in healthcare were purposively recruited through patient organisations and social media to achieve maximum variation regarding symptoms and diagnoses.
Results
Participants described not being taken seriously as a cross-cutting healthcare phenomenon occurring across diverse symptoms, diagnoses, medical specialties, and healthcare settings. Experiences ranged from isolated encounters to cumulative processes that developed over repeated interactions with healthcare professionals (HCPs). Contributing factors were perceived at multiple levels, including healthcare system, HCPs, patient, disease, and interactional factors, which frequently interacted. Consequences extended beyond the initial consultation and included psychological distress, loss of trust, delayed or inappropriate diagnosis and treatment, reduced healthcare utilisation, occupational consequences, and impaired social well-being. Participants identified opportunities for prevention at different levels, highlighting structured feedback mechanisms. 
Conclusions
Medical invalidation is a multifactorial phenomenon that extends across diseases and healthcare settings. Patients emphasized that medical invalidation depends not only on clinical decision-making but on being heard, having their illness perceptions acknowledged, and receiving transparent communication. Strengthening these elements of patient-centred care may improve healthcare experiences.

articles.title: Congenital visual impairment does not impede the development of infants’ ability to reach to the self
articles.authors: GIULIA CAPPAGLI; Matej Hoffmann; Lisa K Chinn; Jason A.M. Khoury; Jeffrey J. Lockman; Sabrina Signorini; gori monica
articles.abstract: While early visual deprivation can hinder some spatial skills, it can also lead to sensory enhancements. Evidence from visually impaired infants is sparse but suggests preserved unisensory orienting and greater reliance on touch alongside reduced multisensory spatial integration and delayed spatially guided action.1,2 Reaching to touch on the body is a spatial task requiring touch to be remapped relative to body posture. Visual impairment could therefore delay this ability if vision calibrates spatial representations, or preserve or enhance it if attention to somatosensory input supports compensation. We tested sighted, low-vision, and blind infants (6–24 months) reaching to vibrotactile targets. Reaching success was comparable across groups and increased with age. Low-vision infants reached more slowly than sighted infants, whereas blind infants did not differ from sighted infants. Thus, body-centered tactile localization can develop without typical visual experience, although degraded visual input may selectively slow somatosensory guidance of action.

articles.title: A Megastudy of Behavioral Interventions to Increase Voter Registration Ahead of the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Katherine Anne Mason; Kayley Okst; Don Green; Robb Willer; James Druckman; Jan G. Voelkel; Yash Patel; Claire Robertson; Wooyoung Choi; Jasmine Sanchez
articles.abstract: In the United States, voter registration is required for participation in most elections, yet many eligible individuals remain unregistered. Relatively little is known about how to increase the likelihood that an eligible adult registers to vote. We evaluated 10 expert-crowdsourced interventions among eligible but unregistered U.S. voters (N = 12,927) in an online survey experiment conducted before the 2024 presidential election. The study was powered to detect small attitudinal effects and effects on voter registration and turnout of roughly 3 percentage points. Nine interventions increased self-reported voting intentions, and five increased clicks on the official voter registration website. Escalating Commitment, a social pressure strategy, produced the largest absolute effect on these proximal outcomes. However, none of the interventions significantly increased voter registration or turnout. These findings highlight the challenge of translating shifts in intention into registration behavior, but also identify potentially promising messaging strategies for future large-scale field evaluation.

articles.title: Caregiver prosody coincides with infant sustained visual attention
articles.authors: Manash Sahoo; Valerie Bambha; Chen Yu; Linda B. Smith; Jeremy Isaac Borjon
articles.abstract: Prosodic modifications in caregiver speech are related to infant attention, word learning, and long-term language development, yet how moment-to-moment caregiver prosody relates to infant attentional dynamics during naturalistic interaction remains unclear. Here, we used unsupervised learning to categorize 12,311 caregiver utterances produced during free play across the second year of life (12-24 months) into four prosodic contour types: fall, hill, rise, and valley. Infant visual attention was measured using head-mounted eye-tracking. Proportions of contour types were stable from 12 to 24 months. Despite this stability, specific contours were temporally coordinated with the onset and offset of infant sustained visual attention (SVA). Rise contours coincided with the initiation of SVA in older infants, beginning approximately one second before onset, and valley contours coincided with the period following SVA offset in both age groups. At the dyad level, two patterns emerged. Caregivers who produced higher levels of vocalizations that coincided with the onset or offset of SVA had infants with more SVA episodes and total SVA time overall. Further, caregivers who exhibited a specific prosodic pattern in the two seconds following SVA disengagement, a fall contour in the first second and a valley contour in the following second, had infants with longer average SVA episodes.  These results dissociate two facets of dyadic temporal coordination: a broad association between caregiver prosody and the quantity of SVA episodes, and a specific post-disengagement prosodic pattern linked to the duration of SVA.

articles.title: Orthographic retrieval unfolds in parallel with single-word production
articles.authors: Jens Roeser; Pablo Aros Muñoz; Markus Damian; Gary Jones; Mark Torrance
articles.abstract: Written word production is often assumed to begin after the relevant spelling has been retrieved. We challenge this pre-onset assumption by asking whether spelling-related processing can continue during output. Across four picture-word interference experiments (Ns = 60, 72, 96, 93), participants typed or spoke picture names while ignoring pronounceable non-word distractors. Distractors either preserved the target-compatible spelling pattern or introduced a phonologically plausible alternative spelling; only the latter should disrupt writing if phonology makes alternative spellings relevant during orthographic retrieval. Bayesian mixed-effects mixture models estimated the probability that response-onset latencies and post-onset intervals came from a longer-duration component. Spelling-mismatch distractors sometimes facilitated onset responses but increased long-duration probability at later timings and within typed words. These late mismatch effects disappeared for spoken responses. These time-course data challenge the classical assumption that written words are mentally prepared as complete spellings before output begins; instead, orthographic retrieval can remain vulnerable to phonologically plausible alternatives during written production.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of artificial intelligence anxiety on academic burnout: A comment on Long et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Long et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking artificial intelligence anxiety to academic burnout. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported artificial intelligence anxiety, perceived stress, rumination, and academic burnout are conceptualized as negative indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Sampling Thoughts During Music Listening: A Systematic Comparison of Probe-caught, Self-caught and Retrospective Thought Reporting Methods
articles.authors: Nao Toyama; Kelly Jakubowski
articles.abstract: Music listening experiences dynamically unfold over time. However, as previous research has relied predominantly on short music excerpts and retrospective post-listening self-reports, how qualitative thought content unfolds during extended listening remains underexplored. Crucially, addressing this requires effective real-time sampling, yet direct empirical comparisons of such methods––i.e., experimenter-led versus participant-led approaches––and their impact on data quality and listener experience are remain lacking. To address these gaps, the present study systematically compared three experience-sampling methodologies (probe-caught, self-caught, and a retrospective control) using participants’ own smartphones during an 18-minute video of a classical music performance. While the control group yielded significantly fewer thoughts, both experimental groups (probe- and self-caught) reported a comparable total number of thoughts. The probe-caught method exhibited greater inter-participant stability and generated significantly more detailed qualitative descriptions. Importantly, participants’ subjective perceived interference on their listening experience was low and did not differ across groups, confirming that real-time thought reporting did not disrupt the natural listening experience compared with traditional retrospective reporting. By validating the efficiency, stability, and minimal invasiveness of the probe-caught method, this study provides an empirical foundation for future research investigating real-time subjective experiences across diverse listening environments.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of police work stress on life satisfaction: A comment on Qiu et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Qiu et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking police work stress to decreased life satisfaction. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported police work stress, perceived social support, sleep disturbance, and life satisfaction are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: Made in the Culture, Not the Voice: Lyrical Camp, Production Texture, and the Queer Anthemization of Popular Songs
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Why do some popular songs become queer anthems while others, including many by openly queer artists, do not? We tested musical affordance and historical contingency accounts in a purposive corpus of 100 songs (69 artists) designed to dissociate queer authorship, explicit queer lyrical content, and community adoption. Adoption was measured as an evidence-coded anthemization score from URL-verified documentation of Pride, drag, ballroom, club, activist, and queer-media use. Anthemization was unrelated to whether artists were publicly queer (rs = −.02) and only weakly related to explicit queer lyrics (rs = .22). Among 16 language-model-coded lyrical themes, camp potential predicted anthemization after family-wise correction and controls for era, genre, authorship, and explicit content (partial r = .40, n = 55). The association replicated with masked lyrics, among songs the coding model could not identify, with a second coding model, and with two independent outcome coders (partial r = .45–.54, n = 46), although it was not robust when the model's own anthem judgements were also partialled out. Full-mix acoustic descriptors related to formant energy and voicing predicted anthemization (|rs| = .38–.43, family-wise p < .05) but vanished when computed on Demucs-separated vocal stems (n = 80), locating the acoustic signal in production texture rather than the singer's voice; spectral brightness was confounded by genre and era. Outcome reliability was moderate (weighted κ = .57). The results support reception-centred accounts of musical queerness. They implicate lyrical camp and production as affordances for queer adoption, not a characteristic queer voice.

articles.title: Willpower or Choice? A Within-Country, Cross-Linguistic Comparison of Free Will Judgments
articles.authors: Alison Oliver; Paulius Rimkevičius; Renato Cesar Cardoso; Marcel Brass; Uri Maoz
articles.abstract: Does the language we speak influence how we think about free will? Previous work has often compared free will judgments across linguistic and cultural groups without isolating language from broader cultural differences. More recent work has found cross-cultural variation, but these designs could not determine whether language itself contributed to that variation. Here we report two exploratory studies in which language was varied while culture was held relatively constant. In Study 1, monolingual English- and French-speaking Canadians rated comics depicting choice and willpower on whether they represent free will. The English phrase free will makes will, and so willpower, salient; the French phrase libre arbitre makes choice salient (as in “to arbitrate”). If language shapes the concept, English-speakers should associate free will relatively more with willpower, and French-speakers relatively more with choice. They did not: the two groups showed almost exactly the same preference for choice, and equivalence testing rules out anythingbeyond a small difference. Study 2 asked why choice comics were favored. Participants rated thesame comics on choice, willpower, doing what one wants, and absence of constraints. Across thenine comics, free will judgments closely tracked ratings of doing what one wants and of choice, but tracked absence of constraints less closely. Free will might therefore be associated most closely with choice and doing what one wants.

articles.title: Wrong Note, Wrong Time: Age and Musicianship-Related Influences on Rhythmic and Melodic Timing
articles.authors: Logan Barrett; Sarah Anne Sauvé; Andrea Rita Halpern; Benjamin Zendel
articles.abstract: Musical expectancy theory posits that listeners anticipate both the pitch that will occur and when it will occur; however, the interaction between these dimensions across age and expertise is less understood. In this study, 175 adults (ages 18–82; musicians and non-musicians) rated the final note of short monophonic melodies on its melodic and temporal fit. Endings were systematically manipulated in terms of pitch (tonal, chromatic, or atonal) and timing deviations. Results showed a strong effect of melodic expectancy: pitch deviations substantially reduced goodness-of-fit ratings, whereas timing shifts had comparatively weak effects. Musicians gave lower ratings overall, indicating heightened sensitivity to expectancy violations, whereas non-musicians were more lenient. Although age alone did not predict ratings, an age × musician interaction emerged: older musicians diverged most strongly from older non-musician peers, suggesting that expertise sharpens expectancy sensitivity across the lifespan. These findings demonstrate that pitch dominates expectancy judgments, while also revealing how aging and musicianship jointly influence the perception of musical errors—an area that remains underexplored in music cognition.

articles.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to estimate how common alcohol references and alcohol-related brand references are among influencers on Instagram
articles.authors: Jack Delmenico; Dan Anderson-Luxford; Emmanuel Kuntsche; Jingda Du; Zhen Du; Megan Cook; Charlotte Jonhston; Paula O'Brien; Simone Pettigrew; Benjamin Riordan
articles.abstract:
Background: Young people spend hours on social media every day, where following influencers is the norm. Influencers post frequently about alcohol and alcohol brands and there has been a rise in influencer marketing. However, prevalence estimates rely on manual analyses of only a small number of posts. We used a large language model (LLM) to estimate at scale how often top Australian Instagram influencers reference alcohol and alcohol brands, and whether this varies by influencer type.
Methods: We identified 988 of the most-followed Australian Instagram influencers and retrieved all 667,531 of their posts that were visible to all users, including those under 18 (i.e., not age gated). An LLM classified whether each post referenced alcohol and these were screened manually to record brand references. Influencers were coded into 14 types (e.g., athletes, actors).
Results: Most influencers (87.45%) referenced alcohol and 47.10% referenced an alcohol brand in at least one post. Overall, 20,448 posts (3.06%) referenced alcohol and 2,869 (0.43%) a brand (14% of alcohol-related posts). Food influencers posted the most alcohol and brand-related content, while athletes posted the least alcohol-related content but had the highest proportion referencing a brand.
Conclusions: Influencer alcohol-related and alcohol-related brand content is pervasive on Instagram and reaches audiences of every age, including those under 18 who should not see alcohol advertising.
So what: Given the link between exposure and use, health promotion should aim policies and strategies at reducing alcohol-related content, particularly branded content that likely reflects influencer marketing.

articles.title: How Adults in Spain Perceive Love:  Individual Differences in Cultural Attunement and Evaluative Style
articles.authors: Saida Heshmati; Lindy Williams; Dana Hussein; Jaymes Paolo Rombaoa; Royce Anders; Zita Oravecz
articles.abstract: Love is culturally universal in presence, yet highly variable in how people perceive it. The present study examined individual differences in cultural attunement and judgment styles related to love. Adults (N = 502) living in Spain rated 61 everyday scenarios according to how likely each would make most people feel loved. Using the Continuous Response Model within Cultural Consensus Theory, we captured individuals’ alignment with the shared understanding of love (i.e., their cultural attunement) in Spanish culture. Greater attunement was observed among women, individuals with higher perceived support from a significant other, those with lower anxiety, and those who valued benevolence. Weaker attunement, on the other hand, was associated with endorsement of power and traditional values. In addition, individuals differed in how they expressed their judgments: older adults and men used a narrower range of responses, whereas those higher in extraversion and conscientiousness showed greater differentiation across scenarios. More educated individuals were less likely to judge situations as loving overall, whereas those higher in agreeableness were more likely to do so. These findings highlight that judgments of love experiences reflect not only shared cultural knowledge but also systematic individual differences in how that knowledge is applied.

articles.title: When Humor Lands or Flops: Exploring Positive and Negative Aspects of Dad Joke Experiences
articles.authors: Paul Joseph Silvia; Vi Bui
articles.abstract: What do people experience when they encounter jokes? Feelings of comic amusement—finding something funny—are the heart of effective humor, but emotional reactions to humor can be complex, as studies of sexual, disparaging, dark, and cringe humor have found. The present research explored a range of experiences to dad jokes, a joke genre marked by clean, affable content and comedic devices founded on wordplay, particularly puns and literalism. A sample of adults (n = 541) read 24 jokes from a large pool and rated each one on several dimensions (funny, interesting, irritating, boring, and confusing). Individual differences in these joke experiences formed two factors related to appeal and aversion, and stable lasso models found that people who found the jokes more appealing were distinguished by demographic features (having children and being more educated, religious, and subjectively affluent), humor self-concepts (identifying as a funny person and having a background in humor), and personality traits (being higher in agreeableness and lower in openness to experience). No stable predictors were found for joke aversiveness. The findings support the 3-WD model of humor, which proposes funniness and aversiveness as general dimensions of humor experience, and illustrate the value of studying specific joke genres instead of an abstract category of verbal humor.

articles.title: Accounts Balanced: The Contingent Role of Rhetoric in Who Survives Political Scandal
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Marti Hope Gonzales; Allison Williams; Elliot Weiner; Rafael Aguilera
articles.abstract: When accused of misconduct in their private or public lives, people choose whether to apologize or to defend their character or reputation. Previous experiments have found that when misconduct is severe or offends outgroup members, transgressors may benefit by defending themselves and denying culpability for wrongdoing. In this study, we explore whether these tendencies can successfully reduce politicians’ accountability for wrongdoing in the context of a U.S. congressional election. We constructed a novel dataset documenting Representatives’ public remarks in response the 1992 House Bank Scandal, during which Representatives from both major parties were accused of misusing funds. Contrary to predictions, conciliatory remarks were not associated with electoral failure among more severe House Bank “offenders.” Consistent with predictions, defensive remarks (refusals) lost their typical association with electoral failure when the incumbent’s party controlled the district. Results suggest that groups may allow their leaders to escape blame for wrongdoing and retain power.

articles.title: Estimand or estimator? Comparing vowel overlap measures against a known ground truth
articles.authors: Grant M Berry
articles.abstract: Deciding how much two vowel categories overlap is a core problem in laboratory phonology and sociophonetics, and the field has proposed several metrics to quantify overlap: the Pillai trace, Bhattacharyya distance, and Euclidean distance, among others. Researchers rarely compute multiple metrics on the same data, and what look like distinct overlap definitions are sometimes different estimates of the same quantity. I introduce Phontrast, an open-source R toolkit that computes multiple overlap metrics on the same tokens, and I simulate distributions with known overlap to disentangle each measure's estimator from its estimand. Two public vowel corpora show how measures behave on real data, in F1 × F2 space and thirteen-dimensional MFCC space. Mean- or Gaussian-based measures are precise but unresponsive to separation in higher moments. Kernel estimates are biased and bandwidth-dependent, but within the simulation's operating region they recover the ordering on average, whatever the mechanism. Pillai is the most precise for small samples and whenever separation is driven by means. Since this is rarely known a priori, I foreground Jensen–Shannon distance, a distribution-free distance between the two vowels' probability distributions that registers separation however it arises, for ordering speakers and contrasts—with Pillai beside it to show movement in category means.

articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones

articles.title: Cultural and Personality Predictors of Attitudes Toward AI Chatbots: A Systematic Literature  Review
articles.authors: Michelle Ming Ertl; Katherine Moore
articles.abstract:
As AI chatbots are becoming increasingly relevant in our daily life, understanding what shapes
people’s attitudes toward them is becoming more important. This systematic literature review
brings together the findings of 34 articles (from across multiple countries) to examine how
personality traits and one’s cultural background predict attitudes towards AI chatbots. The
review suggests that culture works as a primary filter that sets a person’s starting position when
they encounter AI. Western users tend to approach chatbots with more skepticism and stronger
privacy concerns, while on the other hand East Asian users show higher comfort with social AI
interaction. Within each of these cultural settings, individual personality traits fine-tune these
responses, but which trait matters most changes depending on the culture. Agreeableness
drives trust in Western samples, while Conscientiousness drives trust in Arab ones. Technology
specific variables like Personal Innovativeness in Information Technology (PIIT) and AI
configuration anxiety turned out to be stronger predictors than broad personality traits overall.
The review also identifies a persistent global gender gap in AI adaptation that operates
differently depending on cultural setting. Limitations include the overrepresentation of young
university educated participants in existing research, the Western bias present in both study
samples and AI training data, and the ongoing confusion between physical robot findings and
text-based chatbot research. The paper concludes that effective chatbot design and AI policy
require culturally adapted approaches rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

articles.title: Caregivers’ multimodal actions scaffold word learning in the preschool years
articles.authors: Antonia Jordan-Barros; Francesco Cabiddu; Ed Donnellan; Yan Gu; Gabriella Vigliocco
articles.abstract: Children learn language in face-to-face interactions with their caregivers where they are continuously exposed to multimodal input in which verbal content is combined with non-verbal signals (e.g., caregivers looking and pointing at an object while naming it). However, little is known about how caregivers’ use of the full range of multimodal behaviours is linked to children’s word learning. Using the ECOLANG Corpus, we examined how caregivers’ multimodal behaviours predict children’s word learning during a semi-naturalistic parent-child interaction. Thirty-seven caregivers (age: 29-48, 36 female; British and American English speakers) interacted with their child (age: 3-4, 19 female) talking about 12 unknown objects for 30 minutes. Caregivers’ verbal (e.g., label repetitions, speaking rate) and non-verbal (e.g., points, gaze, gestures) behaviours were annotated and used as predictors in regression analyses of children’s learning of the novel object labels along with child vocabulary scores. Results showed that, in the verbal domain, caregivers’ use of high pitch and more lexically diverse speech were associated with better word learning, while caregivers’ use of representational gestures was a significant non-verbal predictor. In particular, using more representational gestures when labelling unknown objects predicted better word learning specifically for children with lower vocabulary scores, suggesting that non-verbal cues such as manual gestures can provide additional support for children with less advanced linguistic abilities. This work presents the first comprehensive investigation of the combined role of verbal and non-verbal caregivers’ behaviours and provides robust evidence that multimodal caregiver communication can shape preschool-aged children’s lexical development.

articles.title: ‘The difference between us is that I am an optimist and you are a pessimist.’ An autoethnographic study on suppression of critical scholarship
articles.authors: P. Matthijs Bal; Mehmet A. Orhan; Yvonne van Rossenberg
articles.abstract: Critical scholarship constitutes an important part of business and management research, including related fields such as work psychology. However, critical work is also often met with resistance from colleagues and gatekeepers within the discipline. Yet, there is little insight into how this resistance manifests in daily academic practice. This autoethnographic study by multiple critical scholars in work and organizational psychology analyzed 34 events whereby their critical work was suppressed and silenced. Thematic analysis of the events revealed ten different mechanisms through which critical work is suppressed, which could be ordered within four sequential stages of suppression: closing space, discrediting work, discrediting research(-ers), and disciplinary control. Jointly, these stages represent an escalating process of how alternative perspectives, including critical work, are suppressed and silenced in hegemonic fields. The paper contributes to existing critical scholarship by being the first to empirically elucidate how and through which strategies critical work is silenced. The study has important implications not only for the development of critical perspectives within scientific fields, but also for academia more widely, as political and societal forces that undermine academic freedom call for a better understanding of how critical work is suppressed, and how it could be nurtured for a more dignified, equal, and democratic society.

articles.title: Two sides of the same coin in memory: Speech and its accompanying gesture are remembered together
articles.authors: Yang Liu; Tilo Kircher; Luyao Chen; Yifei He; Benjamin Straube
articles.abstract: When a speaker gestures, speech and gesture form one multimodal event. Memory research mostly asks how gestures help people remember speech, not how the gesture is remembered or how the two relate. Participants watched videos of an actor speaking sentences with a related gesture or none (Experiment 1, N = 20), or a related or unrelated gesture (Experiment 2, N = 43). They recognized written sentences and, for each called old, judged whether a gesture had been present (Experiment 1) or related (Experiment 2), with confidence ratings. Recognition was better after related than unrelated gestures, but not better after related gestures than none. Gesture judgments were above chance and more accurate for confidently recognized sentences; for these, participants also tended to report non-matching gestures as matching (Experiment 2). Gesture reports thus appear partly retrieved with the sentence and partly inferred from it: memory for speech and gesture is closely coupled.

articles.title: Labvanced Eye Tracking 2.0: validation of webcam eye tracking with 494 unsupervised online participants
articles.authors: Caspar Goeke
articles.abstract: Webcam eye tracking has already become a powerful tool for online behavioral research, and the first generation of Labvanced's system was validated against an EyeLink 1000 in the laboratory at an accuracy of about 1.4° of visual angle (Kaduk et al., 2023). Several questions remained open. How much of that accuracy survives the uncontrolled conditions of a real online study? Why do some participants deliver far worse data than others, and can they be identified before a researcher pays for them? Can the calibration be shortened to make it more practical in ordinary online studies? And what should happen to participants who do not pass it, or otherwise do not qualify? Here we show how we improved eye-tracking accuracy, while simultaneously shortening the calibration, simplifying the setup, and optimizing the whole procedure for real online data collection with our partner Prolific. We then validated the system in seven recording batches with about 500 completed participants of a 45-target accuracy task, and publish their anonymized data so that every result can be verified. With our new standard calibration (about 2 minutes) and balanced screening, the median participant's error was 5.2 % of the screen diagonal, 1.8° of visual angle on a laptop at 60 cm. And with the 5 minute calibration and very strict screening, the median accuracy of online participants reached 4 % of the screen diagonal, which is equal to 1.4° of visual angle at a standard distance. In summary, with this release of Eye Tracking 2.0, we show that the accuracy reported in our peer-reviewed laboratory comparison can be replicated online

articles.title: When the brain can change: effects of neuroplasticity education on beliefs about brain-based mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery. We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs. Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control. The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2. The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall. The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders. In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance. These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.

articles.title: Coming of Age in Polarized Times: Affective Polarization Across Adolescence
articles.authors: Jakob Kasper; Gijs Schumacher; Lysanne te Brinke; Eveline Crone; Bert N. Bakker
articles.abstract: Concerns about affective polarization among young people have grown in political, media, and academic debate. Yet, despite adolescence being a crucial period of identity formation and young people’s central role in shaping the future of democratic societies, little is known about when affective polarization emerges, and how it varies across adolescence and political environments. Drawing on survey data from adolescents (N = 7,031; ages 11–25) and adults (N = 9,997; ages > 25) in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Austria, Poland, and Greece, we examine within-adolescence age differences in affective polarization, adolescent-adult differences, and temporal variation in affective polarization levels around a major political event. We find that affective polarization is already visible by early adolescence and differs remarkably little across adolescent age groups, challenging the expectation that affective polarization increases sharply around the transition to the legal voting age. Comparisons with adults in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and Austria show that adolescents are consistently less affectively polarized than adults. Further, our longitudinal panel evidence from the Netherlands suggests that adolescent affective polarization varies with the broader political environment, increasing around the 2023 parliamentary election and declining thereafter. This illustrates that adolescent affective polarization is not fixed but varies with political dynamics, highlighting adolescence as an important period for educational efforts that foster democratic engagement and constructive political disagreement.

articles.title: Data-Matrix-Based Overall Goodness-of-Fit Testing for Confirmatory Factor Analysis: In-Sample Prediction Error for Observed Variables
articles.authors: Young Ze Kim; Gyeongcheol Cho; Hanjoe Kim
articles.abstract:
Conventional χ²-based tests in confirmatory factor analysis assess overall fit through covariance reproduction and remain the standard inferential tools for overall goodness-of-fit testing. However, they do not directly quantify the magnitude of model misfit and may become unavailable when estimation fails to converge or produces improper solutions.
We introduce and evaluate two data-matrix-based alternatives within structured factor analysis: the in-sample prediction error for observed variables (IPEo) test for a single model and the ΔIPEo test for nested models. IPEo quantifies the proportion of variability in the observed data matrix left unexplained by the hypothesized model, while its bootstrap p value provides an inferential decision. Monte Carlo simulations showed that the IPEo-based tests controlled Type I error, gained power with increasing sample size, and remained available when conventional χ²-based tests frequently failed. An empirical illustration further showed that the IPEo value and its p value provide complementary information about the magnitude and statistical significance of model misfit. These findings support IPEo-based testing as a complementary inferential framework for evaluating CFA model fit directly at the level of the observed data matrix.

articles.title: Ostensive affective feedback and the emergence of the capacity to negotiate communicative content: the psychology of establishing agreement.
articles.authors: Wouter Wolf
articles.abstract: Inferring agreement, that is, inferring that mental content is mutually considered to be sufficiently aligned for the purposes of an interaction, is crucial for many facets of human sociality. Importantly, humans are highly skilled at facilitating such inferences through communication. Yet even within communicative interactions, agreement might fail for interpretive reasons (uncertainty or misunderstanding) or alignment reasons (disagreement). Solving either of these problems often requires iterative communicative interactions during which the content of mental states is negotiated until misunderstandings are repaired and/or disagreements are resolved through compromise. But what social cognitive mechanisms allowed humans’ successful negotiation capacities to emerge, even when conventionalized negotiation and communication systems were not available? Here, I argue that humans developed the capacity to directly negotiate the content of communication by understanding the interactive intent underlying ostension in a previously underappreciated way: To infer a lack of agreement in communicative interactions, a key piece of evidence lies in how the other reacts to one’s communicative act. However, this reaction is often ambiguous. I argue that ostension helps facilitate interpreting such reactions, not only through assumptions of mutual relevance, but in large part due to pragmatic tension that arises from ostensive non-affirmative affective feedback. This tension forces individuals to isolate content as a separate dimension of communicative acts that can be evaluated and negotiated. This facilitates the resolution of interpretive problems through boundary-setting and disagreement through compromise. As such, ostensive feedback has likely played a major role in the emergence of human sociality.

articles.title: Loneliness and Interpersonal Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life
articles.authors: Jasmin Bruna Stariolo; Anh Tran; Kristina Mei; Katharine Helen Greenaway
articles.abstract: Loneliness is a growing public health concern rooted in emotional distress and social disconnection. Interpersonal emotion regulation — managing ones’ own or others’ emotions — is a mechanism for strengthening social bonds and fostering emotional health. Their shared socio-emotional foundation raises the possibility that loneliness may be connected to how people regulate others and are regulated in turn. Accordingly, we investigated whether loneliness is associated with adaptive and maladaptive interpersonal emotion regulation strategies in the moment and over time. To address this question, we conducted a daily diary (N = 170, collected 2020; Study 1) and experience sampling study (N = 239, collected 2021; Study 2). Participants reported on global trait loneliness, then recorded momentary loneliness and use of four strategies as both regulator (regulating others extrinsically) and target of regulation (being regulated by others intrinsically) for seven days. State loneliness predicted greater invalidation as both regulator and target, and global trait loneliness predicted less physical support as regulator and target. Most consistently, the person-level average of momentary loneliness across the week predicted greater use of all strategies — responsiveness, invalidation, reappraisal, and physical support — both as regulator and target. Methodologically, our findings show the importance of assessing loneliness at different time scales. Theoretically, our findings suggest lonely individuals do actively attempt emotion regulation during interactions, yet they may be just as likely to use maladaptive strategies that undermine connection as adaptive strategies that enhance it. This work underscores the importance of interaction quality in understanding how loneliness persists and might be interrupted.

articles.title: Voice Class but Not Fach: Acoustic Correlates of Operatic Voice Types in 8,681 Historical Recordings
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: The German Fach system divides operatic voices into roughly 25 categories within the familiar voice classes, distinguished by tessitura, vocal weight, timbre and agility. Whether these categories are acoustically recoverable has rarely been tested on singers a model has not seen. I analysed 8,681 public-domain 78-rpm recordings by 508 singers in 27 Fächer, labelling each singer with their documented career Fach. After a design audit, 153 singers were locked aside, 12 tests were specified in advance, and the frozen pipeline was evaluated once on the held-out singers. Seven-way voice class was recovered at a balanced accuracy of .54 (chance .15), and female-range versus male-range class at .97 without explicit pitch measures. Within a voice class, the Fach label did not generalise: tenor sub-Fach classification fell from .54 on discovery singers to .38 on held-out singers (chance .34), and no single-aspect model replicated. Treated as a continuous position on the taxonomy's tessitura ordering, however, soprano Fach was predicted on held-out singers (ρ = .44). Female-range voices in electrical-era recordings showed lower singer's-formant prominence and a higher Hammarberg index than male-range voices, differences that a synthetic audit showed are not measurement artefacts of high pitch. The Fach of the role being sung was more recoverable than the singer's label. Coarse voice class is acoustically robust; within a class, the evidence favours an ordering over the discrete categories the labels draw, and points to repertoire as part of what the labels encode.

articles.title: Multi-party simulations with human participants and role-based LLM conversational agents: A design framework and validity evidence for organizational research
articles.authors: Yuki Nozaki; Naho Fujisawa; Yoshinobu Kano
articles.abstract: Dynamic organizational phenomena often unfold through ongoing communication among multiple interdependent actors, yet studying them involves trade-offs among realism, controllability, and scalability. We propose a methodological framework for using role-based conversational agents powered by large language models (LLMs) as multi-party interaction partners in organizational research. It specifies how to create standardized but contingent interaction environments through scenario design, persona prompts, interaction protocols, and iterative testing. In a preregistered illustrative study of leadership communication, we analyzed 394 employees’ text-based simulations powered by GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5 Flash, or Claude Sonnet 4.6. Across models, participants perceived the agents as anthropomorphic and animate, and as acting consistently with their assigned backgrounds, personalities, and linguistic styles. Behavioral coding corroborated and extended these perceptions, with deviations from assigned persona prompts in 2.59% of utterances. Participants’ utterances also yielded codable indicators of theoretically relevant behavior, in this case leadership communication. These findings provide initial validity evidence that multi-party LLM-agent simulations can create plausible interaction environments, deliver persona-consistent stimuli, and elicit behaviorally analyzable responses. We also offer practical guidelines on model selection, replicability, and ethics.

articles_hidden.title: French Validation of the Team Flow Monitor:  Factor Structure and Validity Evidence in Student Teams
articles_hidden.authors: Victoire Vallier; Nicolas Verger; Rebecca Shankland; Roxane Turgon; Quentin Hallez
articles_hidden.abstract: Teamwork is central to addressing tasks whose complexity exceeds the capabilities of any single individual, and the shared optimal experience known as team flow has been linked to collective performance. Validated instruments to measure team flow are, however, only available in Dutch and English. This research aimed to validate a French version of the characteristics subscale of the Team Flow Monitor (TFM). In Study 1 (N = 225), the scale was translated and adapted, and its factor structure, reliability, and convergent and discriminant validity were examined.
