articles_hidden.abstract: Spillover---the influence of previous words on the processing of current words---is widely reported in reading studies, yet population-level findings are mixed. We argue that spillover is neither noise nor a uniform phenomenon; it may reflect systematic individual differences in how processing difficulty carries over across words. We analyze six naturalistic eye-tracking-while-reading datasets and estimate individual-level spillover effects of preceding-word length, frequency, and surprisal using Bayesian hierarchical models. Because studying individual differences requires reliable measurement, we first assess the cross-context reliability of these effects across experimental sessions and reading tasks, operationalized as correlations between individual-level estimates from two measurement contexts. The measured reliability differs across sources and depends on experimental design and signal-to-noise ratio, being strongest for word length and weaker for lexical frequency and surprisal. Crucially, we find that individual differences in spillover vary systematically with reading fluency. Low-fluency readers exhibit greater spillover from low-level lexical properties, such as word length and frequency, whereas high-fluency readers show more pronounced spillover from higher-level contextual difficulty, such as surprisal, which may help explain why population-level spillover findings are mixed. Finally, spillover is related to skipping and regression rates, indicating that some spillover effects may reflect idiosyncratic patterns of gaze behavior. Overall, our findings suggest that population-level effects can obscure divergent reader profiles, motivating theories and models of reading beyond the "average reader".

articles_hidden.title: Effect of Exercise on Cognition, Memory, and Executive Function: A Study-Level Meta-Meta-Analysis Across Populations and Exercise Categories
articles_hidden.authors: František Bartoš; Martina Lušková; Kseniya Bortnikova; Karolína Hozová; Klara Kantova; Zuzana Irsova; Tomas Havranek
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Physical exercise is widely promoted for cognitive enhancement, yet prior syntheses have been questioned due to methodological limitations. 
Objectives: This study evaluated the reliability of evidence supporting physical exercise for general cognition, memory, and executive function, and assessed efficacy across specific population-intervention combinations after adjusting for publication bias. 
Methods: This study is a study-level meta-meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). We included systematic reviews with meta-analyses of RCTs evaluating exercise interventions against non-exercise controls in humans, identified in a meta-meta-analysis published in 2025. We extracted study-level effect sizes and synthesized the data using robust Bayesian meta-analysis which allowed us to evaluate evidence for and against the presence of the effect, between-study heterogeneity, publication bias, while accounting for model uncertainty.
Results: We extracted 2,239 study-level effect estimates from 215 meta-analyses. After excluding suspected duplicates, 1,933 estimates from 201 meta-analyses were included in the overall analyses, which revealed extreme evidence of publication bias and between-study heterogeneity. Adjusted average effects were significantly smaller than unadjusted estimates for general cognition (SMD=0.208; 95% credible interval (CrI) [0.075, 0.318]), and executive functions (SMD=0.088, 95% CrI [0.000, 0.168]). For memory the adjustment differed between adjustment specifications (SMD=0.226, 95% CrI [0.169, 0.282] vs SMD=0.021, 95\%CrI [0.000, 0.217]). While broad prediction intervals spanned substantial negative and positive effects, subgroup analyses identified mostly consistent benefits for specific combinations, such as dance and exergaming for general cognition in non-healthy older adults.
Conclusion: The primary limitations of the evidence are severe publication bias and extreme heterogeneity, which appear to inflate previously reported benefits. Consequently, broad claims of generalized cognitive enhancement from physical exercise appear premature. The results support a shift from blanket public health advice to recommendations tailored to specific population-intervention combinations.

articles_hidden.title: Negative evaluation bias in person perception is linked to interpersonal dysfunction
articles_hidden.authors: Richard Rau; Amina Aissaoui; Johannes Zimmermann
articles_hidden.abstract: Negative evaluations of unfamiliar others have been documented in personality pathology, but it remains unclear whether they reflect a broader perceiver tendency linked dimensionally to interpersonal dysfunction. In a community sample assessed in 2026 (N = 590; n = 226 with close-other reports), we measured a generalized bias toward evaluating unfamiliar others negatively across four standardized person-perception tasks combining personality ratings and adjective selections with vignette and video targets. Stronger negative evaluation bias was associated with greater interpersonal-problem severity when problems were reported by participants themselves (r = .14) and especially when reported by close others (r = .34). Exploratory analyses showed a self-reported shift toward high-agency problems but no corresponding close-other pattern or systematic association with communion. In secondary analyses, negative evaluation bias showed a positive but imprecise association with overall personality-functioning impairment and the expected pattern of lower self-certainty and, conditional on self-certainty, higher certainty about others. These findings support viewing negative evaluation bias as a broader perceiver-level correlate of interpersonal dysfunction, including difficulties apparent beyond the perceiver’s own perspective. Generalizability to more severe personality pathology remains to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the psychometric properties of the Czech versions of Illinois Bully Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Štěpán Komrska; Alžběta Váňová; Martin Dolejš; Jaroslava Suchá
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: The main objective of the study was to adapt and verify the psychometric properties of the Illinois Bully Scale (IBS) in Czech 
adolescents.
Methods: The analysis utilized quantitative data from 1,321 respondents, aged 12 to 14 years, who were enrolled in 7th grade of lower second-
ary or grammar school. Descriptive and inferential statistics, including chi-square tests and Mann-Whitney U tests, were used to examine group 
differences.
Results: The IBS demonstrated strong internal consistency and construct validity across all subscales (Victim: 0.84, Bully: 0.80, Fight: 0.79, 
total IBS: 0.87). Boys and elementary school students reported significant victim and bully experiences. The supplemental cyberbullying scale 
showed significant correlations with the IBS subscales, supporting its criterion-related validity.
Conclusions: Adaptation of the IBS confirmed that it is a useful tool for assessing the frequency and experience of different types and severity 
of bullying. Its Czech adaptation allows for population screening as well as identification of severe cases and planning of interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Distribution across Age of Raw and Scaled Intelligence Scores - the DARSIS model
articles_hidden.authors: Y Cramer
articles_hidden.abstract: On heavily g-loaded subtests of intelligence tests, the mean raw score rises steeply in childhood and levels off in late adolescence. How the entire raw score distribution changes with age is far less well documented, even though norm tables of standardized tests contain exactly this information. This study shows that the relationship between age, raw score and scaled score follows a regular, mathematical pattern that is shared across tests, constructs, countries and decades. Using digitized norm tables from 60 subtests of 19 intelligence tests normed in five countries between 1984 and 2020, the scaled score belonging to a given raw score is modeled as a continuous function of age with three coefficients that are common to all subtests and a single ’difficulty’ parameter p per raw score. The model, termed DARSIS (Distribution across Age of Raw and Scaled Intelligence Scores), explains between 90% and 99.9% of the variance in the norm tables, with root mean square errors between 0.07 and 0.38 standard deviations, roughly half of which is attributable to rounding in the published tables. Leave-one-test-out cross-validation yields nearly identical results. Errors are smaller around the mean of the norm tables and for higher levels of performance, but do not depend on age or on the year of standardization. The model gives a parametric form to the mental growth curves described in the early literature on absolute scaling and can be regarded as a strongly restricted special case of the location-scale models used in modern continuous norming. Applications are discussed: norms for above-level testing, extended norms for the upper and lower tails, a reduced parameter space when norming new tests with item response theory, and the computation of reference ages.

articles_hidden.title: Masturbation Satisfaction: A Machine Learning Investigation of its Most Important Predictors
articles_hidden.authors: David Cornelius de Jong; Maximiliane Uhlich; Nantje Fischer; Laura Marika Vowels
articles_hidden.abstract: The subjective experience of solo masturbation has rarely been studied, and satisfaction with solo masturbation has been particularly overlooked. Studying masturbation satisfaction and its correlates may help clarify why individuals experience masturbation so differently. Moreover, understanding the correlates of masturbation satisfaction may help illuminate how and why solo masturbation is related to well-being. The goal of the present study was to identify the most important predictors of masturbation satisfaction using random forest, a machine learning algorithm that can model many predictors, non-linear associations, and complex interactions more effectively than traditional statistical approaches. Using data from a large representative U.S. national sample (N = 2,486), we developed random forest models that explained 35-46% of the variance in masturbation satisfaction. We used SHAP values to estimate the magnitude and direction of predictors’ contributions to predicting masturbation satisfaction. The most important predictors of masturbation satisfaction included experiential characteristics of the masturbation event (i.e., vividness of the sensory qualities of pleasure and orgasm, cognitive absorption, use of sex toys), sexuality-related dispositions (e.g., sexual desire, attitudes towards masturbation, motives for masturbating), and more general individual differences (e.g., life satisfaction and happiness, awareness of emotional responses). These constructs warrant attention in future investigations of masturbation and well-being.

articles_hidden.title: An Idiographic Examination of Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviors Using Ecological Momentary Assessment and Network Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah M Johnson; Eric Lee
articles_hidden.abstract: Body-focused repetitive behaviors are a class of behaviors including problematic hair pulling (i.e., trichotillomania) and skin picking (i.e., excoriation). Little research has examined how body-focused repetitive behaviors manifest at the individual level and how individuals may differ from group averages. The current study used idiographic observational methods to investigate the internal cognitive and emotional processes and functioning of individuals with body-focused repetitive behaviors. Four women participants with body-focused repetitive behaviors of varying severities participated in the study. EMA data were collected five times daily over two weeks. Individual contemporaneous network analyses were conducted examining the role picking/pulling had on functioning and internal states. Network structure differed markedly between participants. Each participant displayed different central processes including cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety, shame, and distress intolerance. Findings support individualized assessment and case conceptualization of body-focused repetitive behaviors.

articles_hidden.title: Charting Expectations About Economic Gains and Losses Across Adulthood
articles_hidden.authors: Sebastian S. Horn; Alexandra M. Freund
articles_hidden.abstract:
Expectations about changes of one’s economic situation impact motivation and decision making. Yet, little is known about how people think about economic changes across adulthood. In this
study, participants (N = 1,045) aged 18–88 years from Germany and Switzerland charted their expectations about (a) normative income and wealth trajectories for average adults of different
ages, (b) their personal past, present, and future trajectories, and (c) anticipated trajectories with and without active investment. Participants also reported their motivational gain, maintenance,
and loss-avoidance orientation for financial goals. Normative economic expectations of all age groups followed an inverted-U pattern of gains into midlife followed by losses in older
adulthood. Bayesian multilevel models showed that participants differentiated income and wealth, with an earlier peak and steeper decline for income than wealth. In contrast to normative
expectations, personal expectations differed markedly by age, with older participants judging their economic development less favorably than younger participants. These judgments covaried
with motivational orientation. All age groups expected future active investment to improve their economic prospects, but older adults anticipated smaller benefits and even losses under active
investment. Participants’ normative judgments corresponded well to representative income and wealth data (German Socio-Economic Panel; Swiss Household Panel), suggesting that adults of
different ages hold shared and relatively realistic expectations about age-graded economic gains and losses. At the same time, the findings highlight substantial age-related differences in
personal expectations.

articles_hidden.title: The Emergent Structure of Memory Phenomenology Depends on Whether Memories Are More Episodic or Semantic
articles_hidden.authors: Tabatha Blaney-Gale; Jordan Poppenk
articles_hidden.abstract: Phenomenological characteristics are central to theoretical distinctions among modern memory constructs. The scene construction framework proposes that episodic remembering involves the construction of coherent scenes, such that the structure of phenomenology may reflect the engagement of the hippocampus and related regions during recall. However, most phenomenology research relies on instruments with content and scoring schemes that embed theoretical assumptions into their measurements. Here, we explored whether phenomenological characteristics emerge from self-reported memory experiences as anticipated by episodic memory theory. We solicited memories from a large online sample, following each response with a novel questionnaire designed to evaluate the phenomenology of individual memories. We used folded bottom-up factor analyses to examine and validate the global latent factor structure of participants’ memory experiences. Consistent with Tulving’s declarative memory framework, our analyses produced five stable dimensions: imagery, autonoetic consciousness, mental time travel, relational memory, and semantic memory. In order, these dimensions reflect multi-modal perceptual reexperiencing, personal meaning, sense of reliving, detailed spatiotemporal context, and conscious use of semantic knowledge during recall. The semantic memory dimension has no clear predecessor, suggesting the strategic use of general knowledge during recall is a distinct and previously uncharacterized aspect of remembering. This factor structure generalized across memories elicited by recent and remote episodic prompts. However, distinct versions of mental time travel and relational memory emerged in response to the semantic prompt, suggesting these dimensions of memory are context-sensitive rather than fixed. While our findings validate the link between episodic memory and its theorized phenomenological elements, they also invite broader investigation of how phenomenology may vary across different classes of memory.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Construal, Culture, and Cognitive Dissonance Using the Induced Compliance Paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Figureau; Daniel Priolo; Willem W. A. Sleegers; Kenneth G DeMarree; Omid Ghasemi; Amélie Gourdon-Kanhukamwe; Maxime Mauduy; Asil Ali Özdoğru; Robert M Ross; Bjørn Sætrevik
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive dissonance, traditionally conceptualized as a fundamental psychological process involving discomfort from inconsistent cognitions, may vary across cultures. These variations could be attributed to self-construal, or how individuals define themselves in relation to others. Although previous cross-cultural research has predominantly used the free-choice paradigm, significant concerns have been raised regarding its procedural validity and the robustness of its findings. To address this issue, this registered report presents secondary analyses of a large-scale international dataset. We investigated the moderating role of cultural variables on dissonance effects within the induced-compliance paradigm across 18 countries (N = 3,804). We hypothesized that dissonance effects would be stronger for participants with higher individuallevel self-construal scores (H1), in more individualistic countries (H2), and in countries with higher country-level self-construal scores (H3). Our results did not support these hypotheses, suggesting that cultural moderation may not generalize to the induced-compliance paradigm. We discuss the necessity of reassessing the procedure’s reliability and clarifying the theoretical role of choice.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping the Representational Basis of Object-Based Guidance: How Colour Availability Shapes Contributions Across the Hierarchy
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Massironi; Emanuela Bricolo; Marco A. Petilli
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous research has shown that colour is one of the most robust attributes guiding attention during visual search and can dominate guidance, with its removal prompting substantial reweighting toward alternative features. However, naturalistic object search differs in several respects from the simplified displays and controlled designs typically used to investigate the role of colour: observers often do not know exactly how the target will appear, and even when its colour is preserved, many candidate objects may share that colour, reducing its diagnostic value and increasing the relevance of information that generalises across variations in appearance. Does colour retain the same importance under these more naturalistic conditions, and how does the relative contribution of other guiding information change when colour is unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational approach to characterising the representational basis of object-based guidance in natural scenes across multiple representational levels and examine how this profile depends on colour availability. Using eye-movement data from the Potsdam Eye-Movement Corpus, we related fixation-by-fixation object selection to cue-object similarity across multiple computational representational spaces, including layer-specific image representations from a deep convolutional neural network, category-level visual prototypes derived within the Vision Spaces framework, and distributional semantic representations derived from linguistic and scene-based spatial statistics. Image-based, category-level visual, and semantic information made complementary contributions to object selection in both colour and grayscale scenes, while cue-object colour similarity explained only part of this broader representational profile. Critically, removing colour altered the strength of some image-based associations but left the broader pattern of multilevel representational contributions largely preserved. These findings suggest that, in more naturalistic search scenarios, object-based guidance draws on target-relevant evidence across multiple representational formats and levels, with colour accounting for only a limited part of the information supporting guidance. At the methodological level, the computational framework introduced here allows us to characterise the representational basis of object-based guidance across perceptual and semantic levels and to track how the contributions of these representations vary across experimental conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Visual search shifts weight up the visual hierarchy from attentional guidance to verification
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Massironi; Emanuela Bricolo; Marco A. Petilli
articles_hidden.abstract: When searching for target objects among distractors, observers exploit information contained in the attentional template, a memory representation of target features that supports both search guidance and verification for target selection or distractor rejection. The good-enough framework proposes that, because guidance and verification serve distinct computational goals, the precision of the template varies within a given feature dimension: guidance relies on a coarser, relational code that optimizes the reduction of the search space to candidate target locations, whereas verification relies on a more precise, optimal code for target-identity decisions. However, in searches involving real-world, multidimensional stimuli, it remains unclear whether the representation in the template also varies along the depth of the visual hierarchy, from low-level visual features to more abstract information related to object identity. Here, we used a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) to estimate target–distractor similarity at different levels of the visual hierarchy. We then manipulated this similarity in a target-present versus target-absent two-alternative forcedchoice (2AFC) task while recording eye movements. Guidance, operationalized as which of the two stimuli was fixated first and modeled as a function of their relative similarity to the target, was predicted primarily by low-level similarity, with a smaller contribution of high-level similarity. Verification, operationalized as dwell time on each distractor and modeled as a function of its similarity to the target, was also predicted by both low and high-level similarity, but showed a clear shift toward high-level similarity relative to guidance. Critically, the relative weight of high-level similarity nearly doubled from guidance to verification. Together, our findings reveal a shift in representational depth up the visual hierarchy. Beyond template precision, representational depth therefore constitutes a further axis along which template information is selectively exploited according to the computational demands of different epochs of visual search.

articles_hidden.title: Intrusive and voluntary memory from a single system: A retrieved-context account of selective interference in the trauma-film paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Jordan Gunn; Richard Henson; Emily A Holmes; Tommy Mcconnell; Deborah Talmi
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory theory must explain why interference can affect deliberate and involuntary remembering differently. Studies using distressing films show that a film reminder followed by an imagery-competing task such as Tetris can reduce later spontaneous memories of the film (intrusions) while leaving voluntary memory relatively intact. This selective interference effect is often interpreted through clinical theories of traumatic memory in which intrusive and voluntary remembering depend on different memory representations. We develop an alternative account in an emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval (eCMR) model that predicts sequences of film and non-film recall events. Events become associated with context, a changing internal representation of experience. A film reminder reinstates film-associated context, so mental imagery generated during the subsequent task becomes associated with that context. During later retrieval, task memories compete with film memories cued by the same context, reducing film recall without weakening the original film associations. During deliberate recall, however, we propose that people pursue the goal of remembering the film by constructing and maintaining a retrieval cue that distinguishes film from task material. In simulations, sustained support from this cue was required to reproduce the selective-interference pattern across reminder and task conditions, protecting deliberate recall relative to involuntary retrieval. These results suggest that competitor learning and retrieval cueing can produce selective interference within a shared memory system, motivating tests in other memory tasks.

articles_hidden.title: How perceived social, emotional, and behavioral skills differ across the life span
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher Napolitano; Christopher J. Soto; Madison Nicole Sewell; Heejun Roy Yoon; Brent Roberts
articles_hidden.abstract: We investigated age-related differences in perceived social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills and gender variations using a large cross-sectional sample (N=31,315, ages 10-70). Using generalized additive models (GAMs), we identified four key findings. First, modest, temporary negative age gradients emerged during early adolescence, consistent with the “disruption principle”. Second, despite this disruption, mean levels across all five domains—Self-Management, Social Engagement, Cooperation, Emotional Resilience, and Innovation—were positively associated with age, showing steep age gradients consistent with maturation during middle adolescence and early adulthood. Third, facet-level analyses uncovered significant heterogeneity in age-related patterns otherwise obscured at the domain level. Fourth, gender differences emerged: men and women varied in age-related patterns for Cooperation and Innovation, while non-binary participants—despite lower baseline levels—exhibited significantly steeper positive age gradients than male and female counterparts across several domains. Collectively, these results highlight both parallels and distinctions between SEB skill development and established personality trait principles. This comprehensive map informs future longitudinal research and the design of developmentally appropriate interventions across the lifespan.

articles_hidden.title: Mental health of preadolescents in western Ukraine: feasibility and acceptability of a school-based psychosocial intervention during war
articles_hidden.authors: Oleksandr Avramchuk; Olha Germanovych; Olha Ivanenko; Olga Uralova; Marina Lisenberg; Olena Mukha; Yuliya Stadnytska; Richard Davidson; Perla Kaliman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Children living in conflict zones experience high levels of psychological distress. Schools can provide an accessible setting for support, yet evidence on the effectiveness of school-based interventions in active war contexts remains limited.
Objectives: To evaluate children’s well-being and internal coping resources during the war in Ukraine and to examine the feasibility of a school-based program designed to enhance psychological well-being in preadolescents.
Participants and setting: The study involved 81 children aged 10–12 years from schools in Lviv, Ukraine. 
Methods: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms, quality of life, self-compassion, and mindfulness traits were assessed using standard questionnaires and validated psychometric scales. The intervention program, delivered at school, focused on mindfulness, self-compassion, social connection, sense of purpose, and trauma processing. Acceptability and perceived impact were explored post-intervention among children, families, and school staff. 
Results: 42% of children reported four or more ACEs. 39.5% of children exceeded the clinical cutoff for probable PTSD on the Children’s Revised Impact of Event Scale CRIES-8, with differences observed between boys and girls. Higher levels of self-compassion and mindfulness were associated with lower PTSD symptoms. Children, families, and school staff reported improvements in children’s well-being, emotion regulation, and social functioning after the intervention.
Conclusions: Our work provides preliminary evidence of the feasibility and acceptability of a school-based intervention designed to promote children’s psychological well-being and mental health during ongoing war, with positive perceived impacts reported by children, families, and school staff. Interventions incorporating mindfulness and self-compassion training may represent promising approaches for reducing trauma-related symptoms in children exposed to adversity. Larger controlled studies using standardized measures are needed to assess effectiveness before broader dissemination can be considered.

articles_hidden.title: Preventing teacher and parental violence against children: A cluster-randomized controlled trial of a school-based intervention approach in Tanzanian primary schools
articles_hidden.authors: Eliud Kabelege; Katharina Mattonet; Lena Kolwey; Getrude Mkinga; Mabula Nkuba; Manuela Fritz; Faustine Bwire Masath; Katharin Hermenau; Janina Isabel Steinert; Tobias Hecker
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Violence against children (VAC) at homes and schools remains highly prevalent in low- and middle-income countries. We tested the effectiveness of a preventive intervention addressing teacher and parental violence simultaneously.
Methods: In this two-arm, cluster randomised controlled trial, 16 public primary schools in Morogoro, Tanzania, were randomly allocated (1:1) to receive either the Interaction Competencies with Children (ICC) programme or no intervention. Children (aged 8–15 years), their parents, and teachers were enrolled. The ICC intervention targeted teachers and parents focusing on non-violent behaviour management strategies and positive adult–child interactions. Interviewers at follow-up were blinded. The primary outcome was emotional and physical VAC, measured by children and adults’ reports at baseline and follow-up. All randomised participants were analysed. Missing data were estimated through multiple imputation. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT#06369025).
Findings: In total, 410 and 427 children, 380 and 394 mothers, 253 and 246 fathers, and 244 and 235 teachers were assigned to the intervention and control condition, respectively. Participants were recruited between 15 April to 24 August 2024 for baseline and between 1 October 2024 to 21 February 2025 for follow-up assessment. Participants in intervention schools reported significantly greater reductions in emotional and physical violence by mothers (child report (CR): Cohen’s d = 0·227 for emotional violence (EV), 0·134 for physical violence (PV); adult report (AR): 0·343 for EV, 0·473 for PV), fathers (CR: 0·180 for EV, 0·215 for PV; AR: 0·222 for EV, 0·187 for PV), and teachers (CR: 0·089 for EV, 0·164 for PV; AR: 0·336 for EV, 0·607 for PV). No adverse events related to the intervention were detected.
Interpretation: By leveraging the infrastructure of public schools, ICC offers an effective and scalable multi-sectoral model for VAC prevention.

articles_hidden.title: MBB-AVR: a mind-brain-body dataset with dynamic affective states in immersive virtual reality
articles_hidden.authors: Antonin Fourcade; Anthony Buck Ciston; Lucy Roellecke; Jeroen de Mooij; Hector Leos; Arno Villringer; Sara Carletto; Francesca Malandrone; Michael Gaebler
articles_hidden.abstract: We present MindBrainBody-AffectiveVR (MBB-AVR), a multimodal dataset capturing continuous affective experience and both central and peripheral physiological responses during naturalistic emotional stimulation in immersive virtual reality. Forty-seven healthy adults (24 female, 22 male, 1 non-binary; age = 27.1 ± 5.4) viewed a 23-minute stereoscopic 360° video sequence, composed of computer-generated, language-free content designed to elicit high affective variability over time, presented via a head-mounted display (HTC Vive Pro Eye). While immersed, participants continuously rated their momentary valence and arousal using a previously validated rating tool with real-time visual feedback. Synchronized recordings include 64-channel EEG, ECG, respiration, photoplethysmography, galvanic skin response, and head and eye tracking with pupillometry. Participants additionally completed questionnaires including interoceptive sensibility and alexithymia. The dataset is organized following the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) and includes extracted low-level audio and video features of the stimulus. It may support research on the temporal dynamics of affect, multimodal physiological correlates of emotion, and affective computing. The dataset is available at https://gin.g-node.org/fourcade_a/mbb-avr.

articles_hidden.title: Increasing cerebellar beta rhythms shifts cerebral oscillatory signatures of context-driven language processing
articles_hidden.authors: Sandra Ambichler; Tessa Portier; Vitória Piai; Jana Klaus
articles_hidden.abstract: While there is growing consensus that the cerebellum is part of the cerebrally centred network underlying language processing, the direct nature of its contribution to comprehension and production remains unknown. In particular, while both processes require lexical access, production additionally involves motor processes linked to articulatory planning, which has fuelled the view that the cerebellum is primarily involved in motor control in language production. Cortically, both lexical access and articulatory planning are known to be driven by alpha-beta power decreases. To disentangle cerebellar involvement in language, this study investigated the modulatory effect of transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) over the right cerebellum on context-driven language comprehension and production. In a cross-over, double-blind, sham-controlled within-participants design, 32 healthy volunteers received 20 minutes of 20-Hz tACS (2 mA peak-to-peak) targeting the right posterior cerebellum. Immediately afterwards, they performed a context-driven language task while EEG was recorded from 32 channels. In the task, visually presented lead-in sentences creating a constraining or unconstraining context were followed by a picture depicting the final word of the sentence. Participants were instructed to name the picture (production) or judge its animacy (comprehension). Responses became slower overall following active compared to sham tACS, and this increase was more pronounced in the comprehension task. In line with previous work, reliable context-related oscillatory power decreases were observed in response to the context manipulation, but exhibited a different pattern across tasks and stimulation conditions. For production, beta-centred power decreases following sham shifted to temporally and spatially extended alpha power decreases following active tACS. By contrast, alpha-centred power decreases following sham tACS in the comprehension task increased following active tACS. Increasing beta activity in the right posterior cerebellum thus affected early stages of context-driven language processing linked to lexical access in both language domains. The stimulation-induced spectral, spatial and temporal shifts suggest recruitment of alternative cortical resources as a consequence of cerebellar network modulation. This interpretation is consistent with the cerebellum functioning as a network node coordinating temporal dynamics across distributed language regions.

articles_hidden.title: Is Guessing to Blame? Comparing Two Accounts of Attenuated Monitoring Accuracy in Recognition-Based Metamemory Judgments
articles_hidden.authors: Franziska Magdalene Leipold; Constantin Gregor Meyer-Grant
articles_hidden.abstract: The relative accuracy of prospective metamemory monitoring is typically assessed through the association between judgments of learning (JOLs) and subsequent memory performance. In recognition paradigms, however, manifest correlations can vary across task structures, and prior work insinuated that such differences may reflect guessing processes rather than differences in underlying monitoring ability. We formally derived model-implied predictions for the manifest JOL–recognition correlation under two competing theoretical frameworks: the two-high-threshold model (2HTM), which explicitly allows for guessing, and signal detection theory (SDT), which does not. We tested these predictions in an original experiment that manipulated response bias. The observed difference in the manifest JOL–recognition correlation between conditions was well accounted for by the 2HTM under a single latent correlation, whereas SDT clearly failed to do so. These findings suggest that guessing contaminates manifest correlations commonly used as proxies for monitoring accuracy, and that adequately modeling the underlying process can recover the latent association those proxies are meant to capture.

articles_hidden.title: Visual Deprivation Alters Parent-Specific  Autonomic Tuning During Infancy
articles_hidden.authors: GIULIA CAPPAGLI; Marta Guarischi; Guido Catalano; FEDERICA MORELLI; gori monica; Sabrina Signorini
articles_hidden.abstract: Parents' touch regulates infants' physiology, and vision may be essential for identifying social partners, but whether the absence of visual feedback affects this physiological effect has never been tested. We examined whether visual deprivation alters infants' autonomic responses to affective touch from a parent versus a stranger. Eighteen infants aged 8–13 months (9 with peripheral visual impairment, 9 sighted) received slow stroking (3 cm/s) on the right shin while the parent or an unfamiliar adult sat in front of them as the apparent source of touch. Typically developing infants showed a larger heart-rate deceleration during parent than stranger touch. Infants with visual impairment did not differentiate between adults and showed higher heart-rate responses than typically developing infants in the parent condition (Group × Parent Identity interaction). Visual experience may help link affective touch to its social source. The small, clinical sample limits generalizability, and replication is needed.

articles_hidden.title: Effects of Stoic Training on Fear of Negative Evaluation and Responses to Social-Evaluative Stress: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Michael William Lewis; Charles Kalarchian; Alexander MacLellan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Stoic philosophy has influenced cognitive and behavioral therapies, but Stoic training has received limited empirical evaluation. This preregistered randomized controlled trial examined whether Stoic training reduced fear of negative evaluation (FNE), improved broader psychological outcomes, increased Stoic attitudes and behaviors, and altered subjective and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress.

Methods: Undergraduate students (M age = 19.16 years, SD = 1.05; 81% women) were randomized to eight days of online Stoic training or an active control involving literary-fiction readings. Ninety-eight participants completed pretraining and posttraining self-report assessments (Stoic training, n = 46; control, n = 52). Seventy-eight subsequently completed a modified Trier Social Stress Test (TSST), of whom 66 provided usable electrocardiography data for the preregistered cardiac analyses. Before speech preparation, participants in the Stoic condition completed a five-minute Negative Visualization exercise, whereas control participants waited quietly.

Results: Relative to the active control, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining FNE when controlling for pretraining scores, b = −2.77, p = .016, adjusted d = −0.50, and higher posttraining Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale scores, b = 6.06, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.43. Exploratory subscale analyses suggested possible effects on Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness, although neither remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Between-condition effects on resilience, self-efficacy, and rumination were not significant. During the TSST, cardiac effects were contrary to prediction: Stoic training was associated with higher heart rate, b = 4.13, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.53, and lower heart rate variability, although the latter effect narrowly missed statistical significance, b = −0.17, p = .053, adjusted d = −0.49. Subjective distress and state-anxiety responses to the TSST did not differ significantly by condition.

Conclusions: Stoic training led to significantly greater reductions in FNE and increases in Stoic attitudes than an active control, whereas broader psychological outcomes did not differ significantly between conditions. These findings provide initial evidence that brief Stoic training may modify a cognitive vulnerability relevant to social evaluation while engaging the attitudes and behaviors it is intended to cultivate. The unexpected cardiac effects may reflect the broader training, the acute Negative Visualization exercise administered before the stressor, or their combination, highlighting the need to disentangle the cumulative and acute effects of Stoic practice and determine how the timing and context of Negative Visualization influence responses to social-evaluative stress.

articles_hidden.title: Acute Self-Reported and Objective Physical Activity Moderate the Association of Daily Stress with Affective Wellbeing and Self-Esteem
articles_hidden.authors: Justin Hachenberger; Malin Brueckmann; Usama EL-Awad; Elke Wild; Sakari Lemola
articles_hidden.abstract: Daily stress can have detrimental effects on affective wellbeing and self-esteem. Previous research suggests that both the general physical activity level and acute physical activity, may reduce the adverse consequences of stress. However, studies investigating these associations in the context of daily life have typically focused on either acute physical activity or the general physical activity level alone and have largely relied on self-reported measures, which may be subject to recall bias and difficulties in accurately quantifying the duration and intensity of daily physical activity. The present study addresses these limitations using a 28-day experience sampling design combined with ambulatory accelerometry to assess physical activity not only subjectively but also objectively via accelerometry. A total of 96 young adults (81.2% female; 14.6% male; 4.2% diverse or preferred not to report their gender) aged 18 to 30 years participated in the study, overall providing complete questionnaire and accelerometry data for 2,194 and 2,175 days, respectively. Multilevel analyses revealed that acute physical activity, but not the baseline physical activity level moderated the adverse association of stress experiences with state-levels of positive affect, negative affect, and self-esteem. The stress-buffering effect of acute physical activity was not moderated by the severity of depressive and anxiety symptoms at baseline. Overall, these findings extend existing evidence on the role of physical activity in potentially reducing the adverse consequences of stress by differentiating between acute physical activity and the individual’s baseline physical activity level, considering between-person moderators such as affective symptom severity, and including self-esteem as an additional outcome variable.

articles_hidden.title: Looking into the scientist’s mind: The effects of disclosing scientists’ rationale on students’ scientific reasoning and epistemic beliefs
articles_hidden.authors: Katharina Düsing; Vanessa van den Bogaert; Till Bruckermann; Hannah Greving; Julia Cathérine Thomas; Miriam Brandt; Anke Schumann; Daniel Lewanzik; Christian Voigt; Ute Harms
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated the effects of systematically developed video variations on students’ scientific reasoning (SR) and epistemic beliefs (EBs). Drawing on a novel video development framework, we evaluated four video variations that differed in (i.) how scientific practices were presented—either in a cookbook style (focusing on declarative “what” information) or in a scientific reasoning style (integrating declarative, procedural, and epistemic knowledge) and (ii.) how scientists’ thought processes were presented—either as science-in-the-making (concurrent think-aloud insights) or as ready-made science (post hoc reconstruction of thought processes). In a pre–post design, 512 secondary students each engaged with a digital learning environment in which one of the video variations was embedded. Multivariate analyses of covariance (MANCOVAs) that were conducted to control for pretest performance revealed significant main effects of the presentation formats. The scientific reasoning style fostered more elaborated EBs regarding the source of scientific knowledge compared to the cookbook style. Presenting scientists’ thought processes as science-in-the-making improved EBs (again, regarding the source), whereas ready-made science led to higher SR performance in planning and conducting investigations. These findings demonstrate that fine-grained design choices in video representations of scientific practices support SR and EBs to different degrees. We discuss the implications for future research and for education.

articles_hidden.title: Synchrony under uncertainty. The effects of auditory context on the perception of the temporal location of quasi-musical sounds
articles_hidden.authors: Anne Danielsen; Sabine Leske; Justin London
articles_hidden.abstract: Auditory perception and sensorimotor synchronization always occur within a specific auditory context, a fact that is often overlooked when they are studied in the laboratory. Here we address the question of how our perception of a given sound's temporal characteristics is modulated by the sounds surrounding it. Previous research has highlighted the importance of acoustic factors like attack and duration in defining both a sound's perceived temporal position ("P-center") and the temporal range in which it is heard as synchronized with another sound ("beat bin"). Our experiment investigated whether the same probe/target pair is perceived differently when situated in contexts of sounds with different acoustic features, from contexts of mostly clear, sharply defined sounds to contexts of mostly “muddy,” noisy ones. Our findings reveal that the P-center of the target sound shifts progressively later as the context becomes dominated by sounds with softer onsets, and the variability of P-center location—indicative of the width of the beat bin—also increases under such conditions. These results significantly advance our understanding of how sonic environments influence the perception of a sound's temporal characteristics, and shed light on its underlying neural mechanisms. The study offers new insights into the intricate nature of temporal perception in complex auditory environments and sets the stage for further exploration of the mechanisms underlying auditory processing and synchronization.

articles_hidden.title: The Limits of Identifiability in the Self-Exciting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Model
articles_hidden.authors: Hannah Pongratz; Constantin Gregor Meyer-Grant
articles_hidden.abstract:
Evidence-accumulation models play a central role in the field of decision-making research, offering a comprehensive framework for understanding choice behavior and response times, including speed–accuracy tradeoffs (SATs). In this framework, the dominant explanation for SATs has long been that prioritizing speed lowers the boundary separation, meaning less evidence is needed to make a choice. Recently, however, an alternative account has been proposed according to which emphasizing speed induces a confirmation bias toward the currently favored option. Such a behavior can be formally captured by a self-exciting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. However, drawing on asymptotic arguments and extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, key parameters of the resulting evidence-accumulation model are not jointly identifiable. We explain the underlying cause of this identifiability issue, examine its practical consequences for model-based inference, and
present potential strategies to resolve or mitigate it.

articles_hidden.title: Creating Online Cognitive Assessment Platform for Children’s Literacy and Math Skills: A Case Study Illustrated with the ACE Kids Platform
articles_hidden.authors: Vince S. H. Ngan; Jianhong Mo; Oscar Kwun Pok Wong; Melody Chi Ying Ng; Jana Chi-san Ho; Tomohiro Inoue; Catherine McBride; Urs Maurer
articles_hidden.abstract: Computerized versions of paper-and-pencil tests made behavioral assessments of children more automatic and precise. The COVID-19 pandemic further demonstrated the need for assessments to be offered online to allow for remote data collection. However, the design and implementation of computerized tests in an online environment come with various challenges. This article probes the issues, needs and challenges for the development of online assessment of reading and maths, and related cognitive abilities. The paper aims to inform researchers about logistical and technical considerations of developing a customized platform for online child data collection, including (a) technical considerations, (b) interface design, (c) data management, and (d) planning for validation against paper-and-pencil measures. These issues are illustrated with experiences gleaned from the development of an online assessment platform (ACE Kids platform), designed to deliver over 40 tests and questionnaires related to Chinese and English literacy as well as mathematics abilities in K3 – P6 children. The paper also highlights the unique challenges surrounding building online, self-directed biliteracy assessment involving a large assessment battery. Furthermore, we discuss features that improve the ease of use, instructional clarity, and retention of attention. We discussed the use of questionnaires to sample child usage experience during early stages of assessment development to optimize design. Finally, we give consolidated advice for the planning, development and data collection stages for such a customized assessment platform.

articles_hidden.title: The World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statement: 2026 Update
articles_hidden.authors: Stephen V. Faraone; Alison E. Pritchard; Mark Bellgrove; Jan Buitelaar; Li Yang; Luis Augusto Rohde; Brooke S. G. Molina; David Coghill; Jeffrey H.Newcorn; David W. Goodman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: In the 5 years since the publication of the original ADHD International Consensus Statement, a great deal of new evidence has emerged. This updated consensus statement reflects the current state of the science with respect to ADHD, with a goal of reducing misconceptions and stigma around the disorder.
Methods: Studies eligible for inclusion were published between January 1, 2021 and July 1, 2025 and were either: 1) large cohort studies of 2000 or more participants, or 2) meta-analyses of at least 5 studies or 2000 participants in which publication bias was considered. Eligible studies were summarized and consolidated by theme. Manuscript contents were reviewed and approved by 118 authors from 29 countries and 6 continents.
Results: Two hundred and fifty empirically-supported statements were generated from these studies, offering readers an up-to-date understanding of the most robust findings in the areas of prevalence, how genes and environmental factors shape ADHD, psychiatric and somatic comorbidities, cognitive and neurological differences among individuals with ADHD, functional outcomes, and treatments for the disorder. 
Conclusions: Many of the conclusions of the original Consensus Statement are supported, but this update adds important nuance to some findings as a result of more recent evidence. It also highlights a few areas in which the balance of findings has shifted in the last 5 years, providing a transparent overview of the current scientific state of the field.

articles_hidden.title: When Habits Dominate in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: Tracking the Temporal Dynamics of Habitual and Goal-Directed Control
articles_hidden.authors: Chenyu Yuan; Yinqing Fan; Chaoyi Wu; Jingyi Zhang; Binxin Huang; Tingyue Bai; Trevor William Robbins; Tristan Bekinschtein; Zhen Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Patients with Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder (OCD) often struggle to suppress maladaptive habitual behaviours, yet the temporal dynamics of habit–goal arbitration remain unclear. Here we address this question using an intensive four-day training protocol followed by a time-resolved forced-response test, combined with computational modelling. OCD patients and healthy controls (HCs) showed comparable learning trajectories, indicating intact basic associative learning and perceptual–motor speed in OCD. Critically, when previously learned stimulus–response mappings were remapped, OCD patients exhibited a selective increase in habitual errors, but only within an early time window. At longer preparation times, differences disappeared. Computational model comparison showed that OCD patients were more likely than HCs to be best described by a habit model. Within this model, OCD patients showed reduced variability in habitual preparation latency, reflecting more temporally consistent, sharply tuned habit behaviour. Exploratory analyses linked greater symptom severity to more variable goal-directed preparation. Together, these findings suggest that precisely timed habitual responses are more likely to be expressed during early preparation in OCD. This early-expression bias offers a possible account of ego-dystonic compulsions as a biased race in response preparation, without treating the task as a direct test of competition between independent systems

articles_hidden.title: Citation Fabrication and Accuracy in AI-Generated Psychiatric Research: A Comparative Evaluation of Four Contemporary Large Language Models
articles_hidden.authors: Jake Linardon; Cleo Anderson; Tayarna Bolger; Claudia Liu; Olivia Marie Soliman; Zoe McClure
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives. LLMs are increasingly used to support academic writing, but their tendency to hallucinate citations raises concerns about the integrity of AI-assisted scholarly work. This study provides a timely snapshot of citation reliability in LLM-generated academic reviews by testing whether citation fabrication and accuracy differ across four LLMs and review topic specificity.  

Method. ChatGPT-5.4 Plus, ChatGPT-5.3 Free, Gemini-3, and Claude Sonnet-4.6 were tasked with generating 16 literature reviews on mental health, divided into general topics (broad areas with substantial evidence bases) and specialised topics (narrower areas with smaller evidence bases). 

Results. Only 6.1% of the 825 LLM-generated citations were fabricated, with fabrication absent for ChatGPT-5.4 Plus (0%), very low for Claude Sonnet-4.6 (0.5%) and ChatGPT-5.3 Free (5.5%), and highest for Google Gemini-3 (20.2%). A similar model-level pattern emerged for citation accuracy (real citations containing no bibliographic errors). Review topic specificity was not associated with citation fabrication or accuracy. 

Conclusion. Findings suggest possible improvements in citation reliability relative to estimates from prior studies testing older model iterations, while also showing that current performance is strongly model-dependent. These findings highlight the need for rigorous human verification of LLM-generated references and stronger safeguards to protect research integrity as LLMs are integrated into research.

articles_hidden.title: Values and Political Preferences in Childhood
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher Johnston; Martín Opertti; Turgut Keskintürk
articles_hidden.abstract: Studies of youth political development focus primarily on political socialization and salient events, while paying relatively less attention to important individual differences among children themselves, such as values. We administer an original survey to a sample of 10-to-12-year-olds and show that children's value priorities strongly predict their political preferences, and that one dimension of value priorities continues to predict political preferences even after adjusting for parental values and political preferences. Taken together, our findings suggest that pre-teens already connect their domain-general value priorities to evaluations of political candidates and policies. Our work is consistent with a more agentic view of childhood political development, and lends support to the idea that personal values provide a foundation for the development of political belief systems.

articles_hidden.title: Do bilinguals avoid ambiguity or minimise processing effort? Insights from an online eye-tracking study in spoken Mandarin
articles_hidden.authors: Yajun Liu; Antonella Sorace; Kenny Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Previous research shows that bilinguals tend to choose more explicit referential forms (e.g., overt pronouns over null pronouns) compared to monolingual speakers, but the mechanisms driving this tendency remain debated. By conducting two experiments examining lexical ambiguity in spoken Mandarin, we tested two hypotheses: 
Hypothesis 1: bilinguals would rather be redundant than ambiguous in general; 
Hypothesis 2: bilinguals avoid ambiguity only when doing so helps reduce cognitive load. 
In Experiment 1, L1 Mandarin L2 English speakers in the UK and more-monolingual speakers in China completed a picture naming task, where we manipulated whether the context in which a picture is named makes the preferred label ambiguous (e.g., do speakers avoid saying “fen3 si1” when describing a picture of glass noodles when it appears alongside a picture of fans which shares the same label?). Experiment 2 extended this task by incorporating online eye-tracking using WebGazer. Our results showed that, contrary to Hypothesis 1, bilinguals were more likely than more-monolinguals to use ambiguous expressions. Eye-tracking analysis revealed that bilinguals tended to direct early attention toward image pairs with more accessible labels, indicating a preference for linguistic choices that are cognitively less demanding; by contrast, more-monolinguals showed proactive monitoring of ambiguity depending on their responses. These findings support Hypothesis 2 and shed light on cognitive constraints in bilingual lexical access and early signs of lexical attrition.

articles_hidden.title: Yes, ChatGPT (and other models) need a psychiatrist: parallels between experimental neuropsychiatry and AI alignment science
articles_hidden.authors: Karthik V Sarma
articles_hidden.abstract: AI chatbots (such as ChatGPT or Claude) sometimes state false information with confidence, a behavior popularly termed “hallucination.” In their recent perspective, de Boer et al. [1] compared these errors to confabulation in patients with memory disorders, and asked whether ChatGPT needs a psychiatrist. I argue that it does, but for different reasons. False statements from chatbots may be better explained by how they are trained: first to produce contextually consistent text rather than true text, and later by being rewarded to produce answers. The more meaningful parallel lies elsewhere: because these systems learn to simulate human characters, they may also reproduce human personality traits and patterns resembling the symptoms of mental illness. Understanding them may require the methods of experimental psychiatry and psychology, and could advance our understanding of the human mind.

articles_hidden.title: Bodily Experience Shapes Evaluative Judgements and Attentional Engagement with Affective Touch in Art
articles_hidden.authors: Ionela Bara; Gianluca Saetta; David Crevillén Hernández; Cosimo Gentile; Emanuele Gruppioni; Emily S. Cross
articles_hidden.abstract: Affective touch plays a central role in social interactions by conveying emotion and interpersonal closeness. Yet little is known about whether differences in bodily experience following upper-limb amputation are associated with the emotional, evaluative, and attentional processing of observed affective touch. Across two pre-registered experiments, we examined the extent to which affective touch in art shapes emotional, aesthetic, and attentional engagement, and whether these responses differ following upper-limb amputation. In Experiment 1, artworks depicting touch evoked more positive and intense emotional responses than artworks not depicting touch, with little evidence for a difference in aesthetic appreciation. In Experiment 2, artworks depicting touch received higher ratings across all three measures compared to those not depicting touch, with the amputation group showing greater sensitivity to depicted touch in judgements of aesthetic appreciation than controls. Artworks depicting touch were also fixated later and viewed for less time than artworks not depicting touch, with comparable effects across groups. Furthermore, within artworks depicting touch, the upper region of paintings (depicting facial information) was fixated earlier and viewed for longer than the middle region of paintings (featuring more arm and torso information), suggesting preferential visual attention to socially informative body content. These findings demonstrate that observed affective touch in art carries emotional and aesthetic value beyond direct tactile experience. They further highlight that limb loss selectively reshapes the aesthetic evaluation of touch, rather than its emotional or attentional processing. Together, this work advances our understanding of observed touch by demonstrating that its social-affective meaning, aesthetic importance, and attentional prioritisation are partly dissociable, and that bodily experience selectively shapes its evaluation.

articles_hidden.title: No evidence that positive outcomes elicit a stronger sense of agency once correcting for publication bias: a commentary on, and re-analysis of, Mariano et al. (2025)
articles_hidden.authors: Robrecht van der Wel; Shaheed Azaad; Pernille Hemmer; John Michael
articles_hidden.abstract: In a recent meta-analysis, Mariano et al. (2025) conclude that people experience a stronger sense of agency over positive than negative outcomes, indexed by temporal compression. In this commentary, we evaluate that claim and identify several concerns about its validity. First, we argue that temporal compression effects should be standardized before being combined, because values in milliseconds are not necessarily comparable across different paradigms. When we analyzed standardized effects, evidence for a valence effect was absent once adjusting for publication bias. Second, we identified data integrity issues, identifying several studies that were included but either (1) did not manipulate outcome valence at all, or (2) contained only a positive or negative condition compared to a neutral condition. Excluding these studies meant that even unstandardized effects did not support Mariano et al.’s headline finding.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Factors that Influence Acceptability of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy: Experimental and Correlational Approaches
articles_hidden.authors: Claire Whiting; Jesus A. Arroyo; Erik C Nook
articles_hidden.abstract: Objectives. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are widely used treatments that aim to increase clients' awareness and acceptance of their present-moment experiences. Although delivered as secular treatments, their practices have roots in East and South Asian religious traditions, raising concerns about acceptance among diverse religious or atheistic clients. Other MBI features, such as meditation and group-based formats, may also pose barriers to participation. We report two pre-registered experiments examining factors influencing acceptability of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT). Methods. Study 1 (N = 305) tested whether scientific versus religious framings of MBCT influenced treatment acceptability, and whether effects were moderated by religiosity, existential quest (tendency toward exploratory engagement with existential questions), and scriptural literalism. Study 2 (N = 705) examined whether addressing participants' concerns about MBCT increased acceptability. Results. Contrary to hypotheses, Study 1 found no effects of scientific or religious framing on acceptability. However, regardless of framing, MBCT acceptability was higher among participants with greater existential quest (significantly) and greater religiosity (marginally). In Study 2, addressing participants' concerns (whether tailored to their specific concerns or covering all possible concerns) reduced concerns about MBCT and increased acceptability relative to no intervention. Similar to Study 1, religiosity was positively associated with acceptability regardless of condition. Conclusions. Together, these findings suggest that religiosity and existential quest may shape receptivity to MBCT, and that addressing client concerns, rather than adjusting how treatment is framed, may offer a promising route to increasing acceptability. Understanding these individual differences can inform strategies for engaging diverse populations in MBIs.

articles_hidden.title: Barriers and Facilitators to Implementing Digital, Self-Guided Youth Mental Health Tools in Rural Clinics
articles_hidden.authors: Erica Szkody; Alyssa N Gorkin; Juan Pablo Zapata; Eric Arzubi; Jessica L. Schleider
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Rural youth experience significant barriers to accessing timely and effective mental health care, and digital self-guided interventions may help expand service reach in resource-constrained settings. However, little is known about the implementation determinants influencing adoption of such tools by providers and community partners in rural contexts.
Method: The current study used a rapid qualitative approach to examine barriers and facilitators to implementing a self-guided digital mental health intervention for youth across rural Montana. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with outpatient mental health providers (n = 8) and school-based providers (n = 8) in Montana. Interviews explored experiences with implementation, perceived feasibility, and factors influencing the recommendation and use of the tool with youth. Data were analyzed using a rapid analytic approach and mapped to the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation–Behavior (COM-B) model and the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) to identify implementation determinants.
Results: Findings indicated that capability-related determinants included uncertainty about crisis response procedures, need for clearer implementation guidance, and challenges translating digital tools into practice workflows. Opportunity-related determinants reflected structural and contextual barriers, including limited time, workforce constraints, broadband and access limitations, and concerns regarding privacy, data security, and alignment with rural community needs. Motivation was shaped by a tension between perceived liability and professional risk and strong interest in expanding access to care for underserved youth. Across domains, participants emphasized the importance of trust, transparency, and community alignment in shaping implementation feasibility. Conclusion: Findings informed the development of a dissemination toolkit designed for providers, youth, and caregivers to support implementation of digital mental health tools in rural settings. By translating COM-B- and TDF-informed determinants into practical resources, this work demonstrates how implementation science frameworks can guide real-world strategies to support adoption of digital mental health interventions in underserved communities.

articles_hidden.title: More Data, Worse Inference: How the Imputation Model Decides an Interaction Effect
articles_hidden.authors: Adam Y. Shavit
articles_hidden.abstract:
Interaction hypotheses are central to psychology, and predictors are often incomplete.
Standard guidance recommends multiple imputation (MI), yet "MI" denotes different
procedures once the model contains a product term. We quantify how the imputation model
governs recovery of a continuous × continuous interaction when one predictor is missing.
The simulation spans N = 20–160, 20% and 40% missingness, and both missing-at-random
(MAR) and missing-completely-at-random (MCAR), with 1000 replications per cell and Monte
Carlo standard errors. We compare six methods: listwise deletion, mean imputation,
deterministic regression imputation, and three MI variants — naive,
Just-Another-Variable (JAV), and substantive-model-compatible (SMC-FCS). Congenial
SMC-FCS recovered the interaction with near-nominal coverage; JAV's bias crossed zero
under MAR, reaching +0.017 at N = 160 (4.1 Monte Carlo standard errors), as Seaman et
al. (2012) predict. Under MAR, naive MI — whose imputation model omits the interaction —
attenuated the coefficient by approximately the missing fraction (bias ≈ −π·β₃; about
three-quarters of π under MCAR). Because this bias persists while the standard error
shrinks, 95% coverage collapsed to 0.758 at the largest sample size — worsening, not
improving, as data accrued. Deterministic regression imputation manufactured a spurious
interaction, inflating Type I error to 0.276 under MAR against a nominal 0.05; it is
absent under MCAR and governed by one verified selection moment, the shift outcome- or
covariate-dependent missingness induces in the observed moderator. For interactions,
"multiple imputation" and "full-information maximum likelihood" (Lüdtke et al., 2020)
name families, and the member matters more than the label.

articles_hidden.title: Neural Correlates of Beat Processing in Infancy and Their Association With Later Grammar Development: Evidence for the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis
articles_hidden.authors: Eniko Ladanyi; Srishti Nayak; Catherine T. Bush; Youjia Wang; Tiffany G. Woynaroski; Miriam D Lense; Matthew K. Leonard; Reyna L Gordon
articles_hidden.abstract: Infants show evidence of beat processing from birth, but its neural correlates in infancy remain poorly understood. Moreover, although rhythm and grammar abilities are closely linked in older (school-aged) children, it is not known whether individual differences in infant beat processing lay the foundations for those associations. This longitudinal EEG study examined neural correlates of beat processing in 6–12-month-old infants (N=37) and their relation to sentence comprehension skills in the same children at 4 years. We analyzed infants’ evoked time–frequency responses to rhythmic tone–tone–rest sequences presented in physically accented conditions and in inferred-beat conditions, in which accents were removed after an initial exposure phase.. Analyses revealed a significant increase in power to physically accented beats (9–24 Hz, p < .001). Individual differences in this response were positively associated with receptive grammar performance at age 4, assessed with the TROG-2 (r = .48, p = .005), and remained significant after controlling for infant age, parent education, and home music environment (β = .45, p = .011). The inferred beat effect was not related to later sentence comprehension performance. These findings indicate that infant neural activity tracks beat structure, with neural correlates broadly similar to those reported in adults, and that early neural sensitivity to beat is associated with later grammar development, supporting the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis.

articles_hidden.title: Outcomes of Preregistered Studies Related to Extra-Sensory Perception, and Mind-Matter Interaction: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Patrizio Tressoldi; Lance Storm
articles_hidden.abstract:
This review systematically investigated preregistered studies concerning extra-sensory perception (ESP) and mind-matter interaction (micropsychokinesis; i.e., micro-PK). The primary aims were to evaluate their outcomes and compare the percentage of positive findings with those observed in mainstream psychology. Our methodology adhered to the PRISMA Guidelines. We searched major preregistration repositories, including the Open Science Framework and the Koestler Parapsychology Unit (KPU) Study Registry, and relevant meta-analyses. Inclusion criteria focused on completed studies with available preregistration and final results only for confirmatory hypotheses. A positive outcome was defined as the support of at least one confirmatory hypothesis, strictly following preregistered procedures and statistics without deviation. A total of 46 studies met the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Of these, 15 studies (32.6%) reported a positive outcome, and 17 confirmatory hypotheses out of 81 (21%) were positive.
Interestingly, and contrary to some expectations, a broader comparison indicated that preregistered studies concerning ESP and PK did not necessarily exhibit a much lower proportion of confirmed hypotheses when compared with results for preregistered studies in mainstream psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Infants’ ability to learn novel sound patterns changes with age
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Alejandrina Cristia
articles_hidden.abstract: Learning native language phonotactics could render infants somewhat more inflexible with respect to novel pattern learning. Reanalyses of previously published data and a new study aligned to support this hypothesis: performance in phonotactic learning becomes erratic at about 7 months of age.

articles_hidden.title: The existential function of spiritual yearning
articles_hidden.authors: Daryl R. Van Tongeren; Patty Van Cappellen; Joshua Adam Wilt; Julie J. Exline
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans seek to address existential concerns and strive for equanimity in light of potential threats. Across the (non)religious spectrum, people long for existential comfort and satisfaction—namely, they experience spiritual yearning (Wilt, Van Tongeren, et al., 2026). Across five studies (i.e., four experiments, one longitudinal study; N = 5,791), we examined the existential functions of spiritual yearning. Studies 1-3 (n = 462, n = 922, n = 988) revealed that threats to meaning led to greater reported spiritual yearning to the degree people felt existentially insecure. Study 4 (n = 424) demonstrated longitudinally how spiritual yearning was affected by the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election. To clarify inconsistent small effects, an internal mini-meta-analysis revealed a modest yet significant effect of existential threats on spiritual yearning.  Study 5 (n = 2,995) provided evidence that fulfilled spiritual yearnings enhance existential security, whereas unfulfilled yearnings undermine security. Spiritual yearning may serve existential functions.

articles_hidden.title: Do Ocular and Facial Features Reflect Listening-Related Fatigue and Predict Rest Decisions in Adults With and Without Hearing Loss?
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Dreneva; Johannes Sebastian Wienen; Alina Schulte; Cora J. Caron; Dorothea Wendt; Tobias May; Hamish Innes-Brown; Lorenz Fiedler
articles_hidden.abstract:
Listening-related fatigue is common in individuals with hearing loss and may affect decisions to continue with or disengage from listening, yet its objective assessment remains challenging. We used an effort-based decision-making paradigm to investigate whether subjective fatigue ratings predict objective eye- and face-related measures and whether the combination of subjective and objective measures predicts listen-or-rest decisions during a listening task.
Twenty-seven German-speaking adults with normal hearing (NH; 35.7±13.1 years) and thirty Danish hearing-aid users (HA; 73.7±7.1 years) each completed 126 speech-in-noise trials with varying difficulty and reward, while on each trial they could decide whether to listen or to rest. Subsequently, subjective fatigue ratings were collected after each trial. Eye and facial features were recorded throughout the entire study. Analyses were conducted within groups and proceeded in two stages. First, linear mixed-effects models examined how subjective fatigue, task difficulty, reward, and response correctness predicted each eye and facial metric. Second, these metrics, along with the same predictors, were used to model trial-by-trial rest decisions.
In NH participants, greater subjective fatigue was consistently associated with reduced eye openness and increased gaze velocity (small-to-medium effects), as well as higher blink rates (small effect). In HA users, greater fatigue similarly predicted reduced eye openness and increased gaze velocity (small-to-medium effects), together with a small increase in negative facial expressions. In both groups, rest decisions were more likely when task difficulty was higher, reward was lower, and subjective fatigue was higher. In NH participants, incorrect response and greater eye openness in the preceding trial additionally increased the probability of choosing rest.
This work supports the assumption that ocular and facial indicators may serve as promising markers of preceding subjective fatigue and decisions to rest in people with hearing impairment. Recognizing these markers could play an important role in assessing and managing listening‑related fatigue.

articles_hidden.title: Sleep Helps You Make Good Social Decisions, Even If You’re Not Sure Why
articles_hidden.authors: Lewis Vincent Ball; Yicheng Qiu; Heather Jane Ferguson; M. Gareth Gaskell
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory supports trust decision-making in social encounters. We investigated whether this support is influenced by sleep, given the beneficial effect of sleep on episodic memory. Participants encountered images of cooperative and cheating partners during exposure. Item (is this person old/new?) and source memory (did they cooperate/cheat?) were then measured, before participants chose whether to cooperate with old and new partners. Experiment 1 ruled out time-of-day influences on our measures. In Experiment 2, a ~12 hr delay separated exposure and memory/cooperation phases. The Sleep group slept overnight in between whilst the Wake group experienced a day awake. Experiment 3 replicated the paradigm and measured trust in a contextually-novel task relative to exposure, measuring the extent to which participants would accept each partner as their neighbour. In a combined analysis across Experiments 2 and 3, participant-level item and source memory correlated with the frequency of adaptive decisions. Recognition of cheating partners was enhanced in the Sleep group (item memory), but there were no group differences in recalling the past behaviour of partners (source memory). Participants were more likely to cooperate with cooperators than cheaters and more likely to accept cooperators than cheaters as their neighbours (Experiment 3). Importantly, both effects were enhanced in the Sleep group. These findings are consistent with sleep promoting socially-adaptive decision-making.
