Given there was no significant evidence that sleep influenced explicit memory for behaviours, sleep may facilitate decision-making by integrating new memories into generalised knowledge structures in long-term memory, supporting more flexible decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Motor precision shapes information seeking in perceptual decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Alessandra Loretani; Claire Bédé; thibault gajdos; Andrea Desantis
articles_hidden.abstract: Adaptive behavior relies heavily on the confidence we have in our decisions. For instance, in the absence of explicit feedback, the confidence associated with a decision determines whether we seek additional evidence or are likely to change our mind. Recent studies suggest that confidence estimation also depends on motor processes involved in implementing perceptual decisions. However, whether motor-induced changes in confidence meaningfully affect behavior, such as by altering information-seeking, remains uncertain. The present study addresses this question. Participants performed a perceptual task requiring discrimination of the orientation of Gabor patches. The motor cost of the perceptual response was manipulated by varying the size of the response circles that participants had to reach to report their judgment. Consistent with previous findings showing that easier motor responses are associated with lower confidence ratings, we found that such responses were also linked to a greater tendency to seek additional evidence compared to more costly responses. Importantly, this increase in information-seeking behavior was not accompanied by any change in perceptual accuracy. These findings support the idea that the motor costs associated with perceptual decisions modulate confidence, and that such motor-induced changes in confidence play a functional role in guiding subsequent behavior.

articles_hidden.title: ADHD symptoms, rejection sensitivity and the mediating role of peer rejection: A longitudinal study
articles_hidden.authors: Nina Chmielowice-Szymanski; Antonius H. N. Cillessen; Leentje Vervoort
articles_hidden.abstract:
In addition to challenges explained by neurocognitive differences, young adults with ADHD also
experience challenges related to psychosocial processes. Heightened levels of rejection
sensitivity among young adults with ADHD symptoms may be explained by peer rejection
experiences in adolescence. In the current study, which is part of the Nijmegen Longitudinal
Study, we examined among 116 young adults whether peer rejection experiences in adolescence
(age 16) mediated the association between previous ADHD symptoms (age 12) and rejection
sensitivity (age 20). ADHD symptoms were not significantly associated with peer rejection (β =
0.21, p = .200), which were also not associated with rejection sensitivity (β = 0.05, p = .747). There
was no significant direct effect (β = -0.04, p = .817) or indirect effect (β = -0.01, BCa CI = [-0.02,
0.09]) of ADHD symptoms on rejection sensitivity. The current study provided no evidence for an
association of ADHD symptoms with rejection sensitivity, or a mediating role of peer rejection.

articles_hidden.title: Arousal by Any Other Name? Testing the Specificity of Sexual Arousal in Men’s Cue-Based Judgments of Potential Flirt Partners
articles_hidden.authors: Ingo Landwehr; Alexander F. Schmidt
articles_hidden.abstract: Inferring whether a woman is showing romantic or sexual interest can be challenging, especially when multiple cues conflict or cue integration is influenced by physiological states such as arousal. Building on research linking sexual arousal to men’s overreliance on global cues (OGC) when assessing women’s sexual interest, this preregistered study tested whether a similar cue-weighting bias would emerge under nonsexual arousal. Heterosexual men (N = 275) completed a decision task judging which of two women was more likely to be flirting with them. Stimuli from a validated image set combined global sexual (clothing) and specific affective (facial) cues in congruent versus incongruent pairings. Error rate (ER) indexed OGC, whereas reaction time (RT) captured complementary decision dynamics. Incongruent trials yielded longer RTs and higher ERs, but nonsexual arousal did not reproduce the OGC-related performance pattern previously observed under sexual arousal. Findings suggest that sexual arousal may exert distinct effects on cue weighting and conflict-related processing, highlighting the importance of specifying the conditions under which arousal alters the integration of global sexual and specific affective cues in social judgments.

articles_hidden.title: A Psychometric Analysis and Primer for Decision Making in Public Third-Party Funding Allocation
articles_hidden.authors: Rima-Maria Rahal; Daniel Leising; Finn Luebber
articles_hidden.abstract: A significant portion of research is financed by public resources, with the expectation that it will deliver societal benefits in return. But how good are current funding allocation processes at effectively identifying and supporting research ideas that will end up contributing to societal good? In this primer, we address the critical challenge of assessing the effectiveness of funding allocation procedures by treating the selection process as a diagnostic procedure and applying psychometric tools to its assessment. We highlight an apparent disconnect between the mission of funding beneficial research and prevailing practices in funding allocation, emphasizing a lack of understanding regarding how to measure and predict the quality of research proposals. We advocate for greater transparency in funding decision processes, and for empirical investigations of how funding systems may yield optimal outcomes under existing constraints and objectives.

articles_hidden.title: “If you look at my collection, you get a real flavour of who I am.”  The influence of identity on collectors’ behaviours.
articles_hidden.authors: Tom Robert White; Luke Hodson
articles_hidden.abstract: Collecting is common human behaviour, characterized by purposeful selection of items, forming interrelated sets, and valued beyond their utilitarian use. The extant literature offers insight into collector categories, motivations, and behaviours. However, a paucity of research exists on the specific decisions collectors make and how they are informed by identity. To explore this, the present study utilized semi-structured interviews with ten self-identified collectors of mass-produced products. Thematic Analysis identified an overarching theme: “Habits and Hierarchy,” encapsulating the related, but distinct themes of “Collections Dictate Behaviour” and “Better Than You,” plus further themes: “Need for Control,” with a sub-theme “As Intended?” and “Sacred From The Profane.” These themes illustrate links between specific collecting decisions our sample makes and the influence of self and social identities. The study evidences the connection between identity formation, augmentation and enhancement with decision-making. Specifically, how ‘collector’ identity competes with other self-identities, and how collectors compete amongst themselves, by illustrating how collections are reflective of, and enhance collectors’ individual identities, and how this creates a perceived hierarchy within collector communities.

articles_hidden.title: External and internal attention: Mind the role of switches for memory functioning
articles_hidden.authors: Anaïs Servais; Emmanuel Barbeau
articles_hidden.abstract: Attention continuously shifts between information arising from the external environment and internally generated representations such as thoughts and memories. Episodic memory retrieval provides a particularly relevant case in which attention must be redirected from ongoing perceptual processing toward internal memory representations. In this chapter, we examine this transition through the framework of the Attentional Switch to Memory (ASM), a construct proposed to describe the reorientation of attention from the external world toward the internal mental space supporting episodic memory retrieval. We review elements about the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying this switch and discuss how ASM may differ between strategic (i.e., voluntary) and involuntary memory retrieval. In strategic retrieval, the switch is proposed to occur early, following the establishment of the episodic retrieval mode and before controlled memory search. In involuntary retrieval, by contrast, the attentional shift may occur only after a memory representation has already been partially activated. We further discuss candidate behavioral and physiological markers of the ASM, with a particular focus on gaze aversion, eye movements, pupil dynamics, and changes of vergence. Together, these findings highlight attentional switching as a potentially critical but understudied component of episodic memory retrieval and provide directions for future research aimed at characterizing its temporal, cognitive, and neural dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: ChatGPT Dots for Educators and Students in Psychology  Education
articles_hidden.authors: Oleksii Nalyvaiko
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study examines the conditions for using persistent AI agents in higher education, with ChatGPT Dots and psychology education as its analytical focus. An exploratory documentary analysis was conducted on eight public OpenAI documentation pages: six describing Dots and two providing contextual information on ChatGPT and ChatGPT Work. Sixteen purposively selected source statements were coded and recorded in a ledger that distinguishes documented functionality from 
educational interpretation. The analysis develops the Continuing Educational Delegation (CED) 
framework, consisting of six documented conditions: bounded continuity, separation of task completion from verified achievement, distinction between access and permission, audience boundaries across communication channels, explicit control over continuing work, and recognition of capabilities shared with adjacent ChatGPT workflows. Four constructed scenarios apply the framework to seminar preparation, rubric and feedback development, fictional psychological case analysis, and student research planning. The resulting propositions specify how continuing assistance can be 
organised while preserving assessable student reasoning and educator judgment. A prospective comparative protocol defines twenty-four workflow trajectories and distinguishes artifact quality, human review effort, and student learning as separate evaluation targets. The contribution is a source grounded analytical framework and a reproducible specification for subsequent evaluation. No live Dots trials, participant observations, or measured learning effects are reported; the framework therefore requires empirical examination before claims of educational effectiveness can be made.

articles_hidden.title: The Cultural Logic of Honor and Antisocial Punishment in Social Dilemmas: A Multi-Lab Study Across Three World Regions
articles_hidden.authors: Shuxian Jin; Dina Rabie; Jinkwon Lee; Jinkyung Na; Rania Miniesy; Vivian L Vignoles; Ayse K. Uskul
articles_hidden.abstract: Punishment can sustain cooperation by targeting free riders (prosocial punishment), but it may also backfire by triggering retaliation; and when punishment is directed at cooperators (antisocial punishment), it can lead to a decline in cooperation. Samples exhibiting greater antisocial punishment in previous research have tended to come from societies where honor is believed to play a stronger role in shaping social behavior. Here, we tested the role of honor in antisocial punishment through a preregistered multi-lab experiment conducted in Egypt (n = 266), South Korea (n = 212), and the United Kingdom (n = 192), using public goods games with and without punishment. While the level of antisocial punishment was higher among the Egyptian sample, compared to the South Korean and British samples, individual-level honor values and norms were not associated with antisocial punishment across all three samples. Nevertheless, individuals with stronger personal honor values exhibited heightened retaliation, particularly targeting cooperators after being punished unfairly. These findings suggest that honor is not a cultural aspiration that provokes, nor a norm that prescribes, aggression toward cooperators, but rather a cultural logic that shapes when and for whom punishment becomes a tool of harmful retaliation rather than cooperation enforcement.

articles_hidden.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Qualitative Research Training: Opportunities, Limitations and Lessons from Case Studies in Bilingual Autism Research
articles_hidden.authors: Naomi Portillo; Arisa Rincon Rodgers; Stacey L Bevan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background—Interviews are a fundamental method of qualitative research, yet the opportunity to train interviewers may be limited by time and costs. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new possibilities for generating realistic interview simulations that may support training and skills development for researchers.

Purpose—To explore the feasibility of using a Large Language Model (LLM) to simulate qualitative interview responses and describe the strengths and weaknesses of AI-generated interactions as a training tool for researchers.

Methods— Using clinical case studies from caregivers of autistic children, we created a series of AI-generated interview simulations. Research assistants engaged with simulations in both English and Spanish to evaluate the model’s capacity for multilingual responses to a qualitative interview guide. We present a summary of the responses’ thematic relevance, coherence, and conversational authenticity. A focus was given to the model’s ability to maintain consistency across languages while reflecting the experiences represented in the source data.

Results—AI-generated simulations demonstrated the ability to produce coherent, contextually relevant responses in both English and Spanish, suggesting potential training opportunities in multilingual qualitative research studies. 

Conclusions / Implications for Practice—The findings indicate that AI may support researchers working with linguistically diverse populations by providing accessible opportunities to practice interviewing across languages. Additionally, our team found the simulations especially useful for familiarization with the interview format, question flow, and overall process of conducting qualitative interviews. However, simulations lacked several features characteristic of authentic human interaction, including spontaneity, silence, vocal fillers, and nuanced emotional expression. Despite these limitations, we conclude that AI-generated interview simulations have considerable potential as a supplemental tool for qualitative research training and cross-cultural research applications.

articles_hidden.title: Week-to-Week Variability in Daytime Cortisol Output and Internalizing Problems During the Transition to Preschool
articles_hidden.authors: anonymous; Ke Shen; Zibin Sheng; Ziyin Xiao; Jingmei Wang; Jinliang Qin
articles_hidden.abstract: Entry into preschool is a sustained ecological transition that may challenge young children’s psychobiological adaptation. This study examined whether children’s average daytime cortisol output and its week-to-week variability were differentially associated with internalizing and externalizing problems during preschool transition, while also considering parenting context. Participants were 108 Chinese preschool children. Salivary cortisol was assessed twice during the preschool day on one day in each of three consecutive weeks, allowing us to characterize both average daytime cortisol output and variation in that output across weeks. Parents reported authoritative, authoritarian, and permissive parenting as well as children’s internalizing and externalizing problems. The results showed that young children whose daytime cortisol output varied more from week to week showed more internalizing problems, even when differences in their average cortisol output were taken into account. By contrast, average cortisol output showed little independent relation to internalizing problems, and neither cortisol characteristic was related to externalizing problems. Higher authoritarian and permissive parenting were also associated with more behavioral problems, whereas there was limited evidence that cortisol altered the strength of parenting–behavior associations. Together, these findings suggest that children’s HPA functioning during preschool transition may be characterized not only by how much cortisol they produce, but also by how their cortisol output varies across time.

articles_hidden.title: Formal training in a visual aesthetic domain increases shared taste in a domain-specific manner
articles_hidden.authors: Edward A. Vessel; Claire Reymond; Nancy Etcoff
articles_hidden.abstract: Although there is strong agreement for aesthetic preferences (“shared taste”) for natural kinds such as faces and landscapes, preferences for cultural artifacts such as artwork and architecture are more individual. These differences in aesthetic tastes may reflect differences in how individuals parse their perceptual world. We examined the aesthetic preferences of students enrolled in training programs for visual communication and architecture and hypothesized that formal training in an artistic domain would lead to shifts in which features individuals use to aesthetically evaluate that domain, causing changes in which images are preferred and to an increase in shared taste (convergence) across individuals. In a longitudinal study, 27 architecture and 21 visual communication students viewed images of buildings, posters, and artworks and rated them for both understanding and aesthetic appeal at 3 timepoints spread over two years. A single set of ratings were also collected from 69 online control participants. After two years of training (T3), a double-dissociation pattern emerged: architecture students agreed more on which buildings were aesthetically pleasing and understood, but visual communication students agreed more on which posters were aesthetically pleasing and understood. Average aesthetic ratings, on the other hand, were higher for the domain of study only at T1. These findings demonstrate a clear link between the development of expertise, a key form of learning, and aesthetic appeal. Rather than solely being a function of stimulus-computable features, aesthetic appeal is a function of how a person understands their visual world, reflecting personal biographies of visual experience and knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: Generative AI use and the 2022–2025 decline in PISA performance across countries
articles_hidden.authors: Ernesto Guerra; Ivan Aslanov
articles_hidden.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has spread rapidly among students since 2022, and PISA 2025 recorded its lowest results. In a preregistered study, we related four independent country-level AI-use measures to the mathematics, reading and science PISA performance of 15-year-olds. Countries with more AI use scored higher, but, critically, they also tended to show larger declines or smaller gains between 2022 and 2025, as predicted. This association was no longer detectable after adjusting for 2018 performance, before generative AI existed. AI use was unrelated to change from 2015 to 2018, but some measures were associated with declines from 2018 to 2022, during the pandemic, mainly in mathematics. The spread of country means, stable since 2015, narrowed by 7–9% from 2022 to 2025, as upper-middle performers lost and some low performers, which tend to use AI less, gained relative ground. These patterns suggest AI may have contributed to the recent decline.

articles_hidden.title: Young Children Make Rapid Behavior-to-Behavior Inferences from Costly Social Choices
articles_hidden.authors: Bill Pepe; Lindsey J Powell
articles_hidden.abstract: People’s actions provide insights into their motives and traits. Adults can use just one observed action to make social inferences that guide predictions for how the actor will behave in the future. However, previous work suggests young children require significantly more evidence than older children and adults before they will make such generalized inferences. Here we test whether young children can make rapid behavioral generalizations when a single observed action provides diagnostic evidence about a social motive relevant to later behavior. Building on evidence that children employ a naive utility calculus to understand the values underlying others’ choices, children were introduced to a protagonist who could choose to provide costly, non-obligatory help to a needy target. The protagonist either helped, pursued their own goal, or hindered the target. When asked if the protagonist would help the same target (Exp 1) or a new person (Exp 2) in new scenarios, children were more likely to predict help, toward both same and new targets, from the protagonist who previously helped, and less likely to predict help from the hinderer, relative to a neutral protagonist who did not intervene. These findings provide novel evidence that children can use a single instance of prosocial or antisocial behavior to guide predictions about a person’s future actions, and connect this evidence to current theories of social cognitive development. Overall, results suggest children can rapidly infer motives or traits that guide their expectations for people’s future actions.

articles_hidden.title: Cerebellar contributions to social learning in autistic and nonautistic adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Yen-Wen Chen; Shannon Cahalan; Nicole Grace Treece; Ann Clawson; Alyssa Verbalis; Christoph Korn; Gabriela Rosenblau; Allison Jack
articles_hidden.abstract:
The role of the cerebellum in social learning remains poorly understood. Although the cerebellar posterior lobe (CPL) has been implicated in social decision-making and autistic traits, its contribution to social prediction and prediction-error (PE) processing during learning is unclear. We focused on adolescence, a critical developmental period for social decision-making and learning. 71 autistic (AUT) and 75 non-autistic (N-AUT) participants completed social and non-social learning tasks during fMRI. Preregistered hypotheses predicted that the CPL would be involved in prediction and PE processing, with effects differing by diagnostic status and age.

We found no group differences in social learning. Across participants, PEs decreased more steeply during non-social than social learning; in the AUT group this difference between social and non-social learning was more pronounced. In the cerebellum, PE-related activity in the CPL (lobules Crus I/II, VI, and VIIb) showed group- and age-related differences. Contrary to our hypothesis, PE-related activity during social learning was greater in AUT than N-AUT participants in right Crus II. Across several other CPL regions, PE-related activity increased with age in N-AUT participants but showed the opposite pattern in AUT participants. Mirroring the marginally steeper behavioral PE reduction in the non-social condition in the AUT vs. the N-AUT group, PE-related brain activity was greater for non-social than social PEs in left Crus I and right lobule VI in the AUT group. Exploratory searchlight analyses showed greater PE-related connectivity between left Crus II and prefrontal cortex in AUT than N-AUT participants. 

These findings suggest that AUT adolescents may engage CPL differently during learning, particularly for social versus non-social information. Greater CPL activity and connectivity during social learning in AUT may reflect compensatory mechanisms supporting comparable behavioral performance to N-AUT youth.

articles_hidden.title: Intentional Forgetting of Autobiographical Memories: Current Neuroimaging Evidence and Moving Towards an Integrationist EEG-fMRI Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal; Palmer Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Intentional Forgetting (INF) is one of many human memory processes which has gathered academic intrigue in emergent literature. Understood as a conscious and voluntary cognitive effort to suppress the recall of, or remove certain memories, INF has been extensively studied in associative paradigms. However, its application to autobiographical memory (AM) remains under-investigated, especially within neuroimaging studies. First, we summarize existing neuroimaging literature on intentional forgetting of autobiographical memories (INF-AM). Upon reviewing, we found evidence to be fragmented, providing no clear consensus around the neural bases of INF-AM. We argue this fragmentation is, in part, a result of a reliance on single-modality applications of electroencephalograph (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) methodology. 
EEG and fMRI, however, are complementary in their respective temporal and spatial superiority. Subsequently, we propose the application of an EEG-fMRI integrationist approach to INF-AM. We discuss how its application may help address conceptual, paradigm-level, and methodological concerns. Since human AM and the process of forgetting are inherently longitudinal, we contrast the popular cross-sectional design with a longitudinal alternative. We then present the application of the integrationist approach to longitudinal INF-AM designs. Though cognizant of the limitations that may accompany such an approach, we present the integrationist approach as a much needed and promising way forward in decoding the neuroscience of INF-AM.

Keywords: intentional forgetting, autobiographical memory, neuroimaging, EEG-fMRI, integrationist

articles_hidden.title: Longitudinal associations between adverse childhood experiences and alcohol use and misuse among Mexican-origin adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Jenny Zhen-Duan; Nubia A. Mayorga; Lulu Zhang; Mario Cruz-Gonzalez; Margarita Alegria
articles_hidden.abstract: Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are potentially traumatic childhood stressors associated with elevated risk for problematic alcohol use and alcohol use disorder (AUD). Mexican-origin adults exhibit high rates of heavy drinking, underscoring the importance of identifying early risk and protective factors. This study examined prospective associations between family- and community-level ACEs and alcohol outcomes among Mexican-origin adolescents and evaluated familism and family cohesion as potential protective factors. Data came from a three-wave longitudinal community study of 344 Mexican-origin youth assessed between April 2021 and October 2024. Linear and logistic regression models examined prospective associations between Wave 1 ACEs and alcohol outcomes (problematic drinking and probable AUD) at Waves 2 and 3. Familism and family cohesion were tested as main effects and moderators. Family-level ACEs at Wave 1 were associated with higher problematic drinking and increased odds of probable AUD at Wave 3. Community-level ACEs were not significantly associated with alcohol outcomes. Higher family cohesion at Wave 1 was associated with lower alcohol use and reduced odds of probable AUD at Wave 2, and higher familism was associated with lower odds of probable AUD at Wave 3. However, the interaction effects between ACEs and protective factors were nonsignificant. Results underscore adolescence as a critical period for trauma-informed prevention and interventions, when the behavioral consequences of maltreatment and family dysfunction may already be emerging, but trajectories of alcohol-related harm are not yet established.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental and social variation in spatial behavior among BaYaka hunter-gatherers
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Pope-Caldwell; Lee Gettler; Adam Boyette; Yann R. Ouamba; Alyssa N. Crittenden; Sheina Lew-Levy
articles_hidden.abstract: Effectively choosing between exploring alternative strategies versus exploiting familiar ones is a keyaspect of adaptive behavior. Previous research suggests that exploration in early life gives way tomore targeted exploitation with age. Further, group composition can shape one’s propensity forexploration   and   exploitation.   Yet,   few   studies   have   investigated   how   individual   cognitivedevelopment and collective intelligence articulate to help resolve the explore-exploit dilemma in real-world contexts. Here, we investigated spatial behavior in BaYaka hunter-gatherer children and adultsfrom the Republic of the Congo. We used 337 foraging GPS tracks collected across 42 days toinvestigate how individual age and group composition (child-only, mixed-age, adult-only) predictedsix spatial behaviors during real-world foraging bouts. We found that children's foraging paths weremore sinuous—that is, most exploratory—when travelling with peers than with adults. In contrast,mixed-age groups travelled further and covered more unique ground than child-only groups. Wesuggest that this may be indicative of distinct learning goals across foraging social contexts. Wefurther propose that child-only exploration alongside more adult-like exploitation may operate ascomplementary components of an age-graded division of cognitive labor, with discoveries made bychildren during exploratory foraging informing adults' subsequent resource exploitation.

articles_hidden.title: A Taxometric Analysis of the Three-Item UCLA Loneliness Scale in the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project
articles_hidden.authors: Savannah M. Boyd; David Sbarra
articles_hidden.abstract: Loneliness is a well-established risk factor for physical and mental health in later life. This work responds to recent calls to examine the dimensionality of the UCLA Loneliness Scale among older adults. In a preregistered secondary analysis using three measurement occasions from the publicly available National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project (NSHAP), we applied taxometric analyses (i.e., mean above minus below a cut, maximum eigenvalue, latent mode factor analysis, and comparison curve fit index) to examine the latent structure of the 3-item UCLA Loneliness Scale. Results supported the preregistered hypothesis, showing the mean comparison curve fit index (CCFI) was below 0.45 on each measurement occasion (CCFI range: 0.23 – 0.35). Therefore, loneliness, as measured in this sample, likely follows a continuous rather than categorical distribution, with no clear cut point. These findings inform statistical decision-making regarding loneliness classification and use of this scale in this sample.

articles_hidden.title: Morpho-phonetic adaptation is realised in multiple cues: evidence from articulography
articles_hidden.authors: Motoki Saito; Jessie S. Nixon
articles_hidden.abstract: A critical issue in models of speech production concerns the modularity of processing: for example, can information from morphology influence the articulation of phonologically identical segments? A phenomenon that has the potential to help shed light on this question is what we term morpho-phonetic adaptation: systematic phonetic differences in identical segments patterning with morphological differences. Previous studies have been largely inconclusive, finding longer (enhancement) and shorter (reduction) duration of affixes, as well as null effects. The occurrence of morpho-phonetic adaptation for affixes suggests that morphological information can indeed influence segment articulation. However, to date, most studies have involved acoustic realisations in English. If it is the case that morphology interacts with phonetics, such morphological effects should also be observed in languages other than English. We also hypothesise that effects should also occur in articulatory realisations such as tongue movements. In the present study, we compared acoustic duration and tongue movements between two German suffixes -er [ɐ] and -t [-t]. We found that the suffixal -er [ɐ] was significantly longer in duration and significantly lower in tongue positions than its segmentally identical non-suffixal counterpart, and the lower tongue position could not be simply attributed to longer duration. Importantly, however, no effect of morphological status was found for -t [-t] for either duration or articulatory trajectory. These findings show that morpho-phonetic adaptation manifests in multiple cues and may depend on segment identity, with implications for models of speech production.

articles_hidden.title: The limits of ensemble perception: Hierarchical grouping and object-based encoding
articles_hidden.authors: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth; Bilge Sayim
articles_hidden.abstract:
The visual system can efficiently summarize information by extracting ensemble statistics such
as the average of visual features. However, it remains unclear how ensemble perception
operates when individual features are grouped into meaningful objects. In the present study,
we investigated whether ensemble statistics of local features can still be extracted when
oriented line segments form letters. Across two experiments, observers estimated the average
orientation of line elements either as unconnected lines in a typical ensemble display, arranged
into intact letters, or transformed into pseudo-letters. Although the number and orientation of
line elements were identical across conditions, grouping into meaningful letters systematically
impaired performance. Grouping interfered with observers’ ability to estimate average
orientation when intact letters did not provide a useful global orientation cue, leading to larger
errors and greater response variability than pseudo-letters or ungrouped lines. However, when
the average orientation coincided with the mirror-symmetry axis of a letter, observers could
rely on this global structure, resulting in improved performance. Crucially, these effects
replicated in peripheral vision, indicating that ensemble extraction is constrained by perceptual
organization even when access to local feature information is limited. Together, these results
show that ensemble perception is modulated by object-based grouping and perceptual
organization.

articles_hidden.title: Do ‘tortured phrases’ exist in the psychology literature, and are there psychology-specific ‘tortured phrases’?
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick Nebl; Mark G McCoy; Jaime A. Teixeira da Silva
articles_hidden.abstract: Objectives: The psychology literature is occasionally quoted as being in a replication crisis due to the inability to replicate key findings caused by either integrity issues, or weak scientific protocols. This paper focuses on an unexplored topic in psychological science, ‘tortured phrases’, first to appreciate whether any psychology literature might contain such ambiguous terms, even if they are not related to psychology per se. Methods and Results: The Tortured Phrases Detector (TPD) of the Problematic Paper Screener revealed 36 journal articles (including one proceedings paper) with tortured phrases, 14 of which have been retracted to date (10 October 2025). We then induced, using a free online paraphraser, a novel methodology for detecting ‘tortured phrases’, by converting 50 standard psychological terms that started with the letter “A” into purposefully created ‘tortured phrases’. We employed Google Scholar to detect whether any of these created ‘tortured phrases’ might actually exist in published literature. The second method, with only 50 terms, was able to detect at least one potential ‘tortured phrase’ (“evaluation utensil” used to represent “assessment instrument”). Conclusions: The exploratory nature of the methodology was prone to false positives but had success. It is our hope that this study will inspire further attempts to detect tortured phrases in psychology literature in order to further increase the scientific and ethical rigor in the field of psychology.

articles_hidden.title: CortexLume: Rapid Geometry-Adaptive Cortical Feedback for Target-Informed fNIRS Design
articles_hidden.authors: Ruiyi Huang
articles_hidden.abstract: Target-informed functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) probe design requires repeated evaluation of how candidate source-detector geometries sample the cortex, but full photon-transport modeling is too costly for interactive revision. We developed CortexLume, which couples an editable target-patch-placement representation with a geometry-adaptive cortical surrogate for rapid spatial assessment. The surrogate adapts its center, orientation, and anisotropic extent to fitted source-detector geometry and local scalp-cortex relationships, and is intended to approximate normalized cortical spatial allocation rather than absolute optical sensitivity. We benchmarked the method against MCX photon transport assembled through AtlasViewer on the ICBM152 anatomical model and then evaluated the frozen formulation on the independent Colin27 model without retuning. On ICBM152, mean channel-centroid discrepancy was 2.35 mm, 90%-mass Dice was 0.746 per channel and 0.826 per patch, and Jensen-Shannon distance was 0.330; the complete formulation improved Dice in 370 of 396 channels relative to a restricted reference. On Colin27, mean channel Dice was 0.748 and patch Dice was 0.812 across 88 retained channels. Patch-field construction required a median of only 75.81 ms. These results support CortexLume as a rapid cortical surrogate for iterative probe drafting and candidate shortlisting, with subject-specific photon modeling retained for final optical refinement.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing psychological, neural and AI-based representational geometries across multiple similarity properties
articles_hidden.authors: Johan Alejandro Gamba; Megan A. K. Peters; Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel; Brian Odegaard
articles_hidden.abstract: Assessing similarity between objects is a fundamental cognitive process, and similarity judgments can assess many different attributes, including objective properties (color, shape) or subjective appraisals (preference, scariness). Here, we investigated how psychological similarity across eight different properties relates to neural representational geometries and artificial models. We first collected large-scale pairwise similarity ratings for 280 objects. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and multidimensional scaling, we identified three mental representational spaces: one defined by multiple object features and general similarity, a second by affective evaluations, and a third by color. Combining fMRI and RSA in 80 participants, we found that object feature ratings significantly correlated with representational structures in visual and prefrontal cortices. Unexpectedly, affective ratings also correlated with patterns in visual cortices. Crucially, regional variability strongly shaped these correspondences: visual cortices exhibited high noise ceilings and consistent alignment with behavior, whereas associative regions showed greater across-subjects variability and weaker correlations. Finally, algorithms and neural networks with high classification performance on specific properties strongly correlated with behavioral and fMRI RSA matrices. Together, these results demonstrate that similarity is a multidimensional construct that comprises multiple representational spaces whose neural correspondence is shaped by representational content, regional variability, and modeling methodology.

articles_hidden.title: Ready and Willing? Psychological Conditions for Demand-Side Climate Policy in a High-Income Country
articles_hidden.authors: Alaa Aldoh; Jan Michael Bauer; Joachim Peter Tilsted; Mads Ejsing; Cameron Brick; Kristian Steensen Nielsen
articles_hidden.abstract: Climate policy in high-income countries disproportionately prioritizes supply- over demand-side solutions requiring citizen behavior change. This skew partly reflects policymakers’ skepticism about citizens’ readiness and capacity for behavior change. Yet, it remains unclear whether this skepticism reflects actual conditions for demand-side engagement, how climate-relevant perceptions interrelate, and which factors predict perceived feasibility of changing high-impact behaviors. We address these questions using a nationally representative survey of 2,005 adults in Denmark—a high-income, climate-progressive country where supply-side solutions dominate despite ambitious mitigation targets. We map climate-relevant perceptions using network analysis and estimate associations with perceived behavioral plasticity across eight high-impact behaviors using Bayesian ordinal regression. The Danish public is highly concerned about climate change and expresses a strong personal responsibility for mitigation. Perceived behavioral plasticity closely tracked perceived (but not objective) climate footprints of behaviors. Carbon footprint literacy was low: participants overestimated footprints of low-impact behaviors (e.g., waste sorting) and underestimated high-impact ones (e.g., dietary change). Network analysis revealed a dense interconnected system with personal responsibility as the most central node; perceived behavioral plasticity clustered with measured psychological factors, suggesting a mutually reinforcing system. Regression models indicate that personal responsibility, climate change concern, perceived behavioral impact, and social norms consistently relate to the plasticity of eight impactful climate-relevant behaviors; higher-income households reported lower plasticity of several behaviors. Together, these findings challenge the dismissal of demand-side solutions. Psychological conditions for behavioral engagement are favorable; realizing this potential requires pairing communication strategies that strengthen norms and correct misperceptions of behavioral impact with structural policies that make high-impact change affordable and accessible.

articles_hidden.title: Vision and body representation: Insights from blindness
articles_hidden.authors: Dominika Radziun; Luke E. Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Body representations arise from the integration of multiple sensory signals that provide information about the body’s size, posture, and internal states. Vision often plays a dominant role, calibrating and aligning signals from touch, proprioception, and interoception. Yet, individuals born without sight still construct coherent and functional body representations, suggesting that the role of vision in building these representations may be more flexible than previously thought. Here, we synthesize recent behavioral and neuroimaging findings on body representations in blind individuals. We argue that blindness offers a powerful case study in how body representations can emerge through non-visual pathways, revealing the brain’s capacity to flexibly reorganize the sensory inputs supporting its internal models of the body. In doing so, we highlight the broader relevance of visual loss for understanding the plastic and multisensory nature of body representation.

articles_hidden.title: More Than a Keypress: Continuous Key-Actuation Dynamics for Decomposing Speeded Responses
articles_hidden.authors: David Levi Tekampe; Philip Samuel Santangelo
articles_hidden.abstract: Conventional keypress measurement reduces a continuous motor action to a discrete event, typically represented by reaction time (RT) and accuracy. The present study evaluated continuous analogue key-actuation as a method for characterising the unfolding response while retaining a conventional two-choice keypress format. Seventy-seven adults completed the Attention Network Test-Revised (ANT-R) while response-key depth was recorded continuously. We derived target- and press-locked waveforms together with pre-specified measures of response timing, morphology, variability, preparation, and bilateral coor-dination. Established ANT-R manipulations served as experimentally controlled tests of measurement sensitivity. Target-locked waveforms differentiated six of the seven planned ANT-R contrasts after Holm adjustment; location conflict was not significant, and the alerting effect was less robust in sensitivity analyses. No exploratory press-locked contrast survived mul-tiplicity correction. Initiation time and peak-actuation time showed reliable effects across multiple attentional contrasts, whereas ramp time (the initiation-to-peak interval) showed no reliable modulation. Effects in the morphology, coordination, and preparation/control families were more selective and were confined to flanker conflict. Exploratory models further showed that ramp, rise-to-maximum, and return durations and hold jitter predicted trial-level accuracy after controlling for RT, whereas initiation time did not. These findings show that continuous key-actuation can decompose when a speeded re-sponse begins and how it unfolds, while selected key-actuation measures provide response-quality information beyond con-ventional RT. Continuous key-actuation therefore provides an experimentally sensitive measurement approach for extending standard keypress responses, although reliability and cross-device generalisation remain to be established.

articles_hidden.title: The eyes have it: Perceived ocular vitality as a unifying account of eye-region dominance in social perception
articles_hidden.authors: Shiyun Zhang Isabelle
articles_hidden.abstract: The eye region has an outsized influence on first impressions of faces. Its surface features, however, have been studied one cue at a time. This narrative integrative review proposes perceived ocular vitality as a unifying construct: an observer-side inference of youthfulness, health, and alertness drawn from the eye and periocular region. Five cue domains are evaluated: periocular contrast, scleral coloration, scleral exposure, limbal ring prominence, and iris luminance and framing. Evidence ranges from strong (periocular contrast; limbal ring health effects) to contested (the direction of the pupil-size effect). Two experimentally confirmed interactions, one so far shown only with non-human primate faces, suggest that the cues work jointly. Together they also expose confounds that single-cue designs miss. Chief among them, the limbal ring health effect appears to be carried substantially by scleral brightening. Within cue-based overgeneralization theory, the construct has two channels with pre-specified routing. Photometric cues carry youth and health to the valence dimension of face evaluation. Structural cues make the eye legible, which observers read as alertness, and are predicted to reach the dominance dimension as well. The construct is specified precisely enough to be falsified, and an analysis of an existing normed corpus could decide it.

articles_hidden.title: The Association Between SES and Students’ Achievement Motivation in Secondary School: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis Spanning Two Decades of PISA Data
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Grünthal; Lena Keller; Julia Kretschmann; Hanna Dumont; Martin Brunner
articles_hidden.abstract: Major theoretical frameworks of achievement motivation link family socioeconomic status (SES) to students’ achievement motivation in school settings. However, systematic evidence on this association remains limited. This study presents the first meta-analysis on this topic, using representative individual participant data (IPD) from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). The analysis included 485 student samples comprising a total of 3,576,278 15-year-old students, spanning four SES indicators, eight achievement motivation components, four academic domains, 92 countries, and eight assessment cycles across more than two decades (2000–2022). The average meta-analytic association between SES and achievement motivation was small (r = .10, 95% CI [.09, .11]), indicating slightly higher achievement motivation among students from higher-SES families. The magnitude of the association varied meaningfully across SES indicators and motivational components, but only marginally across academic domains. Educational home resources (e.g., books, educational materials) showed stronger associations with achievement motivation than parental education or occupational status, and self-efficacy exhibited the largest association among motivational components. The association increased over historical time but declined following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. After controlling for academic achievement, the meta-analytic average association between family SES and achievement motivation remained statistically significant, but its magnitude was attenuated. These nuanced findings highlight the complex association between family SES and students’ achievement motivation, emphasizing the multidimensionality of both constructs and providing an important empirical foundation for evaluating, refining, and advancing psychological theories that address the link between family SES and students’ achievement motivation.

articles_hidden.title: Validating the Chinese Version of the Manifestation Scale (CVMS): Translation, Cultural Adaptation and Psychometric Extension
articles_hidden.authors: Jiaqi Guo; Lucas J Dixon; Kehan Mei; Mei Shi
articles_hidden.abstract: The Manifestation Scale assesses belief in metaphysically attracting success through positive self-talk, visualization, and symbolic actions. We translated and validated a Chinese version (CVMS) in 1,901 Chinese-speaking adults and compared it with data from 1,023 English-speaking participants. Analyses supported correlated Personal Power and Cosmic Collaboration dimensions within a broader general manifestation construct. Cosmic Collaboration was more distinct in the CVMS, and one item contributed more clearly to the general factor than to specific factors. Findings supported an 11-item Total scale, a six-item Personal Power subscale, and a four-item Cosmic Collaboration subscale, with high internal consistency and three-month stability. Partial scalar invariance supported cross-language latent comparisons. Associations with positive thought-action fusion, hope, perceived success, risk propensity, and get-rich-quick beliefs broadly replicated validity, alongside some cross-language differences in how the scale dimensions were related to metaphysical belief. The CVMS provides the first evidence that manifestation belief can be measured beyond Western contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Calling Development: A Systematic Review of Longitudinal Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Sophie Gerdel; Anna Dalla Rosa; Bryan Dik; Michelangelo Vianello
articles_hidden.abstract: Although career calling is linked to many beneficial outcomes for both individuals and organizations, knowledge on how a sense of calling develops is limited and, in some ways, controversial. To clarify this issue, we conducted a systematic review of longitudinal studies that analyzed the temporal relation between calling and other variables in its nomological network. Across 14 studies, the strongest longitudinal evidence suggests that calling is more often an outcome of career development processes rather than an initiating cause. Specifically, vocational self-definition, agency, and career feedback and appraisal appear to precede calling, whereas personal resources more often follow calling, and life meaning and values appears reciprocally linked with calling. On this basis, we propose a preliminary integrative developmental framework of calling in which calling emerges through recursive cycles of career clarification, agentic engagement, contextual feedback and appraisal, and life meaning- and value-based integration.

articles_hidden.title: La Pirámide del Sueño: desarrollo y difusión nacional de una herramienta de comunicación basada en hábitos para promover un sueño saludable
articles_hidden.authors: Manuel Armayones; Sílvia Gismera; Laura Armayones-Carranza
articles_hidden.abstract: La Pirámide del Sueño es una herramienta de educación para la salud que ordena las recomendaciones de higiene del sueño en cuatro niveles: ritmos y horarios; hábitos y rutinas que ayudan a desconectar; ambiente óptimo para el sueño, y estrategias en la cama. Se desarrolló en la Alianza por el Sueño combinando el formato, ya familiar, de las pirámides alimentarias con el enfoque de diseño de conducta y formación de hábitos de Fogg, que convierte cada recomendación en un pequeño hábito asociado a una rutina. Se presentó en mayo de 2025 con 26 organizaciones colaboradoras y, según el seguimiento de medios, generó 210 impactos informativos y 26 entrevistas, con una audiencia acumulada de 69,9 millones, además de 260 menciones en redes sociales. Unir una metáfora visual conocida y un modelo sencillo de formación de hábitos es una estrategia viable y de bajo coste para promover el sueño saludable; su efecto sobre la conducta está por evaluar.

articles_hidden.title: Face inversion, familiarity and cropping: floating heads are peculiar
articles_hidden.authors: Mia Hanson; Lydia Rebecca Searle; David Pitcher; Mike Burton
articles_hidden.abstract:
Visual processing of faces is widely reported to be disrupted by inversion. Furthermore, this
effect is held to be greater for faces than many other visual stimuli – the face inversion effect
(FIE). However, there have been some recent challenges to the idea that faces are
disproportionately affected by inversion. Here we examine the effects of familiarity and
stimulus-cropping on the FIE. In two experiments we show (i) larger effects of inversion for
familiar over unfamiliar faces; and (ii) much larger effects of inversion for heavily cropped
“floating head” stimuli, by comparison to full photographic images. This raises the
possibility that FIE appears disproportionately large because of the highly artificial cropped
stimuli used in very many perceptual experiments. More naturalistic stimuli, almost never
examined in the literature, give rise to inversion effects, but these are more modest in size.
Finally, the large effect of familiarity highlights the task used to test face perception (a
familiarity decision here) and suggests that a very early processing account of the FIE may
not be satisfactory.

articles_hidden.title: Spatial Aspects of Felt Presence and the Phenomenon of Childhood Imaginary Companions: Peripersonal Space, Embodied Perspective, and Continuity of Agent Propensity
articles_hidden.authors: Burak; Bigna Lenggenhager
articles_hidden.abstract:
Felt presence (FP) refers to the experience of sensing another agent nearby despite the
absence of corresponding sensory evidence, and has been reported across neurological,
psychiatric, and non-clinical populations. However, its potential phenomenological similarity and
continuity with the common childhood experience of imaginary companions (ICs) have received
little attention. The present study characterizes the spatial and perspectival features of
retrospectively reported childhood IC experiences, evaluates their parallels with the
phenomenology of FP, and interprets these convergences within the theoretical framework of
bodily self-consciousness (BSC) and peripersonal space (PPS). Three theory-driven predictions
were tested using retrospective self-reports from a healthy adult sample (N = 185; IC+ = 45; IC−
= 140) excluding participants with psychiatric or neurological diagnoses. First, we examined
whether IC representations were spatially anchored within PPS (Peripersonal Anchoring). Second,
we assessed whether IC experiences were predominantly reported from an embodied, first-person
or third-person perspective. Third, we tested whether individuals reporting childhood ICs show a
greater adult propensity for presence-related experiences (Continuity of Agent Propensity).
Results supported all three predictions. Most spatial distance reports (76.1%) fell within 70 cm of
the body, with an overall median distance of 12 cm, consistent with PPS anchoring. IC experiences
were primarily reported from a first-person perspective (55.6%) and referenced to the body
(88.9%). Furthermore, individuals with childhood ICs reported higher scores on the Sensed
Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ; 15 items, excluding Item 7 due to cross-loading) during
adulthood, whereas dissociative tendencies did not differ between groups. Exploratory logistic
regression identified perceived presence proneness as the only significant predictor of IC history.
Together, these findings suggest that both adult FP and childhood IC experiences may be grounded
in the spatial organization of the bodily action field and reflect a stable disposition for internally
generated social-agent representations.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive reserve differently impacts cognition and metacognition across domains
articles_hidden.authors: Audrey Mazancieux; Lucile Meunier-Duperray; Coline Grégoire; Christine Bastin; Céline Souchay; Chris Moulin; Lucie Angel
articles_hidden.abstract: Preservative effects of cognitive reserve on age-related decline have been widely studied in episodic memory, however less is known about how cognitive reserve influences other domains such as semantic memory or visual perception. Similarly, recent studies suggest that the decline of metacognition observed with age might be reduced by cognitive reserve in the memory domain, but the domain-generality of such effect remains unexplored. This study is part of a published study investigating the effect of age on cognition and metacognition in episodic memory, semantic memory, executive functioning, and visual perception (Meunier-Duperray et al., 2025). Here, we focused on cognitive reserve measured by the CRIq on cognition (i.e., task performance) and metacognition in a subsample of 319 participants (aged from 18 to 79). We expected an effect of cognitive reserve only on tasks sensitive to age-related decline: episodic memory, executive functioning, and visual perception for task performance and episodic and semantic tasks for metacognition. Overall, these results suggest evidence for the null hypothesis for the effect of cognitive reserve on the age-related decline in cognition and metacognition. Only anecdotal to small evidence was found for an effect of cognitive reserve on episodic memory performance across the lifespan suggesting that reserve reflects earlier individual differences rather than differences in the rate of decline. However, the low variability of our high-reserve sample may have masked some effects.

articles_hidden.title: When attention turns inward: Mind wandering reduces perceptual sensitivity across visual fields
articles_hidden.authors: Bianca de Haan
articles_hidden.abstract: We all mind wander from time to time, where instead of being focussed on our task, we start thinking about task-unrelated personal events or concerns. In daily life, however, mind wandering is often associated with reduced processing of external information. This is commonly explained by the decoupling hypothesis, which posits that processing of external sensory information is attenuated when attention turns inward. However, it remains unclear whether perceptual decoupling reflects a global, uniform attenuation of sensory processing, or a spatially-specific reduction linked to lateralised attentional mechanisms. In the current, pre-registered study, we used an online signal detection task to assess the impact of mind wandering on perceptual performance in the left and right visual fields. While performing the task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering or on task. Consistent with the decoupling hypothesis, perceptual sensitivity (d′) was significantly reduced on trials during which participants reported mind wandering compared to on-task trials. However, this reduction in sensitivity did not differ between stimuli presented in the left and right visual field. These findings suggest that perceptual decoupling during mind wandering reflects a global attenuation of sensory processing, and that attentional systems involved during mind wandering may be distinct from those associated with slower fluctuations of attentional resources such as reductions in alertness.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring the Role of Physical Effort in the Rewarding Value of Sedentary Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Silvio Maltagliati; Pam ten Broeke; Philippe Sarrazin; Ryan Rhodes; Erik Bijleveld; Genevieve Fridlund Dunton; Cedrick Bonnet; Benjamin Gardner; David A. Raichlen; Matthew W Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Sedentary behavior is commonly studied based on the value of the higher-order task being performed, such as watching TV, using a phone, or playing video games. However, it is possible that the low physical effort associated with these behaviors also contributes to their appeal. That is, individuals may be drawn not just to the task but to the low effort it is paired with. This study aims to test this possibility by manipulating body position (sitting vs. standing) while participants engage in a familiar sedentary task (i.e., playing Tetris). Methods: To test this hypothesis, we manipulated body position during a smartphone video game task to examine how sitting versus standing affected the rewarding value assigned to the game. Results: Our results (two independent studies, N = 228 and N = 129) show that the rewarding value of this sedentary behavior also stems from the low effort cost associated with sitting. Conclusions: These findings suggest that the perception of effort may contribute to influencing sedentary preferences and provide valuable insights for interventions aimed at reducing excessive sedentary behavior, such as targeted strategies to increase the valuation of physical effort.

articles_hidden.title: Iconicity and Age Make Distinct Contributions to Symbolic Correspondence in Early Childhood
articles_hidden.authors: Keyi Yang; Ruoxi Chen; Suizi Xue; Jiajia Zhou; anonymous; Juan Wang; Jingmei Wang; Jinliang Qin
articles_hidden.abstract: Iconicity has been proposed to support children’s symbolic understanding, yet it remains unclear when iconicity contributes to symbolic correspondence and how this contribution varies across early childhood. The present study examined semantic judgments in 204 Chinese preschool children (Mage = 5.36 years, SD = 0.78; 102 boys) across three representational formats: line drawings, Oracle Bone script, and simplified Chinese characters. Children judged whether sequentially presented picture–symbol pairs referred to the same objects or actions, allowing broad format differences to be distinguished from graded item-level iconicity within each format. Children were consistently more accurate when rejecting mismatches than when confirming matches. Iconicity was especially informative when children had to confirm that different forms shared a meaning. Diffusion decision modeling further showed that this advantage was expressed in the accumulation of decision-relevant evidence during confirmation. Older age was associated with more efficient evidence accumulation for establishing semantic correspondence across representational formats, but age did not systematically strengthen or weaken the iconicity-drift relation. These findings suggest that iconicity and age make distinct contributions to symbolic correspondence: iconicity functions as a task-dependent source of information, whereas age-related differences are characterized by broader gains in the efficiency of establishing correspondence across symbolic forms.

articles_hidden.title: Sentiment Analysis of Clinical Interviews Identifies Language Markers of Identity Diffusion in Adolescents with Personality Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Katarina Lodrant; Filip Melinscak; Ayse Nur Beris; Valentin Schneider; Klara Czernin; Anselm Bründlmayer; Paul Plener; Frank Scharnowski; David Steyrl; Clarissa Laczkovics
articles_hidden.abstract:
Identity diffusion – a fragmented sense of self and others maintained by splitting-based defenses – is a core feature of impaired personality functioning, theorized to involve heightened negative affectivity and affective instability. Evidence from other psychopathologies suggests that markers of affective disturbances can be automatically extracted from spontaneous speech, yet the linguistic correlates of identity diffusion have rarely been examined – particularly in adolescents, the age group in which personality pathology assessment is most challenging but also most consequential for early intervention.
Transcripts of the Structured Interview of Personality Organization (STIPO) for adolescents were analyzed in a sample of 72 German-speaking participants (50 patients, 22 healthy controls) spanning the full spectrum from consolidated identity to severe identity diffusion. An interpretable lexicon-based sentiment analysis framework combined word frequency measures (LIWC) with continuous word-level valence indices (VADER), capturing both the prevalence and the dynamics of emotional tone.
Greater identity diffusion was associated with higher affective variability (r = .48–.55), a more negative overall affective orientation (strongest effect: r = −.62), more frequent negative affective language, and more extreme negative expression, with weaker evidence for reduced positive language. Measures of positive extremes, affective expressiveness, and verbosity showed no significant associations.
Identity diffusion in adolescents is thus associated with a distinctive affective language profile, detectable from clinical interview transcripts using sentiment analysis. The results are consistent with psychodynamic accounts of splitting and affective dysregulation, and support the potential of automated language analysis as a reproducible, scalable complement to clinical assessment.

articles_hidden.title: NICE’s 2026 Consultation Draft Guideline for OCD and BDD (GID-NG10435): A Critical Appraisal with Secondary Analysis of NICE’s Published Data
articles_hidden.authors: Himanshu Tyagi; Mark Paramlall
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. In September 2026 the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) opened consultation on the first batch of its update to the 2005 guideline for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (GID-NG10435). The draft replaces stepped care with matched care and reviews first-line treatment.

Methods. We appraised the draft and its supporting documents against six questions informed by selected AGREE II domains, analysing NICE’s published effect estimates, sample sizes, sensitivity analyses and economic results descriptively; every value was checked against its source document. Comparison guidelines were identified by a documented search.

Results. The adult OCD review included 82 randomised controlled trials and the BDD review 13 studies. The committee cited small samples and wide credible intervals when it did not recommend metacognitive therapy (52 participants) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR; 59 participants). Self-administered cognitive behavioural therapy with therapist support, the second adult option, rests on 61 participants, with a wider credible interval than EMDR’s, and was recommended on other documented grounds. The top-ranked adult option had a probability of 0.17 of being the most cost-effective. The first-listed BDD option ranked fifth of nine in the network meta-analysis. The draft gives no drug-specific dose targets, no consolidated definition of an adequate trial and no primary severity measure for allocation or response. Treatment after non-response to an adequate trial is outside the scope of Batch 1; on the assumptions in NHS England’s 2013 specification, a cascade beginning with 48 million adults in England and Wales yields approximately 48,000 people not responding to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor followed by local graduated exposure. All six selected multimodal OCD comparison guidelines address augmentation; none provides a treatment pathway for BDD.

Conclusions. The draft rests on a substantial evidence synthesis. The published rationale does not fully explain why small samples and imprecision precluded recommendations for some treatments but not others; several operational parameters are not specified; and further-line treatment is outside the first batch.

articles_hidden.title: First Frequency, then Transitional Probability: Insights from primate statistical learning
articles_hidden.authors: Andreas Lazartigues; Thomas Chartier; Frédéric Lavigne; Joel Fagot; Arnaud Rey
articles_hidden.abstract: Statistical learning is a fundamental cognitive capacity, whereby humans and other species extract the structure of sequences based on statistical cues. Among these cues, Transitional Probability (TP) quantifies the probability of the next stimulus given the preceding one(s), while Frequency quantifies the relative occurrence of local sequences. Mechanistic explanations have generally considered TP the prevalent cues, but a role of Frequency cannot be ignored. Yet, the specific contributions of each, and their interaction, are not well understood. Here, we report a simple serial reaction time experiment that 1) provides online, trial-by-trial learning data, 2) allows a clear dissociation of Frequency and TP, 3) excludes the involvement of internal verbalized rules by testing non-human primates (Guinea baboons, Papio papio). Our results show that, contrary to the traditional view, Frequency can be the main cue influencing statistical learning. Indeed, we found learning to be primarily determined by Frequency in the first 2,000 trials of the learning phase, while the usual prevalence of TP emerged only later on. These data provide a better understanding of the interactions between statistical factors involved in sequence processing. They also constitute new constraints for computational models of statistical learning and challenge existing results.

articles_hidden.title: Item-dropping to improve in-sample Cronbach's alpha can harm true reliability: A Monte Carlo simulation
articles_hidden.authors: Ze Freeman; Ian Hussey
articles_hidden.abstract: Cronbach’s alpha is the most commonly reported metric of reliability in psychological measurement, and statistical software encourages a common post hoc revision: dropping the item whose removal most improves in-sample alpha. A Monte Carlo simulation examined what this practice does to true reliability, varying items per scale (5 to 40) and sample size (20 to 1,000), with item pools generated from a loading distribution fitted to 3,783 factor loadings from real psychological scales. Two strategies, always dropping the nominated item or dropping only when in-sample alpha improves, were evaluated against the population alpha and true reliability of the retained items. The bias in the reported alpha itself was modest, overstating true reliability only in short scales at small samples and understating it elsewhere. The decision was another matter: at the smallest scale and sample size, dropping reduced true reliability in 46.7% of the replications in which the conditional rule acted, despite requiring an apparent improvement, and almost the entire apparent gain was selection optimism. Stricter decision rules helped only in large samples: with N of 200 or more, acting only on apparent gains above .02 kept the probability of harming the scale at or below 7%, whereas at N = 20 no threshold examined made the decision safe. Because this risk depends on scale length and sample size, given loadings typical of trait scales, it is knowable before data are collected, whereas nothing inside the alpha-if-item-removed table distinguishes a genuinely weak item from a sampling artefact.

articles_hidden.title: A multidimensional normative database of experiential ratings for German nouns
articles_hidden.authors: Cristina Cara; Christian Bellebaum; Laura Bechtold; Marta Ghio
articles_hidden.abstract: Theories of semantic representation propose that concepts are grounded in multiple forms of experience, yet normative resources capturing this multidimensionality remain scarce, especially in German. We present a database of experiential ratings for 1,985 German nouns, with particularly broad coverage of abstract concepts (a 3:1 ratio of abstract to concrete nouns). In total, 354 native German speakers rated the extent to which the meaning of each word is associated with 16 experiential dimensions spanning perceptual, motor, affective, cognitive, social and magnitude-related domains, complemented by concreteness and familiarity ratings. The database additionally provides the dominant experiential dimension of each word and an exclusivity score quantifying how strongly its profile is dominated by a single dimension relative to the others. Cross-database validation against existing German norms showed strong convergence with our concreteness, valence, and arousal ratings. Longitudinal test-retest assessment of all experiential dimensions, as well as concreteness and familiarity, in a subsample of 36 participants showed moderate to high temporal stability across ratings. To characterize the multidimensional structure captured by the database, we further applied exploratory factor analysis followed by hierarchical clustering in the factor-derived semantic space. These analyses identified three broad factors interpreted as socioemotional, perceptual, and magnitude-related, and four clusters of words with distinct experiential profiles. Summary-level and participant-level data are freely available through the project website, which also provides an interactive interface for exploring the norms. The database provides a resource for research on conceptual representation in psycholinguistics, cognitive neuroscience, and computational semantics.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociable neural oscillations track subjective value under risk and ambiguity
articles_hidden.authors: Shuting Mei; Leyou Deng; Gökhan Aydogan; Christian Carl Ruff; Ya Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: How the brain values uncertain prospects and translates them into choices is a central question in decision neuroscience. Current accounts propose that decisions under risk and ambiguity share a valuation process that integrates outcome with probability information, with ambiguity additionally requiring evaluation of the uncertainty about the probabilities themselves. Here we used computational modeling to estimate trial-wise subjective value and tested whether it was tracked by shared or distinct neural dynamics under risk and ambiguity. Participants accepted or rejected risky and ambiguous monetary gambles while we recorded neural activity using electroencephalography (Experiment 1) and magnetoencephalography (Experiment 2). Across both experiments, alpha-band (9–14 Hz) activity localized to the precuneus and superior parietal cortex tracked subjective value under both risk and ambiguity. By contrast, delta-band (1–3 Hz) activity localized to the ventromedial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices tracked subjective value only under ambiguity. These findings reveal dissociable neural signatures for the two forms of uncertainty and suggest that the brain resolves ambiguity by combining a shared valuation process indexed by alpha activity with an additional process indexed by delta activity that may reflect the motivational salience of options with ambiguous outcome probabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Consistency: A Critical but Often Overlooked Requirement for Causal Inference in Psychological Research
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Junker; Michael P. Grosz
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists are often interested in specific causal quantities (“What is the effect of reducing social-media scrolling by 20 minutes on well-being?”) but tend to focus on vague questions (“Does ‘time spent on social media’ predict well-being?”). There is a mismatch between the causal effects researchers care about and the associations and correlations they compute. In this article, we highlight consistency as a foundational requirement for causal inference that can bridge this mismatch and make statistical estimates causally interpretable. Consistency shows how causal quantities are interpretable only when (a) the causal quantity of interest—the causal estimand—is described precisely enough that it does not bundle different versions of the treatment (e.g., passive scrolling, reading distressing news, or chatting with friends on social media) that have different effects, and (b) the way that the treatment variable changes in the data matches this causal estimand of interest. We clarify these requirements and illustrate how to state and assess them in settings common in psychological research, with a focus on indirect experimental manipulations and multidimensional constructs. Making this step explicit helps researchers articulate their estimands more transparently and is a prerequisite for other concerns such as confounding and model specification.

articles_hidden.title: Health care practitioners’ knowledge, attitudes and perceptions of psychedelic treatments for mental disorders: A scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Jacqueline Samantha Womersley; Gabriela Iacovou; Yumna Kathrada; Marnus Janse van Vuuren; Hannah Lukic; Soraya Seedat
articles_hidden.abstract: Interest in psychedelic treatments for mental health conditions is growing. Health care professionals will be key in the implementation, recommendation, and administration of psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) if and when it is approved for clinical use, making their knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions (KAPs) central to successful translation into practice. We conducted a scoping review of health care professionals’ KAPs toward the psychedelic treatment of mental health conditions. Thirty-nine studies, comprising both quantitative and qualitative investigations, were included. The number of studies, and range of health care professionals surveyed, increased over time, though research remained concentrated in North America, Europe, and Australia. Participants mostly performed well on objective knowledge assessments, but this did not necessarily align with subjective knowledge, which indicated lower self-reported confidence in PAT theory and practice. Attitudes toward psychedelics’ therapeutic potential, safety, and legalisation were generally favourable, although concerns included potential misuse, risk of precipitating subsequent psychiatric disorders, and cognitive impairment. Participants generally perceived psychiatrists and specialised facilities as most suitable for PAT administration, and the need for further research was strongly supported. A lack of trained personnel and resources, and cost, side effect, and misuse concerns, were the most frequently endorsed barriers to implementation. Research into health care professionals' KAPs regarding psychedelic treatment is maturing, but important gaps remain: granular insight into KAPs toward specific compound-disorder combinations is lacking, and geographic coverage does not reflect the global burden of mental illness. Addressing these gaps will be important as PAT moves closer to clinical implementation.

articles_hidden.title: Intentions to Help Friends Across Cultural Groups: The Role of Emotional Connectedness
articles_hidden.authors: Arzu Karakulak; Michael Bender
articles_hidden.abstract: Across five studies (N = 1,859), we examined cross-cultural variation in emotional connectedness and intentions to help a family member, a friend, and a stranger.
