Across two pre-registered studies, participants were exposed to situations designed to elicit compassion for the environment (Study 1; N = 165) or awe at nature (Study 2; N = 117). Participants then reported their emotional experiences, intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective actions, and provided open-ended definitions of the target emotions. Results showed that compassion and awe were successfully elicited and exhibited distinct emotional patterns. Compassion for the environment was significantly associated with higher intentions to engage in pro-environmental collective actions, whereas awe at nature was not, suggesting that eco-emotions may support different forms of social and environmental engagement. Qualitative analyses revealed conceptual overlap between French participants’ spontaneous descriptions and English-language theoretical definitions. However, contrary to recent empirical categorizations, compassion was generally considered to be a negative emotion. Together, these findings highlight the value of experimentally inducing discrete self-transcendent eco-emotions to clarify their specific emotional content and their distinct roles as socially embedded drivers of environmental engagement.

articles_hidden.title: Visuospatial features influencing the evaluation of two-body interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Orlandi; Mohammad Soleyman Nejad; Matteo Candidi
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual evaluation of aesthetic, semantic, and emotional aspects of two-body interactions is fundamental for social cognition, yet the contribution of objective stimulus features to these evaluations remains largely unexplored. This study investigated how different visuospatial features of two-body implied interactions influence their evaluations in terms of aesthetic pleasure, symmetry, emotional valence, meaning, and interest. Across four studies involving 200 participants, we found that visually ‘entangled’ two-body interactions, defined by the extent of shared interpersonal space, were rated as more aesthetically pleasing, interesting, and meaningful than their disentangled versions. Using Representational Similarity Analysis and hierarchical multiple regressions, we identified the contribution of each stimulus feature to these evaluations. These findings suggest that two-body entanglement enhances the perceived dyads’ aesthetic and semantic value, possibly facilitating their configural processing. The study expands prior literature and highlights a dissociation between visuospatial features and mechanisms underlying pleasure and interest in dancing bodies.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring musicality at home: Preliminary validation of the Music@Home questionnaires in a Greek population
articles_hidden.authors: Katerina Drakoulaki; Christina Anagnostopoulou; Angeliki Triantafyllaki; Orianna Bairaktari; Aikaterini Nina Polytimou
articles_hidden.abstract: Music@Home was developed in the United Kingdom as a systematic instrument for the assessment of informal musical interactions in the home environments of children under the age of 5. It has been successfully adapted and validated in German, and widely used in research with typically developing children, children with neurodevelopmental disabilities, and adults reporting their early music exposure retrospectively. In the present study, we adapted and conducted a preliminary validation of the Music@Home Infant and Preschool questionnaires for a Greek-speaking population. A total of 238 Greek-speaking primary caregivers completed either version, along with measures of cognitive stimulation at home and child language and communication development. Both Greek questionnaires demonstrated acceptable to good confirmatory fit, strong internal reliability, and evidence for divergent validity, with test-retest reliability established for the Preschool version, indicating that musical engagement represents a distinct aspect of the home environment rather than general cognitive stimulation. Exploratory analyses revealed modest positive associations between Infant scores and parent-reported language outcomes, consistent with previous research linking early musical experiences and language development. These findings provide initial evidence that the Greek Music@Home is a psychometrically sound tool for assessing the home musical environment in Greek-speaking populations and highlight the value of cross-cultural adaptations for research on music cognition, language, and broader developmental outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Eat your vegetables: Exploring food learning cues in 12-month-old infants
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Rioux; Karola Schlegelmilch; Annie E. Wertz
articles_hidden.abstract: Food learning in early life largely relies on social learning. Previous research has shown that infants learn something is edible when they directly observe someone else eating it. However, the role of other forms of food-related social information remains largely unknown. Food processing actions (e.g., chopping, mashing) are essential components of human food behaviors and a ubiquitous part of infants’ everyday lives. Here we examined whether infants (i) differentially attend to eating and food processing actions compared to control actions and (ii) learn that novel foods are edible after observing eating and food processing actions performed with them. We tested 12-month-olds’ responses to three different actions: eating, food processing, and a control action (touch). First, we showed infants side-by-side videos of an adult performing two different actions with novel foods across three between-subjects conditions and measured their gaze and pupil dilation with an eye-tracker. Then, we offered infants the novel foods shown in the videos and measured their choices and eating behaviors. Our eye-tracking results indicate that infants differentially attend to eating and food processing actions relative to the control action, and show increased pupil dilation for the control action relative to the two actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting). When asked to choose which novel food they could eat, infants chose the novel food they saw an actor eat, but only when that eating action was paired with the control action. These findings help identify important mechanisms that increase acceptance of healthy foods early in life.

articles_hidden.title: Same Effect, Different Magnitude: How the Choice of Pre- or Post-Treatment Standard Deviation Shapes Standardized Effect Sizes in Psychological Clinical Trials
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Anika Buchholz; Anna Suling; Antonia Zapf; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles_hidden.abstract: Standardized mean differences (SMDs) are used to express treatment effects on a common metric, yet there is no consensus on whether mean differences should be standardized using the outcome standard deviation (SD) at baseline or follow-up. This study examined whether this choice systematically affects effect-size magnitude in a reproducible sample of 100 randomized psychological clinical trials. For each trial, SMDs were calculated using either the pooled baseline SD (SMDpre) or the pooled follow-up SD (SMDpost). The unweighted paired mean difference showed that |SMDpre| was, 0.11 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, 95% CI [0.07, 0.14]. In a multilevel meta-regression |SMDpre| was 0.082 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, equalling a 13% increase, 95% CI [0.042, 0.123]. Bland–Altman analysis indicated substantial between-study variation, 95% limits of agreement [−0.25, 0.46]. Secondary analyses including 2,228 effect sizes across all follow-ups mirrored this pattern, indicating a 7% increase of SMD magnitude associated to |SMDpre|, 95% CI [0.021, 0.044]. Moderator analyses suggested that discrepancies were larger in studies applying symptom-threshold eligibility criteria, and in secondary analyses, using the same measure both to determine eligibility and to assess the outcome and with longer follow-up. Importantly, 70% of included studies did not report how SMDs were operationalized. These findings demonstrate that the choice of standardizing SD systematically affects estimated treatment-effect magnitudes and that the discrepancy can become more pronounced under specific design conditions. Researchers should therefore carefully consider the choice of standardizer and explicitly report the time point and method used to derive the SD.

articles_hidden.title: Confirmatory Validation of the Singing Incongruence and Gender (SInG) Scale in an Independent Sample of Transgender and Gender-Diverse Singers
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Singing-related gender incongruence can be a significant source of distress for transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) individuals, yet general measures of gender dysphoria and speaking-voice instruments do not capture this domain. The Singing Incongruence and Gender (SInG) Scale was developed to address this gap, but its four-factor structure had not been confirmed in independent data.
Methods: Participants were an entirely new sample of 232 TGD individuals (141 nonbinary, 48 transgender men, 43 transgender women), with 883 cisgender respondents retained as a comparison group for known-groups validity and measurement invariance. Confirmatory factor analysis used robust weighted least squares on a polychoric correlation matrix. I also examined reliability, construct validity, a 12-item short form, and how the scale should be scored.
Results: The four-factor structure was confirmed, with all standardized loadings between .618 and .925 and better fit than a unidimensional alternative (comparative fit index .841 versus .618). Approximate fit fell below conventional thresholds, reflecting both a low ratio of cases to the 126 estimated parameters and some redundancy of item wording; a 12-item form fit better (.930), retained reliability and validity, and performed similarly in split-half cross-validation regardless of which near-equivalent items were retained. SInG scores predicted singing-voice discrepancy beyond age, identity subgroup, and general gender dysphoria (ΔR² = .192), and TGD respondents scored higher than cisgender respondents (d = 0.59; Misgendering d = 1.12).
Conclusions: The SInG Scale captures singing-related gender incongruence beyond what a general dysphoria measure explains, and is available in a brief 12-item form suited to clinical intake and choir screening. Because the subscales bear different relations to criterion outcomes, they should be reported alongside the total score.

articles_hidden.title: A Non-Parametric Approach to Modeling Accelerated Longitudinal Designs
articles_hidden.authors: Suryadyuti Baral; Jonathan Park; Emilio Ferrer
articles_hidden.abstract: Accelerated longitudinal designs (ALDs) offer an efficient means of studying large developmental periods by combining shorter longitudinal samples across overlapping cohorts. ALDs have been used to study processes that span large developmental epochs, such as cognitive development. However, traditional parametric approaches may impose structural assumptions that limit the accurate reconstruction of individual developmental trajectories. We investigate a nonparametric functional data analytic (FDA) approach for modeling latent trajectories in accelerated longitudinal data. This method allows for the recovery of smooth, continuous time trajectories that account for both shared and idiosyncratic patterns of change. We compare the FDA approach to the continuous time latent change score model with simulations that emulate nonlinear change processes often seen in developmental research. We apply both methods to two empirical datasets with individuals aged 5- to 22-years, where each person is assessed two or three times. Our results demonstrate that the FDA method captures the shape and timing of individual trajectories more accurately beyond the observed data. These findings suggest that FDA offers a robust and flexible alternative for modeling developmental change in ALDs.

articles_hidden.title: The impact of professional development programs on K–12 teachers’ AI literacy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: YING MA; Chloe Gordon; Tingting Li; Ziwen Teuber; Theresa Dicke; Taren Sanders; Michael Noetel; Rebecca J Collie; Kewen Liao; Chengliang Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Teachers' artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is an increasingly important focus of professional development (PD). This systematic review synthesized evidence from 62 empirical studies (61 records), including 36 studies eligible for effect-size estimation, involving pre-service and in-service teachers. Most programs emphasized AI-related knowledge and skills, with less systematic attention to attitudinal and ethical dimensions. Common design features included temporal flexibility (e.g., synchronous and asynchronous learning), role diversification (e.g., co-designers and collaborators), and contextual orientation (e.g., task- and project-based learning). The primary combined-design multilevel meta-analysis after influence diagnostics, based on 212 effect sizes from 34 studies, indicated a significant positive average effect across knowledge, skills, and attitudes/values (g = 0.76, 95% CI [0.50, 1.02], p < .001). Substantial heterogeneity indicated considerable variation across programs and contexts. Although possible small-study effects and publication selection may have inflated the magnitude of the primary pooled estimate, Bayesian selection-model analyses continued to support a positive average effect. No statistically significant moderation was detected by career stage, school level, intervention-duration category, research design, outcome measurement type, or gender composition. These findings provide an important quantitative benchmark for the emerging evidence base and indicate that AI literacy PD can support multiple dimensions of teachers' AI literacy.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Differences in Emotion Regulation May Not Be Unique to Expressive Suppression
articles_hidden.authors: Sooyeon Kim; Katharine Helen Greenaway; Peter Koval
articles_hidden.abstract: Controlling emotion expression is theorized to be more valued and thus more frequently used and beneficial among Easterners than Westerners. However, existing evidence relies on global self-reports capturing culturally informed beliefs about suppression rather than moment-to-moment suppression. Moreover, whether cultural differences are specific to suppression or reflect broader emotion-regulation patterns remains unclear. Using three experience-sampling datasets, we tested cultural differences in suppression across global and momentary self-reports and their specificity. Easterners reported greater suppression at both global and momentary self-reports. Cultural differences were specific to suppression at global levels but generalized to reappraisal and rumination at momentary levels. We found less support for cultural differences in the affective correlates of emotion regulation. However, there was moderate evidence that momentary suppression, reappraisal, and rumination were less strongly associated with negative affect among Easterners than Westerners. We provide the first comprehensive test of cultural differences in suppression and suggest they may reflect broader emotion-regulation patterns.

articles.title: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) for Coding Open-Ended Survey Responses: A Total Survey Error Framework
articles.authors: Laone Maphane; Gabriele Durrant
articles.abstract:
Open-ended questions are commonly used in survey research to supplement closed-ended questions by capturing respondents’ views, reasons, and priorities in their own words. However, coding these responses for analysis remains time-consuming and difficult to standardise. Recent advances in automated coding, especially through large language models (LLMs), have renewed interest in using open-ended responses at scale, but their evaluation is often difficult and framed mainly in terms of classification accuracy and agreement with human coding. This paper develops a Total Survey Error framework for evaluating automated coding of open-ended survey responses as part of survey measurement and data production. Model outputs are assessed using existing human-coded data as a high-quality operational benchmark, with the evaluation examining six complementary dimensions, such as processing agreement, measurement validity, prevalence distortion, coding density, response-form sensitivity, and operational reliability. The framework is applied to data using open-ended survey responses from the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen). The paper aims to inform how automated coding systems, including LLMs, can be assessed in practice, and what issues survey researchers should consider when evaluating their suitability for open-ended survey coding, and how improved coding may enable wider use of open-ended questions in large-scale quantitative surveys.
Keywords: automated coding; large language models; measurement validity; open-ended survey responses; survey data quality; Total Survey Error

articles.title: Where Silicon Samples Go Wrong: Item-Level Coefficient Distortion in LLM-Simulated Chinese Public Opinion
articles.authors: Mingkun Cui; Shenghao Xiong
articles.abstract: Do regressions fitted to survey responses simulated by large language models return the coefficients human data would? We used four 2026 models to generate responses to the full attitude-item bank of two Chinese General Social Survey waves, conditioning on 1,000 respondents’ demographic profiles per wave and requesting each person’s most likely answer. For 10 items analyzed in both waves, we compared human and simulated coefficients on the human-anchored scale, with Holm adjustment across 240 tests. The 28 supported differences concentrate in three patterns: an inflated income gradient in perceived fairness, an urban–rural gradient in premarital-sex morality where the human coefficient is near zero, and an overstated sex difference in gender-ability beliefs. Marginal fit does not locate these distortions. Standardizing each source by its own standard deviation changes 33 test decisions, showing why regression validation requires a declared outcome scale.

articles.title: The Grumpy Meme and Irritability Ecology: How Low-Intensity Negative Affect Spreads, Survives, Sediments, and Becomes a Workplace Climate
articles.authors: Koichi Hiraoka
articles.abstract:
Research on negative affect in organizations has largely focused on relatively visible phenomena such as anger, aggression, abusive supervision, workplace bullying, and incivility. Yet much of everyday organizational life unfolds between overt anger episodes, when no one is shouting but employees still monitor facial expressions, short replies, sighs, silence, or reduced responsiveness and conclude that someone appears grumpy. Such low-intensity signals may alter whether people approach, speak, seek advice, or share information. To theorize this domain, this paper distinguishes Irritability, Grumpiness, and the Grumpy Meme, and introduces Irritability Ecology as an integrative framework.
Irritability refers to a relatively low-intensity internal affective state that need not be externally expressed. Grumpiness refers to socially perceivable expressions through which others infer that a person appears to be in a bad mood. The Grumpy Meme refers to a socio-affective transmission process in which perceived grumpiness alters another person’s affect or behavior and is subsequently re-expressed in another interaction. Thus, irritability may exist without observable grumpiness, while perceived grumpiness does not necessarily demonstrate underlying irritability.
The paper argues that low-intensity negative affect may survive in workplaces because it is inexpensive to express, highly repeatable, difficult to sanction, and often protected by ambiguity regarding both the event and the actor’s intention. Repeated expressions may accumulate through Affective Sedimentation, creating background vigilance, mood-reading, and eventually a workplace climate. A two-axis model of anger and irritability is proposed, yielding four affective climate types: Calm–Stable, Quiet Tension, Eruption–Recovery, and Pervasive Anger–Irritability. The paper further introduces Affective Non-Transmission as the capacity to experience negative affect without automatically transferring it to others, and connects this capacity to post-conflict relational repair.
Irritability Ecology is therefore not a weaker version of Anger Ecology. Whereas Anger Ecology examines the visible fire of workplace affect, Irritability Ecology examines the ambient climate that persists between fires. The framework shifts attention from identifying “grumpy people” to examining how low-intensity negative affect is expressed, transmitted, sustained, sedimented, interrupted, and repaired within organizational environments.

articles.title: The sociolinguistic labor of incarcerated people
articles.authors: Gabriella Licata; Robert Tyler; Mesro Coles; Anthony Habib Watkins; Brian Asey Gonsoulin
articles.abstract: Through participatory action research, we draw on interviews with 40 incarcerated students to examine how linguistic practices are shaped by institutional power in carceral environments. We argue that the magnitude of surveillance under incarceration produces sociolinguistic labor: the effortful management of one’s communicative repertoire. Our analysis identifies a distinctive form of dual-direction sociolinguistic labor, whereby incarcerated individuals are required to extend their repertoires both toward stigmatized vernaculars to gain social capital and toward hyperstandardized registers for institutional capital. We examine this dynamic across educational, social, and procedural domains, with particular attention to boardspeak—an emotionally-constrained, bureaucratic register through which rehabilitation is performed and assessed at a Board of Parole hearing. By situating these practices within broader critical linguistic theories and perspectives, we show incarcerated people self-surveil and create, prompting varying levels of sociolinguistic labor and innovation that are mediated by race, ethnicity, ability, socioeconomic class, and in-group membership. These findings demonstrate how high-stakes, surveilled environments intensify the stakes of language use and reshape the boundaries of communicative agency.

articles.title: Une approche dynamique de la réception des pré-annonces pharmaceutiques dans les réseaux sociaux - Le cas des vaccins contre la Covid-19 sur twitter
articles.authors: Olivier Caron; Christophe Benavent
articles.abstract:
à 90 %. Cette préannonce est à la fois une information et un signal stratégique porté par une entreprise intéressée au succès de son produit. Que deviennent alors le message et son émetteur
dans la conversation publique ? Les travaux sur la transmission sociale établissent qu’un message se transforme à mesure qu’il circule et s’assimile aux préoccupations du milieu qui le reçoit.
À partir de ce cadre, de l’amplification sociale du risque et du Persuasion Knowledge Model, nous étudions les préannonces d’efficacité de Pfizer/BioNTech, Moderna et AstraZeneca sur
le Twitter francophone, comparées à des événements où les mêmes entreprises font l’actualité sans être à l’origine de la nouvelle. Deux temporalités apparaissent. Le contenu du débat se
transforme presque immédiatement, puis se réinscrit dans des préoccupations préexistantes, comme l’obligation vaccinale ou l’actualité politique. Le jugement de l’entreprise apparaît plus
tard : les utilisateurs passent surtout du relais du message à l’évaluation de son émetteur, sans hausse nette de la négativité des jugements déjà exprimés. Cette bascule est absente lorsque
l’entreprise est seulement l’objet de l’information. Une préannonce met en circulation deux objets : un message et celui qui le porte.

articles.title: The geopolitics of academic publishing: the case of Kazakhstan
articles.authors: Eva Hartmann; Aikerim Bektemirova
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Publications in Scopus- and Web of Science-indexed journals have become the global benchmark of academic excellence. This article examines how Kazakhstan has placed this new ‘gold standard’ at the centre of its academic publishing policy, which has become a key part of its university reform agenda since 2010. Using a Gramscian lens on power and knowledge, we show how the government employs this policy to position itself between the West and Russia in a shifting geopolitical context. The adoption of this benchmark not only changes how Kazakhstan's academic community relates to the broader academic world. It also significantly reshapes the hierarchy within Kazakhstan’s academic community. We argue that this has profound implications for the societal role of universities and academic research and their ability to address local challenges. Our study makes both empirical and theoretical contributions to the growing literature on the geopolitics of knowledge, highlighting the interplay among local, national, and global dynamics.

articles.title: Who Manufactured Pseudo-History Theories? The Emergent Collective Creation of Historical Narratives on the Chinese Internet
articles.authors: ZY Liu; Di Yuan
articles.abstract: This paper examines the formation, expansion, and functions of pseudo-history theories (伪史论) on the Chinese internet from the perspective of cultural economics, and proposes the analytical concept of “Emergent Collective Creation.” This concept refers to the process whereby a large number of relatively independent content producers, acting on the basis of their respective local motivations and in the absence of any unified overall plan, generate a collective narrative system that exceeds the original planning and control of any single participant through imitation, competition, the recombination of arguments, and the migration of topics. The paper first investigates relevant figures who possess formal academic credentials or publishing experience and analyzes the pathways through which early pseudo-history resources entered public circulation. It then takes as examples the extension of pseudo-history theories from ancient Greece and Rome to other civilizations, historical figures, and issues concerning Chinese dynastic history, exploring how competition for traffic, content imitation, and the selective recombination of historical materials drive narrative expansion. Finally, using online controversies surrounding the film The Penghu Naval Battle as a case study, it analyzes how pseudo-history theories have been deployed by different participants in conflicts over historical identity and in online opinion confrontation, and discusses possible links between controversial historical discourses and public trust in academic authority. The paper argues that even dispersed individual actions lacking unified coordination may, through indirect interaction, produce collective narrative outcomes and enable pseudo-history theories to move from a form of content competition for traffic into ideological contention. Because this study relies primarily on publicly available online materials, publications, and media reports, and lacks internal platform data as well as continuous records at the creator level, the mechanisms identified remain exploratory explanations whose chains of transmission, causal relations, and actual effects await further verification.

articles.title: Are Women Comedians Less Funny?: Empirical Analysis of Gender Differences in 1-on-1 Competitive Comedy
articles.authors: Yuhei Yamaguchi
articles.abstract:
"Is there a difference in funniness between men and women?'" This study addresses this question. The perception that "women are less funny than men" is widespread, and some studies have indeed shown that men have a better sense of humor. In addition, in industries dominated by men, the presence of women tends to be relatively low. In the comedy industry, where men make up the overwhelming majority, women comedians are thus exposed to a double stereotype of this kind. We examined whether, under such a double stereotype, women comedians are able to be as funny as men comedians. We collected and analyzed data on a total of 3,925 matchups from a television program in which comedians compete directly over funniness in one-on-one contests. The results showed that, although a simple statistical model makes men comedians appear funnier, an analysis using a model that accounts for individual funniness revealed no significant difference in funniness between men and women.
Although concerns remain about the generalizability of the findings, the results call into question existing research on gender differences in sense of humor, as well as the associated stereotypes.

articles.title: A Sociolinguistic Inquiry into Vietnamese Swearing: Regional Variation and Cross-Cultural Parallels
articles.authors: Hàng Hỷ Vinh
articles.abstract: This exploratory, pilot-scale study investigates the Vietnamese swearing construction built from an obscene verb, a kinship term and a second-person pronoun (địt mẹ mày, đụ má mày 'fuck your mother', mả cha mi 'your father's grave') through two questions: how kin-directed swearing differs across regions and which part of the construction reveals the speaker's region (RQ1); and why Vietnamese swearing targets kin and women, viewed against the full repertoire of swearing themes in Vietnamese and neighbouring languages (RQ2). It combines eight Vietnamese dictionaries (1651–2021) and comparative dictionaries of Mường, Cham, Teochew and Cantonese with an online convenience-sample survey of 50 young speakers across four regions, a small Quốc ngữ prose corpus, and a thematic comparison with ten other language communities. For RQ1, the dictionaries show no regional boundary in the verb before 1931, whereas the survey finds a clear North/South split in both the verb and the word for "mother"; regional information is asymmetric, with Southern and Central forms acting as strong markers while standard-compatible forms (địt, mẹ) and online abbreviations (đm, vkl) spread across all regions. For RQ2, sex and kin dominate the free lists; the mother-directed sexual formula occurs in Vietnamese, Chinese, Thai, Hindi and English but is absent from Japanese, so it cannot be attributed to Confucian heritage alone. Kin-directed swearing is rated more offensive than self-directed swearing and triggers more active responses; swears that deny the hearer's descent (đồ con hoang, cả họ nhà mày) are the heaviest and the least mitigated among friends. Young respondents name affection for kin, not family face, as the main reason; we read this as a contemporary synchronic reinterpretation of templates whose diachronic origin lies in honour-based lineage norms. Taken together, the target of kin-directed swearing is the hearer's legitimate standing within the lineage. Results describe young, internet-using speakers and should be read as hypothesis-generating.

articles.title: Standpoint Theory and the Enactment of the Social Relation of Comradeship through Social Research
articles.authors: Ioana Cerasella Chis
articles.abstract: This paper discusses the ethico-political impetus for seeking to establish the social relation of comradeship with socially marginalised research participants of projects concerned with social justice and countering structural oppression. To this end, the paper explores Olufemi O. Táíwò’s (2020) distinction between liberal and constructive approaches to Standpoint Theory, before considering the social relations of allyship and comradeship through the context of a project that examined structural disablement and precarious work in the UK. In light of this analysis, I call on other social researchers to consider the necessity of enacting the social relation of comradeship with socially marginalised participants as a way of affirming mutual recognition, strengthening emancipatory research, and producing socially useful dialogic knowledge.

articles.title: Impact of Social Media Platforms on Youth: An Anthropological Study
articles.authors: Sivakumar A
articles.abstract:
Social media has become a ubiquitous sociocultural phenomenon, transforming how young people communicate, socialize, and construct identities. This anthropological study examines social media use among young people aged 18–25 in urban and semi-urban areas of Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, South India. It explores usage patterns, self-identity expression, maintenance of social relationships, digital literacy, and the influence of gender, education, and socioeconomic background on digital participation. It also considers how young people perceive social media’s everyday effects on their social and cultural lives.

A mixed-methods design was adopted. Quantitative data were collected through a questionnaire administered to 60 youth respondents, while semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 participants. The questionnaire demonstrated high overall reliability (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.91), and its individual scales showed acceptable to high reliability. Content validity was reviewed by experts, while exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were used to assess construct validity. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests of independence; qualitative data were analyzed thematically using NVivo.

Findings indicate that social media is embedded in young people’s everyday lives: 73.3% reported using platforms more than once daily. WhatsApp (93.3%), Instagram (88.3%), and YouTube (81.7%) were the most widely used platforms. Entertainment (90.0%) and maintaining contact with friends (85.0%) were the leading purposes, followed by information seeking (63.3%) and identity expression (35.0%). Digital literacy levels were low for 23.3% of respondents, medium for 48.3%, and high for 28.3%. Differences were particularly evident in advanced skills, including evaluating information and managing privacy.

Hypothesis testing found significant associations between digital literacy and frequency of use (p = 0.048; Cramér’s V = 0.324), digital literacy and platform diversity (p = 0.047; Cramér’s V = 0.283), gender and identity expression (p = 0.037; Cramér’s V = 0.331), and gender and platform choice (p = 0.041; Cramér’s V = 0.326). Other hypothesized relationships were not statistically significant. The qualitative analysis identified five themes: curated identity performance, digital kinship and connectivity, stratified digital competencies, gendered digital surveillance, and ambivalent impression perceptions.

The study contributes to digital anthropology by illustrating how global platforms are locally adopted in South Indian contexts, how social relationships are sustained in digital spaces, and how digital literacy may function as cultural capital. It offers recommendations for educators, parents, policymakers, platform designers, and young people to promote more equitable and beneficial digital participation.

articles.title: Visual Resistance Assemblages: Recurring Multimodal Configurations in Kenya’s Gen Z Finance Bill Protests
articles.authors: Castro Chebukosi
articles.abstract: Social-media protest communication is increasingly multimodal, combining language, imagery, typography, sound, performance and platform-specific features. While existing research has demonstrated how such resources produce meaning within individual artefacts and genres, comparatively less attention has been given to how functionally related multimodal configurations recur across heterogeneous artefacts within the same protest corpus. This study addresses this corpus-level problem through a qualitative multimodal analysis of 72 protest artefacts published or circulated on X during Kenya’s June–July 2024 Finance Bill protests, analysed through multimodal social semiotics and cross-artefact comparison. The analysis identifies five recurring configurations: Constitutional Legitimation, Distributed Agency, Comparative Fiscal Information Design, Visual Witnessing and Collective Identity, and Satirical Recontextualization. These configurations are not treated as mutually exclusive artefact categories; rather, they represent recurring relationships among heterogeneous semiotic resources that retain comparable communicative functions despite variation in genre and surface realisation. The study proposes the concept of Visual Resistance Assemblages (VRA) as a descriptive analytical unit for identifying such corpus-level recurrence. The findings demonstrate how constitutional discourse, distributed participation, comparative fiscal reasoning, collective representation and satirical recontextualisation were organised through heterogeneous multimodal resources. VRA complements existing multimodal, assemblage-oriented and digital activism approaches by shifting attention from multimodality within individual artefacts to recurring multimodal organisation across protest corpora.

articles.title: The Emotional Meaning and Sociocultural Implications of 'Eojunggan-hada' in Korean Society: An Exploratory Study
articles.authors: Heeju Lee
articles.abstract: This study explores how the Korean expression 'eojunggan-hada' (being in-between) extends beyond simple linguistic ambiguity to reflect issues of personal identity and social belonging. Unlike previous Korean linguistics research that focused on linguistic ambiguity and mitigation expressions, this study defines 'eojunggan-hada' as a way of being positioned at the boundaries of identity and belonging, analyzing its sociocultural implications. A survey of 111 respondents revealed that participants frequently experience being in-between in daily life (mean 3.44), perceiving it more as a product of social structural conditions (mean 3.46) rather than personal character traits (mean 3.22). Notably, daily experience of in-betweenness showed a strong positive correlation with attributing it to one's personality (r = .64, p < .001), suggesting that the more frequently people feel in-between, the more they blame their own character for it. Qualitative analysis of open-ended responses confirmed that being in-between functions simultaneously as discomfort and survival strategy. This study conceptualizes 'eojunggan-hada' as a boundary emotion formed within Korea's unique collectivist culture and relational pressures, proposing that it represents not individual indecisiveness but rather a way of existence created by social structures.

articles.title: Manufactured Desire： How Social Media and Influencer Agencies Sexualise and Monetise Pregnant Influencers
articles.authors: Yuting Qin
articles.abstract: This article examines how pregnant influencers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, are sexualised and monetised through the interlocking practices of the platform, influencer agencies and influencers themselves. Taking the 2024 controversy around the appearance influencer YīLìXiǎoShāZi and the # 孕妇摇 (Pregnancy Swing Dance) challenge as its point of departure, the study combines visual analysis of top-ranked Douyin posts, in-depth interviews with an influencer, an influencer agency employee and a platform employee, and sentiment analysis of 4,874 user comments. This article interprets platform monetisation structures and influencer agency production routines as organising influencers’ embodied labour into standardised production roles and measurable commercial attributes. It proposes the “factory of desire” as a framework for understanding how platforms, influencer agencies and influencers mutually enable and constrain the commodification of pregnant bodies. Interviewees described unwritten rules through which sexualised content can remain visible under mainland China's restrictions on pornography: perceived emphasis on skin exposure in automated moderation, a grey zone known as 擦边 (cābiān, "skirting the boundary"), and appeals framed around "pregnancy beauty". The analysis suggests that these commercial and regulatory conditions can encourage pregnant influencers to reproduce porn chic conventions, while constraining their subsequent commercial options. Within the sampled comments on videos criticising the sexualisation of pregnancy, disgust had the highest average model score; these findings describe this selected discussion rather than public opinion as a whole.

articles.title: Generalised Conversational Implicature in Kenyan Generation Z Digital Protest Discourse: Q-, I-, and M-Heuristics in the 2024 Finance Bill Protests on X
articles.authors: Castro Chebukosi; Bernard Kodak; Jane Ombati
articles.abstract: The June–July 2024 Finance Bill protests in Kenya produced a distinctive corpus of digitally mediated political communication in which Gen Z-associated protesters on X (formerly Twitter) relied on omission, shared background knowledge and stylistic markedness to construct political meaning beyond the literal content of their posts. This study examines how such strategies generated Generalised Conversational Implicature (GCI), applying Levinson’s (2000) Q-, I-, and M-heuristic framework to a purposively sampled corpus of 72 protest artefacts retrieved from X in June 2026. Using thematic and pragmatic coding, the analysis shows that condensed slogans, mobilisation language and constitutional citation generated Q-heuristic implicatures through informational economy; shared political, cultural and generational knowledge generated I-heuristic implicatures; and marked linguistic, visual and performative choices generated M-heuristic implicatures, extending Levinson’s lexical account of markedness into a multimodal register. The three heuristics frequently layered within single artefacts, and thematic coding further revealed six protest-specific inferential patterns beyond Levinson’s original typology: anti-co-optation, constitutional-sovereignty, trauma-memory, care-based, data-activism and digital-network patterns. The study demonstrates how GCI analysis can be extended to fast-paced, multimodal, digitally networked political communication when its categories are made explicit and their limits are clearly bounded.

articles.title: The Impact of U.S. Tariffs on European Public Opinion: Evidence From a Natural Experiment
articles.authors: Joseph Noonan
articles.abstract: How do tariff escalations shape public attitudes in targeted countries? This registered report examines how the second Trump Administration's April 2025 tariff escalation affected European public opinion. Leveraging the announcement's timing during the fieldwork of Standard Eurobarometer 103.3 as an unexpected event, I compare respondents interviewed before and after. Drawing on theories of external threat, in-group identity, and cooperative reciprocity, I test whether the escalation strengthened pro-EU sentiment, worsened views of the United States, and shifted cooperation preferences. I find that it reduced favorable views of the United States, while effects on EU attachment and cooperation preferences were small and non-significant. The decline in favorable views of the United States is concentrated in the most negative response category, indicating that negative views intensified. These results suggest that economic threats from an ally can sharpen antagonism toward the threatening actor without producing broad in-group consolidation or shifts in trade cooperation preferences.

articles.title: Watchdog Capture and the Social Licensing of Child Harm: A Case Study of Common Sense Media and OpenAI
articles.authors: Travis Gilly
articles.abstract:
This paper examines a structural failure mode in the validation chain that legitimizes consumer artificial
intelligence products marketed to or used by minors: a child safety advocacy organization that arrives at
each crisis after journalists and litigants have already exposed it, or plays the harm down when it arrives
first, and that enters endorsement, development, and funding relationships with the firm whose product
produced the harm. It documents a twenty-three year response pattern at Common Sense Media (CSM),
a United States based organization that reports reaching more than 150 million users and 1.4 million
educators worldwide each year, across three crisis cycles: YouTube Kids during the Elsagate incidents
of 2017, video game loot boxes between 2017 and 2019, and generative artificial intelligence chatbots
between 2023 and 2026. The paper situates the pattern within Carpenter and Moss’s (2014) account of
corrosive capture, regulatory intermediary theory, and the social license literature. It argues that CSM’s
September 2025 endorsement of OpenAI’s parental controls as “a good starting point,” controls that
contemporaneous reporting described as developed by OpenAI with CSM, and CSM’s January 2026
ballot measure merger with OpenAI, which dropped provisions from CSM’s original ballot initiative that
had tracked its vetoed bill, together constitute a transfer of social license rather than a substantive safety
remedy. It then examines the October 2026 risk assessment in which CSM’s Youth AI Safety Institute,
funded in part by the OpenAI Foundation, rated ChatGPT for Teens an Unacceptable Risk on the strength
of a parental notification mechanism that CSM had helped develop and had endorsed at launch. CSM’s
own October 2025 review had already tested that mechanism, recorded parental alerts arriving more than
twenty-four hours after a tester discussed suicide, and recorded the account bypass, yet described the
product as meaningful progress and kept it rated for teens thirteen and up for a further 349 days. Archived
copies of CSM’s ChatGPT rating page show that the product carried a thirteen and up label from October
2023 and a Moderate risk rating from August 2024 through at least September 2025, so that the rating
available to parents on the day a sixteen year old user died after extended use of ChatGPT was Moderate.
The October 2026 findings were authored for the public by the former newspaper columnist who had
documented the bypass three days after launch, without reference to that earlier reporting. The paper
proposes public record indicators for detecting watchdog capture in other consumer safety intermediaries.

articles.title: Silicon Ethics: Comparing the Dynamics of Human and LLM Responses to Ethical Dilemmas
articles.authors: W. Russell Neuman
articles.abstract: A key element in alignment research is commonly captured by the phrase “alignment with human values.” Human ethical judgment, however, is plural, unstable, affectively charged, socially embedded, and often justified after the fact. This article proposes a systematic comparative methodology emphasizing the potential complementarity of how human and silicon ethics may differ.   Drawing on literature of moral psychology, it identifies five dynamics of human ethical judgment systematically comparing them with their functional analogues in generative models. The goal is not to anthropomorphize LLMs or treat human judgment as a gold standard, but to compare the latent structures of the dynamics in vivo and in silico. The article argues that such comparison can extend alignment research beyond mimetic reproduction of human preferences toward compensatory intelligence: AI systems that help humans notice neglected consequences, test consistency, consider alternative moral frames, and deliberate more responsibly about their own commitments.

articles.title: Apuestas en Chile: regulación y peso económico de un mercado en expansión
articles.authors: Andrés Araya; Fabian Belmar; Xiomara Kuwae; Sebastián Aliaga
articles.abstract: El mercado de apuestas ya no puede entenderse solo como una actividad presencial. La expansión de internet, los teléfonos inteligentes, los medios de pago digitales y la publicidad deportiva trasladó parte relevante del juego de azar hacia plataformas online. Chile reguló históricamente el juego mediante autorizaciones parciales: hípica, loterías, casinos municipales y casinos bajo la Ley N.º 19.995. Ese diseño permitió ordenar segmentos específicos, pero quedó tensionado frente a un mercado digital transnacional. El juego de azar es un problema de política pública, no solo una actividad recreativa. Involucra recaudación fiscal, competencia entre operadores, protección al consumidor, prevención de lavado de activos, integridad deportiva y riesgos asociados al juego problemático. El mercado online no autorizado se ubica en una zona compleja: no forma parte del mercado autorizado, pero tampoco ha sido desplazado de manera efectiva. La Corte Suprema ha declarado ilegales las apuestas online no autorizadas, mientras persisten dificultades prácticas de fiscalización, persecución penal y control de dominios. En 2025, el mercado regulado registró ingresos brutos del juego por $787.281 millones (0,23% del PIB) y generó $148.712 millones en recaudación específica asociada al juego de azar, sin considerar IVA ni impuesto a la renta. Cerca del 70% del mercado regulado corresponde a casinos físicos. Este informe estima el mercado online no autorizado como la brecha entre la tendencia contrafactual del mercado regulado y sus ingresos efectivamente observados. En 2025, esa brecha alcanzó $431.489 millones (0,13% del PIB), es decir, poco más de un tercio de la industria. Bajo una tasa específica de 20% sobre ingresos brutos del juego, la pérdida potencial de recaudación sectorial asociada al mercado online no autorizado se aproxima a $86.298 millones en 2025.

articles.title: Similar disruptions, different reactions? Refugee crises and the politicization of immigration in Sweden and Switzerland
articles.authors: Marco Bitschnau; Didier Ruedin; Anders Hellström; Marie Sundström
articles.abstract: We investigate how major refugee crises affected the immigration debate in Sweden and Switzerland, two countries that have long been among the most popular European destinations for immigrants in general and refugees in particular. Analysing claims from newspapers during two crises, the Balkans refugee crisis of the 1990s and the European refugee crisis of 2015–16 (N=3,593), we find (1) fairly diverse patterns of politicization, with slightly greater polarization in Switzerland but higher salience peaks in Sweden; (2) no significant differences in how actors position themselves in relation to the status quo; and (3) substantial differences in how they use certain frames. We conclude that despite their proximity to immigration matters, refugee crises do not always lead to more politicized debates. There may be some crisis impact—but certainly no reason for crisis determinism. Instead, factors such as the domestic context and the relative shock value of each crisis appear to be relevant and should be given more consideration.

articles.title: Digital capacity in Brazilian municipalities: fiscal autonomy, bureaucratic structure and heterogeneity
articles.authors: Yago Paiva; Lizandro Lui
articles.abstract: Over the past decades, digital transformation has become a central aspect of state modernization. In this article, we treat this process as a form of state capacity building — specifically, of the digital capacity of the state. Our aim is to assess whether, at the municipal level, fiscal capacity and bureaucratic quality account for higher levels of digital capacity. To this end, we adapt to the municipal context a concept originally formulated for national states and construct the Municipal Digital Capacity Index (ICDM), a novel and comprehensive measure built from the seven waves of the Brazilian Survey of Basic Municipal Information (MUNIC) that include an information and communication technology module between 2004 and 2024, covering virtually all Brazilian municipalities in each wave. Using the ICDM as the dependent variable, we estimate panel models designed to recover between-municipality effects. Fiscal autonomy is the strongest determinant of digital capacity, with a magnitude far exceeding that of bureaucratic attributes, whose effects are positive but modest. None of these effects, however, operates uniformly: own-source revenue yields more in low-income municipalities, staff qualification pays off only where there is organizational structure to absorb it, and the share of politically appointed staff, whose average effect is null, is positive in poorer municipalities and negative in wealthier ones.

articles.title: Following the Feedback: Audience Engagement and Politicians’ Issue Attention on Social Media
articles.authors: August Lohse; Tobias Priesholm Gårdhus; Snorre Ralund; Hjalmar Bang Carlsen
articles.abstract: Political representatives increasingly communicate in social media environments where every message generates immediate and quantified audience feedback. Although likes are not a representative measure of public opinion, they provide information about which issues attract attention from politicians' online audiences. We examine whether politicians devote more attention to issues that generate high engagement. Our analysis draws on 128,204 Facebook posts published by 123 Facebook-active Danish Members of Parliament between 2011 and 2018. We find that issues receiving relatively more audience feedback are consistently more likely to appear in politicians' subsequent posts. This pattern is present across political topics and different forms of engagement, but weakens during election campaigns, when heightened electoral incentives and institutional constraints coincide. The findings show that quantified platform feedback is systematically linked to the allocation of political attention, but that this alignment varies with the context in which politicians communicate.

articles.title: My (22m) Girlfriend (23f) Comes Home and Does Nothing”– Gendered Perceptions of Paid and Unpaid Work in Reddit Relationship Discussions over Time
articles.authors: Birgit Zeyer-Gliozzo; Johanna Hölzl; Gundula Zoch; Philipp Doebler
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic reignited longstanding debates around gender inequalities in paid and unpaid work. While survey research has advanced our understanding of these disparities, it typically relies on predefined categories and is susceptible to social desirability and recall bias. Online postings, by contrast, capture intimate experiences in real time but rarely include demographic attributes. We leverage a unique dataset of discussions in Reddit relationship communities that combines rich descriptions of conflicts around (un)paid work with demographic information to examine: Which topics do men and women discuss in relationship conflicts around paid and unpaid work? We use Large Language Models (LLMs) and systematically vary GPT-family models and prompting strategies to classify manifest (demographic information) and latent variables (whether posts discuss romantic relationships, paid, and unpaid work) in Reddit posts. Using classifications from the best-performing approach, we apply Structural Topic Models to explore which topics partners discuss and how discussions evolve over time. We find temporary pandemic shifts in topics, and women more often discuss mental health in paid work-related conflicts, while men more frequently emphasize career objectives. In conflicts related to unpaid work, men more frequently express concerns about sexual intimacy. Our analysis offers new insights into topics driving relationship conflicts around (un)paid work. We also contribute to the growing literature on LLMs’ capabilities and limitations in classifying social-science constructs. By combining demographic information with sensitive narratives, our dataset captures forms of relational conflict rarely accessible in survey or social-media research, opening promising avenues for future research.

articles.title: The Evolutionary Hearth: An Environment-Dependent Game-Theoretic Framework for Javanese Maternal Domestic Pedagogy
articles.authors: Muhammad Sukri Bin Ramli
articles.abstract: This study introduces the Principle of Conditional Cultural Adaptiveness, establishing that the evolutionary performance of cultural strategies depends strictly on environmental state variables and shifts through equilibrium migration as those macro-conditions change. Modernity is formally conceptualized not as cultural erosion, but as equilibrium migration between state-dependent optima. Existing scholarly interpretations of Javanese maternal domesticity and the construct of kanca wingking frequently emphasize patriarchal gender hierarchies, symbolic cosmology, or moral norms without formally modeling how domestic practices dynamically adjust to resource volatility, environmental hazards, and shifting household bargaining power. We develop an environment-dependent game-theoretic frame work linking selected maternal instructions to material resource allocation, homeostatic regulation, risk management, health capital investment, cultural information transmission, and costly signaling. By integrating ethnographic philology with evolutionary game theory, bargaining theory, dynamic optimization, and eco-evolutionary feedback modeling, this research provides a formal computational social science framework for representing cultural persistence and transformation while explicitly differentiating stable household equilibria from equitable distributions of welfare.

articles.title: In Silico Advertising Tests
articles.authors: Marta Trales; Guillaume Hochard; Christophe Benavent
articles.abstract:
This research examines whether large language model agents can produce analytically useful evidence for advertising testing when treated as synthetic respondents rather than as substitutes for human consumers. We report an in-silico comparative post-test of two television advertisements in the French telecommunications market, conducted on a panel of 800 profile-conditioned consumer agents. The study evaluates the synthetic corpus through internal validity criteria: whether the questionnaire covers the main dimensions of advertising response, whether evaluative dimensions form coherent relations, whether the two stimuli are discriminated across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic embeddings, and whether responses vary intelligibly across social profiles.
The results indicate that the synthetic panel produces structured and interpretable evidence. The contribution is not that the analysis discovers a contrast invisible in the advertisements themselves: Bouygues and Orange are clearly built around different persuasive registers. Rather, the contribution is methodological. The synthetic-interview pipeline consistently recovers and differentiates these registers across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic comparisons. Bouygues is associated mainly with creative, humorous and memorable qualities,
while Orange is associated with reliability, informativeness, purchase orientation and overall preference. This structure is visible quantitatively in the main six dimensional coding scheme. Among all 800 synthetic agents, Bouygues leads on creativity (83.6% versus 14.8% for Orange), whereas Orange leads on informationseeking or consideration (76.8% versus 14.8% for Bouygues) and overall preference (54.8% versus 20.6% for Bouygues), with the remaining responses classified as mixed or neutral. The analysis remains deliberately limited to synthetic respondents.
Claims about similarity to human preferences or market behaviour would require external comparison with representative human data or market-level indicators.

articles.title: Why We Cling to Flawed Influencers: Psychological Mechanisms Behind Loyalty to Deceptive Social Media Figures
articles.authors: Asma Alolyan
articles.abstract:
Abstract  
Existing studies on loyalty to social media influencers have mainly focused on cognitive  dissonance, parasocial bonding, halo effect, social identity, and just world belief, each in  isolation. This paper advances another argument: that these five mechanisms occur not  independently but in a predictable sequence, each reducing psychological resistance to the next,  producing loyalties more resistant than any single mechanism alone. We call this the  compounding loyalty model. Cognitive dissonance is the initial motivation causing a follower to  realise something is wrong; parasocial bonding makes rationalisation a requirement, not an  option; the halo effect provides a surface level base for maintaining trust despite misbehaviours;  social identity makes loyalty costly to lose; and just world belief provides a final, motivated  argument that deception did not happen at all. We draw this model from cases including James  Charles (2021) and Ramon Abbas, convicted of fraud in 2022. Media literacy, ethical marketing  and platform policy are discussed. 

Keywords: Influencers, social media, Cognitive dissonance, Para-social relationships, Halo  effect, social identity theory, just world hypothesis, Compounding loyalty model.

articles.title: Cooperation as Routing: A Network-Layer Formalization of How Help Propagates Through Social Networks
articles.authors: kazutaka hayashi
articles.abstract:
Most models of how things spread on social networks are broadcast models: a state
reaches whoever is reachable, and the analysis asks how far it spread. Cooperation often
does not spread this way. A request for help has no xed recipient; a person who receives
it either helps or, unable to help, passes it toward someone who can. Repeated, this for-
warding carries the request across the network hop by hop, much as a packet is routed
toward a host it has never met. Classical work on decentralized search established that
such address-free messages can reach a target through local decisions, and that chains die
mainly because intermediaries stop. We formalize the decision layer of this process: help-
requests are packets, participants are nodes, and each node facing a request acknowledges
it, forwards it, does both, or drops it. We dene an eective forward as one whose next
hop itself acts, and show that crediting only eective forwards, to the immediate previous
hop only, rewards every intermediary on a successful path without backward propagation,
rewards routing quality rather than volume, and gives no reward for acting in isolation. We
specify the provenance records needed to measure these quantities and illustrate, on the
log of an operating mutual-aid platform, how chains that reached four hops could not be
reconstructed because provenance was missing at the second hop. We discuss implications
for cooperative multi-agent systems and for instrumenting platforms that route help.

articles.title: Larger, younger, faster, harder: expansion, transformation, and inequality in YouTube’s creator economy (2019–2026)
articles.authors: Bernhard Rieder; Adrian Padilla; Ariadna Matamoros-Fernández; Òscar Coromina
articles.abstract: The growth of YouTube's creator economy raises a question that accounts of individual success and precarity cannot settle: how are the conditions of participation changing across the platform? Comparing two population-scale crawls from 2019 and 2026, we examine expansion, changes in production, and the distribution of attention across millions of channels. The population above the 1,000-subscriber threshold for advertising monetization grew from 4.4 million to 24.5 million, while its video catalogues grew ninefold. Expansion was strongest in South, Southeast, and East Asia, with India's share of channels declaring a country rising from 10 to 27 percent. This growth accompanied substantial turnover: most channels recorded in 2019 had no recent upload in 2026, and continued participation differed sharply by prior standing. Production also changed fundamentally. Median video duration fell from 247 to 60 seconds, with shortening across every content category and channel size. Among channels above 100,000 subscribers, new entrants accounted for most of the shift toward short form, while most continuing incumbents also shortened their output. Attention became more concentrated even among the same channels observed at both dates, and advertising revenue grew more slowly than the population meeting the subscriber threshold. These findings show how the output imperative extends from producing more to adapting what is produced, while sustained participation remains sharply unequal. They also place the increasingly Asian geography of the creator economy at the center of questions about platform labor, opportunity, and precarity.

articles.title: Perceived Manipulation, Fairness, and Trust in Competitive Mobile Gaming: A Cross-Cultural Analysis of Player Discourse
articles.authors: Hanieh Hatefi Yousefi
articles.abstract:
Perceptions of fairness play a central role in player experience within competitive mobile games, yet the processes through which players develop and sustain beliefs about manipulation remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates fairness-related discourse across two cultural and platform contexts through a five-year longitudinal qualitative analysis (2022–2026) of player-generated content from competitive mobile backgammon games.
The primary corpus consists of more than 52,000 Persian-language player reviews collected from Iranian app distribution platforms, supplemented by anonymised customer support transcripts. The comparative corpus comprises a stratified random sample of 750 negative reviews drawn from 4,116 reviews posted on an anglophone app-store listing over the same period. Using Inductive Thematic Analysis (ITA), the study identified seven recurring themes: dice manipulation, pay-to-win mechanics, bot opponents, connectivity sabotage, predetermined outcomes, statistical anomaly reporting, and support dismissal. These themes were subsequently organised into three higher-order meta-themes: Perceived Agency Erosion, Trust Erosion, and Statistical Misinterpretation.
The findings reveal both convergent and culturally distinct patterns. Beliefs that game outcomes are manipulated through unfair dice behaviour emerged as the dominant theme in both datasets, suggesting common cognitive mechanisms underlying fairness perceptions in stochastic competitive environments. At the same time, the two contexts differed in their developmental trajectories, complaint framing, and institutional response structures. Fairness-related complaints increased substantially across the Persian-language corpus over the study period, whereas comparable concerns remained relatively stable within the anglophone sample. Players in both contexts employed statistical reasoning to support manipulation claims, although the rhetorical and cultural framing of these arguments differed. Institutional responses to complaints also varied structurally, yet both contexts exhibited patterns that players frequently interpreted as dismissive or insufficiently responsive.
These findings contribute to research on player psychology, digital trust, and cross-cultural user experience by demonstrating how perceptions of unfairness emerge through the interaction of cognitive biases, community discourse, and platform communication practices. The study further highlights the importance of transparency design and context-sensitive trust-building mechanisms in competitive free-to-play games.

articles.title: Beyond the Joke: A Thematic Content Analysis of Russian-Linked Meme Pages Targeting Azerbaijan
articles.authors: Gudrat Guluyev
articles.abstract: As internet memes evolved from mere entertainment into a tool of digital propaganda, their role in modern warfare has become increasingly significant. This study examines their role in the case of Russian-linked information operations targeting the Azerbaijani audience on Facebook.  While the existing literature on meme-based Russian propaganda focuses heavily on the United States and Ukraine, the South Caucasus, one of the important regions of Russia’s “near abroad” policy, remains overlooked. The research addresses this critical gap by analyzing how these strategies are adapted to Azerbaijan's specific cultural and political context. The study relies on qualitative, multimodal analysis and emergent coding of 78 memes from nine Russian-linked Facebook pages targeting Azerbaijan between January 2023 and December 2024. The analysis identifies four consistent themes (the negative othering of the West, the discrediting of Western leaders, the reframing of the Nagorno-Karabakh Conflict, and the promotion of Azerbaijani sovereignty) and various propaganda techniques that have already been revealed in existing studies. The research paper concludes that these pages conduct a systematic influence campaign that sophisticatedly blends pro-Russian narratives with culturally conservative and patriotic domestic sentiments to resonate with the local audience.

articles.title: Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s (VIII): Five Ideological Tendencies within Han Nationalism and Their Real-World Demands
articles.authors: ZY Liu
articles.abstract: This article is an exploratory study in the series “Research on Han Nationalism in China in the 2020s.” It examines different ideological tendencies within Han nationalist discourse on the Chinese Internet. Unlike approaches that treat Han nationalism as a single political position, this article argues that contemporary Han nationalism on the Chinese Internet is not a unified movement with a common political program, but a collection of ideological tendencies formed around different real-world problems. Based on long-term observation of relevant online discourse, historical narratives, cultural phenomena, and public discussions, the article identifies five ideal types: establishment Han nationalism, renunciation-oriented Han nationalism, left-wing Han nationalism, cultural Han nationalism, and right-wing Han nationalism. These five tendencies primarily focus, respectively, on policy correction; central–local relations and fiscal responsibility; ethnic and class inequality; Han cultural identity; and population decline and the long-term demographic continuity of the Han. Although they share dissatisfaction with some differentiated ethnic policies and particular historical narratives, they differ substantially in their explanations of the causes of these problems and in their proposed solutions. Some of their demands also overlap with left-wing politics, liberalism, or regional autonomy. Han nationalism therefore cannot simply be equated with nationalism in the conventional right-wing sense. Its internal political demands in fact reflect real tensions in Chinese society concerning employment, working conditions, fiscal pressure, regional governance, population decline, marriage and fertility, and cultural identity. This article does not attempt to estimate the actual social size of these tendencies. Instead, it treats the five categories as analytical ideal types for understanding internal differences within Chinese Internet Han nationalism in the 2020s.

articles.title: Did local authorities lose revenue following banning unhealthy food advertising?
articles.authors: Mark Alan Green; Emma Boyland
articles.abstract: UK local authorities are increasingly exploring restrictions for the advertising of unhealthy foods on their estates to promote healthier food environments. Concerns about effects on revenue can be a barrier to progress. In this study, we provide preliminary evidence that these policies did not negatively affect total advertising revenue across four local authorities in North West England. In some cases, we found that revenue increased post-implementation.

articles.title: Academia as a Mirror of Society: Science in the Age of Capitalist Realism
articles.authors: Philipp Strasberg
articles.abstract: Prima facie, the scientific endeavor seems anti-capitalistic par excellence: a collective, non-profit driven effort of humanity to advance its knowledge in which everyone with enough education is free to participate. But a more detailed look reveals that science and its academic system perfectly mirror our late capitalist society: inequality, exclusivity, overproduction, hypercompetition, exploitation, control, self-optimization, burnout and depression are today’s symptoms, here and there. In addition, missing political agency is not only mirrored in academia---it is cultivated there. A common perspective on both, science and society, can offer the chance to change both for good.

articles.title: Conceptualizing Political Consumerism in the Attention Economy
articles.authors: Christopher Starke; Claes de Vreese; Natali Helberger
articles.abstract: Social media platforms increasingly become targets of politically and ethically motivated user protest, yet existing approaches do not sufficiently explain how deliberate platform use can operate as political participation. This conceptual paper extends the established concept of political consumerism to the attention economy, defining it as individuals’ market-oriented behaviors to punish or reward social media platforms on political or ethical grounds. It argues that three main factors constrain political consumerism on social media platforms: opaque value extraction, limited ethical alternatives, and high switching costs. Because political consumerism can take many forms, the paper suggests distinguishing user actions by their economic impact and whether they signal user preferences to the platform company. It further explains how social media literacy and regulation can improve the legibility and actionability of these practices. Finally, it outlines methodological implications for studying political consumerism through mixed-method designs that combine user motivations with behavioral data.

articles.title: Resilience in a Discordant Security Culture: Georgia between Institutional Continuity and Political Realignment
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili
articles.abstract: Challenging the common understanding in the relevant literature, this study reconceptualizes resilience to hybrid threats as a politically mediated process rather than purely a matter of institutional capacity-building. To examine how policy frameworks and political rhetoric interact to shape resilience, it traces Georgia’s security culture in the aftermath of the Russo-Georgian war. Through intertextual discourse analysis, the article cross-examines the institutional architecture of digital resilience, encompassing cybersecurity (systemic), media regulation (protective) and media literacy (empowerment) measures, with the government’s shifting rhetoric (2023–2025), while interview data provide contextual insights. The analysis reveals a discordant security culture manifested in fragmented governance and discursive struggle over resilience. Although formal policy frameworks normatively align with the West and consistently identify Russia as the principal security threat, governmental rhetoric portrays the same Western actors as sources of foreign interference and prioritizes political autonomy over cooperation while still invoking commitments to the constitutionally enshrined Euro-Atlantic trajectory. This dichotomy between institutional design and political discourse results in strategic ambiguity. It suggests that in hybrid regimes formal frameworks may function symbolically to signal external alignment, while practice is determined by short-term political calculations and discretionary authority, leaving institutions and societies vulnerable to evolving forms of foreign interference.

articles.title: From Desktop to Spatial Interfaces: UX Design Implications of Evolving Interaction Paradigms
articles.authors: Hiromu Tsuruta
articles.abstract:
This study examines how the transition from screen-based interaction paradigms to spatial
interfaces affects established user experience principles and design considerations. The
study is guided by the following research question: How does the transition from
screen-based interaction paradigms to spatial interfaces affect established UX principles and
design considerations? Apple Vision Pro and visionOS are examined as one case. The
corpus consists of 60 selected Human Interface Guidelines pages, 76 WWDC sessions, the
Apple Vision Pro User Guide, and notes from researcher observation. The HIG and WWDC
materials were analyzed qualitatively and coded using four dimensions: consistency,
feedback, affordance, and information architecture.
The analysis suggests that established UX principles remain relevant in spatial interfaces,
although the way they are implemented changes. This study describes that change through
three categories: retention, adaptation, and extension. Some familiar purposes and
structures remain in place, others are adapted through spatial interaction, and some design
concerns expand to include the user’s body and surrounding environment. Familiar
structures such as windows, controls, and navigation remain important, but visionOS adds
gaze, gesture, depth, distance, sound, anchoring, and immersion as additional design
mechanisms. From this pattern, the study proposes selective spatiality: spatial presentation,
immersion, and embodied interaction are most useful when they support the task, not simply
because they are available on the platform.
In the Vision Pro case, effective spatial UX comes from keeping familiar interaction
structures while adding spatial features only where they are useful. Designers must also
consider comfort, attention, accessibility, environmental awareness, and hardware limits.
Because the study examines one platform and does not include independent user testing, its
findings should be interpreted within that scope.

articles.title: From Public Dominance to Private Expansion: Changes in Hospital Infrastructure in Spain (1986–2018)
articles.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez; Margarita Vega-Rapún
articles.abstract: In many countries, the growth of the private hospital sector coincides with a decline in beds per inhabitant. Spain is no exception, showing one of the lowest relative bed provisions in the EU. This study offers an exploratory analysis of the evolution of private hospital bed provision in Spain and its Autonomous Communities between 1986 and 2018. Using historical hospital catalogs from the Ministry of Health, we conducted graphical and cluster analyses to examine trends and classify regions by the share of private hospital beds. Results indicate a national trend toward fewer beds and a growing presence of the private, mainly for-profit, sector, with notable regional differences such as the Catalan model. This research provides comparative and long-term evidence on structural changes in Spain’s hospital system.

articles.title: “AI” as gaslighting – Considering the affordances of stochastic generative systems in relation to anthropo-centered epistemic operations
articles.authors: Daniel Cardoso
articles.abstract:
This paper mobilizes the notion of ‘AI’ as a carcinogen, as developed by Berman, to then inquire and analyze what is the possible human impact that results from the democratization of the use of Large Language Models and Generative Pretrained Transformers, from the perspective of how epistemic frameworks are mobilized as a core component of sociability.
It then advances the proposal that we understand ‘AI’ as a case of the ‘Thomas Theorem’, and that, as such, LLMs and GPTs can effectively operate as systems of non-targeted, non-intentional, gaslighting.
